subtopic_detail: Placenta praevia vs abruption discrimination
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar. A 34-year-old G3P2 at 30+2 weeks presents with a sudden gush of bright red vaginal blood soaking through a pad. She reports no pain and the baby has been moving normally. Both previous births were uncomplicated vaginal deliveries.

She has had no antenatal care since the dating scan at 12 weeks after moving from interstate. She is Rhesus positive with no known medical problems and takes no regular medications.

On examination she is anxious but comfortable. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender with a longitudinal lie and cephalic presentation. Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 128/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7, fetal heart rate 145 with reactive CTG. Speculum examination has not yet been performed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 128/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.7, FHR 145 reactive
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen; longitudinal lie; cephalic; blood pooling on pad
data_table.Obstetric history: G3P2, two prior uncomplicated vaginal births; no antenatal care beyond 12 week dating scan
data_table.Investigations: Group and hold sent; FBC pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Immediate digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation and station
Transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound to localise the placenta before any vaginal examination
Bedside Kleihauer Betke test to quantify fetomaternal haemorrhage before any imaging
Speculum examination first to identify a local cervical or vaginal source of bleeding
MRI pelvis with placental accreta spectrum protocol before any bedside assessment is done

subtopic_detail: Placental abruption recognition and delivery timing
stem:
You are the on call registrar. A 29-year-old G2P1 at 34+5 weeks presents after a low speed motor vehicle collision one hour ago. She was the belted front seat passenger. She describes constant severe lower abdominal pain and reduced fetal movements since the crash.

Her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated. Anti D at 28 weeks was given because she is Rhesus negative. She takes no other medications.

On examination she is pale and clammy. Abdomen is rigid and exquisitely tender with a woody consistency to the uterus. There is a small amount of dark blood at the introitus. Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 88/52, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 97% room air, temp 36.4, fetal heart rate 90 with recurrent late decelerations on CTG. Bedside ultrasound shows a posterior fundal placenta with no praevia and no retroplacental clot visualised.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 88/52, RR 24, SpO2 97% room air, temp 36.4, FHR 90 with recurrent late decelerations
data_table.Examination: Pale clammy; woody rigid tender abdomen; small dark blood at introitus
data_table.Imaging: Bedside USS: posterior fundal placenta, no praevia, no retroplacental clot seen
data_table.Obstetric history: G2P1 at 34+5, Rhesus negative, anti D at 28 weeks given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Transfer by road to a tertiary centre 90 minutes away for management with specialist input
Admit for continuous CTG monitoring and betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular for 48 hours
Repeat formal ultrasound to look for retroplacental clot before deciding on operative delivery
Induce labour with vaginal prostaglandin E2 and augment with oxytocin for expected rapid delivery
Category 1 caesarean section with concurrent maternal resuscitation and massive transfusion activation

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia after SROM
stem: A 32-year-old primigravida at 37+3 weeks was admitted for expectant management of a bilobed placenta with a low lying accessory lobe seen at 32 weeks. Her membranes ruptured ten minutes ago with fresh red blood immediately after the clear liquor.

data_table.Cardiotocography: Reassuring five minutes ago, now a sudden baseline of 70 /min with a sinusoidal pattern
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, presenting part high

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate category 1 caesarean section with the neonatal team
Continuous cardiotocography for 30 minutes before deciding birth mode
Urgent Apt test on the vaginal blood for fetal haemoglobin
Instrumental birth with a Kiwi cup once the cervix is fully dilated
Amnioinfusion with warmed saline to relieve cord compression

subtopic_detail: Tocolysis choice with contraindication
stem:
You are the birthing suite registrar. A 27-year-old G1 at 29+4 weeks presents with regular painful uterine contractions every 4 minutes for the past two hours. Speculum reveals no liquor and no bleeding.

Her pregnancy has been complicated by chronic hypertension controlled on labetalol 200 mg twice daily. There is no history of asthma, cardiac disease, or diabetes. She takes only labetalol and a pregnancy multivitamin.

On examination her abdomen is soft between contractions and non-tender. The cervix is 3 cm dilated and 80% effaced. Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 148/92, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.9, fetal heart rate 145 reactive. Fetal fibronectin is not available. Betamethasone has already been given and magnesium sulfate infusion for neuroprotection has been commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 148/92, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.9, FHR 145 reactive
data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm dilated, 80% effaced; soft non-tender abdomen between contractions
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg BD; pregnancy multivitamin; betamethasone given; magnesium sulfate infusion running
data_table.Obstetric history: G1 at 29+4; no membrane rupture; no bleeding; no diabetes or asthma

lead_in: Which agent is most appropriate for tocolysis?

options.text: Nifedipine 20 mg orally as a loading dose then 20 mg orally every 6 to 8 hours
Salbutamol intravenous infusion titrated to a maternal pulse under 120 beats per minute
Atosiban intravenous 6.75 mg bolus then infusion at 300 mcg per minute for 3 hours
Indometacin 100 mg rectally then 50 mg orally every 6 hours for up to 48 hours
Additional intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g bolus followed by 2 g per hour for tocolysis

subtopic_detail: Magnesium neuroprotection window
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar. A 31-year-old G2P1 at 28+6 weeks with confirmed preterm prelabour rupture of membranes 6 hours ago now has regular contractions every 3 minutes.

Her previous birth was a term vaginal delivery. Antenatal group B streptococcus screen is unknown. She takes no medications and has no allergies.

On examination her abdomen contracts palpably every 3 minutes and is non-tender between. Speculum confirms pooling of clear liquor at the cervix. Cervix is 4 cm dilated. Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 122/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.9, fetal heart rate 150 reactive. Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular was given 3 hours ago. Intrapartum benzylpenicillin has been commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 122/76, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.9, FHR 150 reactive
data_table.Examination: Contractions every 3 min; cervix 4 cm dilated; pooling clear liquor
data_table.Medications: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM 3 h ago; intrapartum benzylpenicillin commenced
data_table.Obstetric history: G2P1 at 28+6; prior term vaginal birth; GBS status unknown

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading dose then 1 g per hour for neuroprotection
Second dose of betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular immediately to complete the loading regimen early
Add clindamycin intravenous to cover intrapartum GBS pending laboratory swab result
Commence nifedipine 20 mg orally as tocolysis to delay birth by a further 48 hours if possible
Perform emergency category 2 caesarean section on the basis of possible intrauterine infection now

subtopic_detail: GBS prophylaxis penicillin anaphylaxis
stem:
You are the labour ward registrar. A 34-year-old G3P2 at 36+2 weeks presents in early labour with contractions every 5 minutes. Her antenatal vaginal rectal swab at 35 weeks grew group B streptococcus.

She has a documented severe reaction to penicillin during a previous UTI treatment: throat swelling, wheeze, and required adrenaline. Antibiotic susceptibility testing on the GBS isolate shows resistance to clindamycin.

On examination her abdomen is soft between contractions and non-tender. Cervix is 3 cm dilated and 60% effaced. Membranes are intact. Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.7, fetal heart rate 140 reactive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.7, FHR 140 reactive
data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm dilated 60% effaced; membranes intact; soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: 35 week GBS swab positive; isolate clindamycin resistant
data_table.Allergies: Penicillin: throat swelling, wheeze, required adrenaline

lead_in: Which intrapartum antibiotic is most appropriate?

options.text: Benzylpenicillin 3 g intravenous loading then 1.8 g every 4 hours until birth
Cefazolin 2 g intravenous loading then 1 g every 8 hours until birth
Clindamycin 900 mg intravenous every 8 hours until birth for penicillin allergic women
Vancomycin 20 mg per kg intravenous every 8 hours (maximum 2 g per dose) until birth
Erythromycin 500 mg intravenous every 6 hours until birth as an alternative macrolide

subtopic_detail: ADIPS OGTT thresholds
stem:
You are the antenatal GP registrar. A 30-year-old G2P1 at 26 weeks attends for review of her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test performed after an overnight fast.

She has a BMI of 24 with no family history of diabetes. Her previous pregnancy was uncomplicated with a birth weight of 3.4 kg at term. She takes only pregnancy multivitamins.

Examination is unremarkable. Symphysis fundal height is appropriate for gestation and blood pressure is 118/72. The pathology report shows fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L, one hour glucose 10.4 mmol/L, and two hour glucose 8.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72; other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: SFH appropriate for 26 weeks; fetal movements normal
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT: fasting 4.9 mmol/L, 1 h 10.4 mmol/L, 2 h 8.2 mmol/L
data_table.Obstetric history: G2P1, prior term vaginal birth, birth weight 3.4 kg

lead_in: How should this result be interpreted?

options.text: Normal result with all three values below the ADIPS diagnostic thresholds for pregnancy
Gestational diabetes based on a one hour value at or above the diagnostic threshold
Impaired glucose tolerance requiring a repeat test in four weeks to confirm the diagnosis
Overt diabetes in pregnancy given the elevated one hour and two hour glucose measurements
Result inconclusive because at least two values must be above threshold for a diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Escalation from metformin to insulin
stem: A 33-year-old G2P1 at 32 weeks with gestational diabetes started metformin four weeks ago after failed dietary control and has titrated to 1 g twice daily. There is no infection or steroid use.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 36 cm
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound at 30 weeks: abdominal circumference 92nd centile, estimated fetal weight 88th centile
data_table.Blood glucose diary: Fasting mean 5.8 mmol/L, two hour post prandial mean 8.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to management?

options.text: Add bedtime isophane insulin with short-acting insulin at meals
Increase metformin to 1 g morning and 1.5 g at night
Add glibenclamide 2.5 mg orally each morning to the metformin
Refer to the dietitian and review again in one week
Bring induction of labour forward to 37 weeks to reduce stillbirth

subtopic_detail: Timing of delivery in insulin treated GDM
stem:
You are the antenatal clinic registrar. A 36-year-old G3P2 with gestational diabetes on insulin presents at 38+3 weeks. Her diabetes has been well controlled since insulin started at 30 weeks with fasting values averaging 4.6 mmol/L and post prandial values averaging 6.3 mmol/L.

Both previous births were normal vaginal deliveries at 39 and 40 weeks with birth weights of 3.7 and 3.9 kg. She has no other medical problems.

Examination is unremarkable. Symphysis fundal height at today's visit is 39 cm. Growth scan two weeks ago showed abdominal circumference on the 65th centile and estimated fetal weight on the 60th centile with normal amniotic fluid volume and umbilical artery Doppler. Blood pressure is 118/72.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72; other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: SFH 39 cm at 38+3 weeks
data_table.Investigations: USS at 36+3: AC 65th centile, EFW 60th centile, AFI normal, UA Doppler normal
data_table.Blood glucose diary: Fasting mean 4.6 mmol/L; 2 h post prandial mean 6.3 mmol/L; on insulin since 30 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate timing of birth?

options.text: Await spontaneous labour up to 40+6 weeks with weekly antenatal review and growth surveillance
Continue expectant management until 41+0 weeks then discuss induction of labour options
Recommend elective caesarean section this week for macrosomia prevention and safer maternal outcome
Offer induction of labour immediately given the SFH of 39 cm suggests fetal macrosomia now
Offer induction of labour between 39+0 and 39+6 weeks with balloon or prostaglandin cervical priming

subtopic_detail: First line pharmacological choice with fertility desire
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 32-year-old woman presents with heavy periods for the past 8 months. She soaks a super pad hourly on her heaviest two days and passes 50 cent piece sized clots.

Her cycle is regular at 28 days lasting 8 days. She is trying to conceive with her partner and has been trying for 3 months. She is otherwise well with no medications or allergies.

Examination is normal including bimanual pelvic examination with a mobile normal sized uterus and no adnexal masses. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal endometrium at 6 mm and no fibroids or polyps. Full blood count reveals haemoglobin 105 g/L (115 to 165), MCV 74 fL (80 to 100), and ferritin 8 microgram/L (15 to 200). Thyroid function and coagulation screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Bimanual normal; mobile normal sized uterus; no adnexal mass
data_table.Imaging: Pelvic USS: endometrium 6 mm; no fibroid or polyp
data_table.Investigations: Hb 105 g/L (115-165); MCV 74 fL (80-100); ferritin 8 mcg/L (15-200); TFTs and coags normal
data_table.Fertility: Actively trying to conceive for 3 months

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine system inserted at the next menstrual period
Combined oral contraceptive pill with 30 mcg ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel continuously
Tranexamic acid 1 g orally three times daily during menstruation for the duration of bleeding days
Norethisterone 5 mg orally three times daily from day 5 to day 26 of each menstrual cycle
Referral for endometrial ablation because pharmacological therapy is unlikely to be adequate long term

subtopic_detail: Structural cause workup with intermenstrual bleeding
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar. A 44-year-old parous woman is referred by her GP with heavy menstrual bleeding for 12 months and new intermenstrual bleeding for 3 months. Cervical screening is up to date and negative.

Her cycle is regular at 28 days and cycles typically last 9 days. She has completed her family and uses condoms for contraception. She has no bleeding diathesis and no medications.

Bimanual examination is normal. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal uterus with endometrial thickness of 14 mm and a discrete 12 mm hyperechoic focus at the fundus with a feeder vessel on colour Doppler. Full blood count reveals haemoglobin 108 g/L (115 to 165) with normal indices.

data_table.Examination: Bimanual normal; uterus normal size and mobile
data_table.Imaging: TVUS: endometrium 14 mm; 12 mm hyperechoic fundal focus with feeder vessel on colour Doppler
data_table.Investigations: Hb 108 g/L (115-165); MCV within normal limits; cervical screen up to date and negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in six weeks to see if the lesion resolves spontaneously
Blind endometrial Pipelle biopsy in the clinic as the primary tissue sampling strategy
Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy and polypectomy of the focal lesion under general anaesthesia
Pelvic MRI with contrast to characterise the focal lesion before deciding further investigation
Commence tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menstruation and reassess in three months

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding TVS threshold
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 62-year-old woman presents with a single episode of light pink vaginal bleeding two days ago. Her last menstrual period was at age 52 and she has had no bleeding since.

She is otherwise well with a BMI of 34, well controlled type 2 diabetes on metformin, and hypertension on perindopril. She has never used hormone therapy. Cervical screening is up to date and negative.

Examination reveals no vulval or vaginal lesion on speculum. Bimanual examination is normal with a small mobile uterus and no adnexal masses. Urgent transvaginal ultrasound performed the same week reports a homogenous endometrial thickness of 6 mm with no focal lesion and no free fluid.

data_table.Examination: No vulvovaginal lesion on speculum; bimanual normal; small mobile uterus
data_table.Imaging: TVUS: endometrium 6 mm homogenous; no focal lesion; no free fluid
data_table.Past history: BMI 34; T2DM on metformin; hypertension on perindopril; never used HRT

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure and review only if further bleeding episodes occur in the next six months
Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in six weeks to see if the endometrial thickness reduces below 4 mm
Commence topical vaginal oestrogen and review response over the next three months
Endometrial Pipelle biopsy in the outpatient setting with hysteroscopy if inadequate or negative
Refer directly to gynaecological oncology for total abdominal hysterectomy after preoperative workup

subtopic_detail: Persistent PMB despite thin endometrium
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar. A 68-year-old woman presents to your clinic with her third episode of postmenopausal bleeding in eight weeks. Her first two episodes were investigated by her GP with transvaginal ultrasound each time showing an endometrial thickness of 3 mm and Pipelle sampling that returned scant benign endometrial tissue.

She has a BMI of 41, type 2 diabetes on metformin, and previously took tamoxifen for five years following breast cancer at age 55. Cervical screening is up to date.

Examination reveals atrophic vulvovaginal changes with no discrete lesion. Bimanual examination is normal. Repeat transvaginal ultrasound today shows an endometrial thickness of 3 mm with a poorly seen endometrial midline echo and a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Haemoglobin is 118 g/L (115 to 165).

data_table.Examination: Atrophic vulvovaginal changes; no discrete lesion; bimanual normal
data_table.Imaging: TVUS today: ET 3 mm with poorly seen midline echo; small free fluid in pouch of Douglas
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L (115-165); prior 2 Pipelle samples: scant benign endometrium
data_table.Past history: BMI 41; T2DM on metformin; prior tamoxifen 5 years for breast cancer age 55

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that thin endometrium excludes malignancy and review in three months if symptoms persist
Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy under general anaesthesia to obtain a definitive histological sample
Third Pipelle biopsy in the clinic with concurrent saline infusion sonohysterography for guidance
Commence topical vaginal oestrogen for presumed atrophic vaginitis and review response over six weeks
MRI pelvis with contrast to stage a presumed malignancy prior to any further tissue sampling

subtopic_detail: Methotrexate eligibility criteria
stem: A 28-year-old G2P0 attends the early pregnancy service 7 weeks after her last menstrual period. She has 3 days of mild right iliac fossa discomfort and light brown spotting. She lives locally with reliable transport and phone contact.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, mild right iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism, cervix closed
data_table.Imaging: Empty uterus, 2.4 cm right adnexal mass, no fetal cardiac activity, no free fluid
data_table.Investigations: Serum bhCG 2100 IU/L, plateaued over 48 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy as definitive surgical management
Suction dilatation and curettage to confirm the diagnosis histologically
Expectant management with weekly serum bhCG until below 15 IU/L
Laparoscopic salpingostomy to preserve tubal function for fertility
Single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre

subtopic_detail: Prior contralateral salpingectomy flip
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar. A 32-year-old G3P0 attends theatre for laparoscopic management of a right tubal ectopic. She had a left salpingectomy 4 years ago for a ruptured left tubal ectopic. Her current pregnancy was spontaneously conceived after 18 months of trying and she strongly wishes to preserve fertility.

At today's laparoscopy the right tube contains a 3.8 cm unruptured ectopic in the ampullary region with an intact serosa and no active bleeding. The left side confirms absent left tube. The uterus and ovaries appear normal. Preoperative bhCG was 7200 IU/L.

data_table.Operative findings: Right ampullary unruptured 3.8 cm ectopic; intact serosa; no bleeding; left tube absent; normal uterus and ovaries
data_table.Investigations: Preoperative serum bhCG 7200 IU/L
data_table.Reproductive history: 18 months to conceive spontaneously; strongly wishes fertility preservation; prior left salpingectomy 4 years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical management?

options.text: Right salpingectomy because the tube is the only remaining tube and future ectopic risk is high
Right salpingostomy with removal of the products and preservation of the tube for future fertility
Abandon surgery and give single dose intramuscular methotrexate given fertility preservation intent
Milk the ectopic out of the fimbrial end of the tube to avoid opening the tube or removing it
Ipsilateral cornual resection with removal of the uterine horn to prevent recurrent ipsilateral ectopic

subtopic_detail: Expectant management thresholds
stem:
You are the early pregnancy assessment service registrar. A 26-year-old G1P0 presents at an estimated 5+3 weeks gestation with 24 hours of very light brown vaginal spotting. She has no pain and has been afebrile.

She is haemodynamically well. She lives 15 minutes from the hospital and has reliable phone contact and transport. She has no significant medical history and takes only a pregnancy multivitamin.

Abdomen is soft and non-tender. Speculum shows a closed cervix with a small amount of dark blood. Vital signs are within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a small 1.2 cm left adnexal mass with no yolk sac or fetal pole, and no free fluid. Serum bhCG on presentation is 480 IU/L and a repeat 48 hours later is 320 IU/L.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen; cervix closed; small dark blood on speculum
data_table.Imaging: TVUS: empty uterus; 1.2 cm left adnexal mass; no yolk sac or fetal pole; no free fluid
data_table.Investigations: Serum bhCG day 0 480 IU/L; day 2 320 IU/L (falling)
data_table.Social: Lives 15 min from hospital; reliable transport and phone contact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with serial serum beta hCG measurement every 48 to 72 hours until under 15
Single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre body surface area
Diagnostic laparoscopy today with proceed to salpingectomy or salpingostomy as indicated
Admit for 48 hour inpatient observation with intravenous cannula and serial abdominal examinations
Suction dilatation and curettage to confirm absence of intrauterine pregnancy before further decisions

subtopic_detail: Postnatal follow-up and long-term cardiovascular risk after pre-eclampsia
stem: A 33-year-old woman is being discharged on day four after a birth at 36 weeks complicated by pre-eclampsia. Her blood pressure is controlled on oral labetalol and she is breastfeeding.

data_table.Investigations: Platelets 214 x10^9/L, creatinine 72 micromol/L, ALT 28 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow-up plan?

options.text: Blood pressure review this week and cardiovascular risk review yearly
Blood pressure review this week and no further follow-up required
Repeat blood pressure only if she develops headache or visual symptoms
Routine six-week postnatal visit with no interim blood pressure check
Referral to a renal physician for annual glomerular filtration testing

subtopic_detail: Uterotonic choice with contraindication
stem: A 34-year-old G4P3 has 1200 mL of continuing blood loss after a vaginal birth. She had pre-eclampsia treated with labetalol, has aspirin-sensitive asthma, and a documented severe reaction to ergometrine at a previous birth.

data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy, placenta complete, first degree tear only
data_table.Given: Oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly and an infusion of 40 units running

lead_in: Which additional uterotonic is most appropriate?

options.text: Ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscularly, repeated every 2 to 4 hours
Carboprost 250 microgram intramuscularly, to a maximum of 2 mg
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously over 10 minutes as the next agent
Misoprostol 800 microgram rectally as a single additional dose
A second oxytocin infusion of 40 units in 1 L over 4 hours

subtopic_detail: Late preterm steroids and asymptomatic bacteriuria
stem:
You are the antenatal ward registrar. A 26-year-old G1 at 32+4 weeks with confirmed preterm labour has been admitted. Cervical examination shows 2 cm dilatation and 60% effacement. Membranes are intact.

Her antenatal course has been unremarkable and she has no medical conditions. She takes only pregnancy multivitamins.

Abdomen is soft between contractions and non-tender. Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.9, fetal heart rate 145 reactive. Midstream urine sent yesterday for asymptomatic screening has returned pure growth of Escherichia coli at 10^8 colony forming units per litre with sensitivity to cefalexin, nitrofurantoin, and trimethoprim.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.9, FHR 145 reactive
data_table.Examination: Cervix 2 cm dilated 60% effaced; membranes intact; soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: MSU: pure E coli 10^8 CFU/L; sensitive to cefalexin, nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim

lead_in: Which combination of interventions is most appropriate?

options.text: Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular repeated at 24 hours, no antibiotic given culture reflects colonisation
No corticosteroids since gestation is beyond 32 weeks and cefalexin 500 mg orally 6 hourly for 5 days
Dexamethasone 6 mg intramuscular repeated 4 times plus nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6 hourly for 7 days
Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular repeated at 24 hours plus trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 7 days
Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular repeated at 24 hours plus cefalexin 500 mg orally 6 hourly for 5 days

subtopic_detail: Perimenopausal HMB with fibroids and IUS choice
stem:
You are the gynaecology clinic registrar. A 47-year-old woman presents with 18 months of increasingly heavy predictable periods. She has completed her family and does not wish to conceive again.

Her BMI is 28 with no other medical conditions. She has no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and cervical screening is up to date.

Bimanual examination reveals a bulky irregular uterus corresponding to 12 weeks gestation size. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates an anteverted uterus with multiple intramural fibroids the largest measuring 4 cm, no submucosal component distorting the endometrial cavity, and an endometrium of 8 mm. Uterine cavity length is 10 cm. Full blood count reveals haemoglobin 102 g/L (115 to 165), MCV 76 fL (80 to 100), and ferritin 6 microgram/L (15 to 200). Cervical screening and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Bulky irregular uterus 12 week size on bimanual
data_table.Imaging: TVUS: anteverted uterus; multiple intramural fibroids largest 4 cm; no submucosal component distorting cavity; endometrium 8 mm; cavity length 10 cm
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L (115-165); MCV 76 fL (80-100); ferritin 6 mcg/L (15-200); cervical screen negative; TFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine system after outpatient endometrial biopsy to exclude hyperplasia
Uterine artery embolisation as a fertility sparing option that avoids surgical morbidity of hysterectomy
Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy as definitive management for perimenopausal HMB
Endometrial ablation using bipolar radiofrequency as a definitive uterine preserving procedure now
Ulipristal acetate 5 mg orally daily for 3 months as a selective progesterone receptor modulator now

subtopic_detail: NCSP HPV primary screening pathway
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman who is up to date with her routine cervical screening. Her last cervical screening test five years ago was HPV not detected. She has had regular menstrual cycles, no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, and is in a stable long term relationship.

Her routine cervical screening test today returns HPV oncogenic types other than 16 or 18 detected. A reflex liquid based cytology on the same sample shows low grade squamous intraepithelial lesion.

She is otherwise well, has never been immunised against HPV, and has no immunosuppression. Vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Prior screening: HPV not detected five years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer for colposcopy within eight weeks for direct visualisation and directed biopsy
Return to routine five yearly HPV cervical screening as the reflex cytology is low grade
Prescribe topical imiquimod cream and repeat cytology alone in six months to assess clearance
Arrange an HPV self collection swab in three months to confirm today's clinician collected result
Repeat the HPV cervical screening test in 12 months to reassess persistence of the current infection

subtopic_detail: Post treatment surveillance after LLETZ
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 38-year-old woman six months after a large loop excision of the transformation zone for a histologically confirmed high grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL, CIN 3). Excision margins were reported as clear of dysplasia and endocervical curettage was negative.

She has recovered well with no bleeding or unusual discharge. She has never smoked, is HIV negative, and is not on any immunosuppressive medication.

Her six month test of cure co test today returns HPV not detected and cytology negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. She asks when she should return for the next screen.

data_table.Procedure: LLETZ six months ago for CIN 3; margins clear; endocervical curettage negative
data_table.Test of cure today: HPV not detected; cytology NILM (co test)
data_table.Risk factors: Never smoker; HIV negative; not immunosuppressed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow up?

options.text: Return to routine five yearly HPV cervical screening as she has cleared her treated lesion today
Annual co test of HPV and cytology for the next 24 months and then return to routine screening
Refer for repeat colposcopy in six months regardless of the negative test of cure result today
Arrange repeat cytology alone at 12 months without HPV testing given the treatment was successful
Offer completion hysterectomy after two children to remove any residual cervical cancer risk

subtopic_detail: Missed COCP rules
stem:
You are the GP consulting a 22-year-old woman who takes a combined monophasic 30 mcg ethinylestradiol pill. She is in week two of her current pack. She forgot to take her pill on Wednesday and Thursday and realised this morning (Friday) when she opened the pack.

She has had unprotected sex on Tuesday evening. She has no other missed pills in this pack or the previous pack. She takes no other regular medications and has no contraindications to hormonal contraception.

She is otherwise well. Vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Missed pills: Two consecutive pills in week two of current pack

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Take the most recent missed pill and offer levonorgestrel emergency contraception because unprotected sex occurred
Discard the current pack, start a new pack today, and use condoms for the next seven days for safety
Take the two missed pills together now, skip the next pill free week, and start the next pack straight after
Take the most recent missed pill now, continue the pack, and use condoms for the next seven days
Insert a copper intrauterine device within five days as emergency contraception given unprotected intercourse

subtopic_detail: Emergency contraception selection
stem:
You are the after hours GP registrar consulting a 27-year-old woman. She had a single episode of unprotected vaginal intercourse 72 hours ago and is worried about pregnancy. Her last menstrual period started 12 days ago and her cycles are regular at 28 days.

Her body mass index is 32 kg/m2. She takes no hormonal contraception and has never had an intrauterine device. She has no known drug allergies and no medical history of note. She specifically declines any device based contraception today for personal reasons and asks for a tablet option.

She is otherwise well and her vital signs are within normal limits. A urine pregnancy test today is negative.

data_table.Cycle position: Day 12 of a regular 28 day cycle

lead_in: What is the most appropriate emergency contraception?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg oral single dose taken as a one tablet regimen this evening
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg oral single dose taken as a one tablet regimen this evening
Levonorgestrel 3 mg oral single dose given her body mass index above 26 this evening
Copper intrauterine device inserted within the next 48 hours by a trained clinician
Mifepristone 200 mg oral single dose taken as a one tablet regimen this evening

subtopic_detail: Long acting reversible contraception counselling
stem:
You are the GP consulting a 24-year-old woman who wants the most effective long-acting reversible contraceptive available in Australia and who plans to try for pregnancy in about two years. She has heavy but regular menstrual periods that soak through a pad every hour on the first two days and cause her to miss work.

Her body mass index is 24 kg/m2, she has never been pregnant, and her blood pressure is within normal limits. She has no history of venous thromboembolism, migraine, or breast cancer. She takes no regular medications.

Her haemoglobin is 105 g/L (115-165) and ferritin is 8 mcg/L (20-200), consistent with iron deficiency anaemia.

data_table.Menstrual pattern: Regular; soaks pad hourly on day one and two
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 105 g/L (115-165); ferritin 8 mcg/L (20-200)
data_table.Reproductive plan: Wants pregnancy in about two years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line long-acting reversible contraceptive?

options.text: Etonogestrel subdermal implant lasting three years and inserted in the upper arm today
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular injection every 12 weeks
52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device lasting up to eight years in Australia
Copper intrauterine device lasting up to ten years and inserted within the next cycle
Combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously to skip withdrawal bleeds each month

subtopic_detail: HRT route selection with VTE risk
stem:
You are the GP consulting a 52-year-old woman with disabling vasomotor symptoms and moderate mood change since her periods stopped 14 months ago. Non hormonal strategies have failed and she wants to try menopausal hormone therapy.

Her body mass index is 33 kg/m2. She has a strong family history of venous thromboembolism, with her mother and sister both diagnosed with an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis in their forties. She has never had a clot herself and thrombophilia screening was declined by her haematologist as it would not change clinical management. She has an intact uterus.

Her blood pressure is 128/78, she has never smoked, and her mammogram three months ago was reported as normal.

data_table.Symptoms: Severe vasomotor symptoms and mood change; 14 months amenorrhoea
data_table.Risk factors: BMI 33 kg/m2; strong family history unprovoked VTE
data_table.Screening: Normal mammogram three months ago; BP 128/78; never smoked

lead_in: Which combined hormone therapy regimen best balances symptom relief against her risk profile?

options.text: Oral conjugated equine oestrogens with medroxyprogesterone acetate in a continuous regimen
Oral oestradiol valerate with norethisterone taken continuously without a break
Transdermal oestradiol patch alone without any progestogen because she is amenorrhoeic
Transdermal oestradiol patch with oral micronised progesterone taken at bedtime each evening
Tibolone 2.5 mg orally daily as a single tablet regimen with no separate progestogen

subtopic_detail: HRT absolute contraindications
stem:
You are the GP consulting a 54-year-old woman about menopausal hormone therapy for hot flushes affecting her sleep. She is 18 months into amenorrhoea and non hormonal measures have not helped enough.

She was diagnosed with oestrogen receptor positive invasive ductal breast carcinoma three years ago. She completed lumpectomy, adjuvant radiotherapy, and is on year three of five of adjuvant tamoxifen. She has no history of VTE, cardiovascular disease, or liver disease.

Her blood pressure is 122/76 and mammograms have been clear post treatment. She asks specifically whether menopausal hormone therapy would be safe for her.

data_table.Oncology history: ER positive invasive ductal breast carcinoma three years ago; on adjuvant tamoxifen
data_table.Symptoms: Vasomotor symptoms disrupting sleep; 18 months amenorrhoea
data_table.Cardiovascular: BP 122/76; no VTE or cardiovascular disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response regarding menopausal hormone therapy?

options.text: Offer transdermal oestradiol only, as the transdermal route avoids the breast cancer risk of oral oestrogen
Offer tibolone 2.5 mg orally daily as it avoids the standard oestrogen exposure in menopausal hormone therapy
Offer combined transdermal oestrogen and micronised progesterone as the safest recognised regimen
Decline systemic menopausal hormone therapy and offer non hormonal pharmacological options
Continue tamoxifen alone as it will treat both her cancer and her vasomotor symptoms adequately

subtopic_detail: Admission criteria and first line antiemetic
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 26-year-old primigravid woman at 9 weeks by dating scan. She reports vomiting more than eight times per day for the past week and cannot keep down even sips of water since yesterday morning. She has lost 4.5 kg from her booking weight of 62 kg.

On examination her lips and mucous membranes are dry and skin turgor is reduced. Her pregnancy is a singleton and she has no history of thyroid disease or previous hyperemesis. She takes no regular medications.

Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6. Urine dipstick shows ketones 3+ and specific gravity 1.030. Serum sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), and thyroid function tests are pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 96/58, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes; reduced skin turgor; 4.5 kg weight loss
data_table.Investigations: Urine ketones 3+; sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge home on oral doxylamine and pyridoxine with a review in 48 hours for symptom reassessment
Prescribe oral ondansetron and arrange outpatient IV fluids in the day therapy unit tomorrow
Arrange urgent ultrasound to exclude molar pregnancy before initiating any parenteral therapy today
Commence prednisolone 40 mg orally daily as a corticosteroid rescue with tapering over two weeks
Admit for intravenous rehydration, potassium replacement, thiamine, and regular antiemetics

subtopic_detail: Ondansetron timing and teratogenicity counselling
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 30-year-old G2P1 at 8+3 weeks with persistent vomiting despite regular doxylamine plus pyridoxine and metoclopramide. She lost 5 kg from her booking weight and has ongoing ketonuria after two litres of intravenous crystalloid.

Her PUQE score is 14. She is otherwise well with no thyroid dysfunction, no molar features on ultrasound, and a singleton intrauterine pregnancy. She takes no other regular medications and has no drug allergies.

She asks specifically whether ondansetron is safe in her current situation. Vital signs are within normal limits after resuscitation.

data_table.Response: Ongoing vomiting despite doxylamine-pyridoxine plus metoclopramide
data_table.Gestation: 8+3 weeks by dating scan; singleton intrauterine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding ondansetron?

options.text: Withhold ondansetron until after 10 weeks and continue current first line therapy in the interim
Offer ondansetron after discussing the small orofacial cleft signal in first trimester exposure
Advise ondansetron is absolutely contraindicated in the first trimester due to cardiac malformation risk
Advise ondansetron is completely safe and there is no signal at all for any first trimester teratogenicity
Switch to droperidol as first choice given the known QTc prolongation risk with ondansetron in early pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Corticosteroid and magnesium neuroprotection window
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 28-year-old G1 at 29+4 weeks with a sudden gush of clear fluid one hour ago followed by ongoing leakage. Speculum examination shows pooling of clear liquor in the posterior fornix and a closed cervix. There are no contractions.

Booking bloods including group and screen and GBS status from 26 weeks were unremarkable, with GBS not detected on rectovaginal swab. She has no fever, abdominal tenderness, or offensive discharge.

Vital signs: pulse 84, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7, fetal heart rate 145 with reactive CTG. Fetal ultrasound shows appropriate growth and no anomalies. She has received no corticosteroids in this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.7, FHR 145 reactive
data_table.Speculum: Clear liquor pool in posterior fornix; cervix closed
data_table.Investigations: GBS not detected at 26 weeks; no infection markers

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management set?

options.text: Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly, magnesium sulfate loading and maintenance infusion, and immediate induction of labour
Oral amoxicillin plus clavulanate, corticosteroids, and expectant management on the antenatal ward
Discharge home with twice weekly outpatient CTG and weekly ultrasound surveillance after 24 hours observation
Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly, oral erythromycin 250 mg six hourly, and admit for expectant management
Tocolysis with nifedipine for 48 hours plus corticosteroids to buy time for lung maturity to develop fully

subtopic_detail: Term PROM and GBS prophylaxis
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 32-year-old G2P1 at 39+2 weeks presenting six hours after a large gush of clear fluid at home. She has had two mild irregular tightenings since arrival but is otherwise not contracting.

Her previous baby was born vaginally at term without complications. She had a positive rectovaginal group B streptococcus screen at 36 weeks in this pregnancy. Her group and hold is on file and she is Rhesus positive.

On speculum a clear liquor pool is seen; the cervix looks 1 cm dilated. Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6, fetal heart rate 140 reactive. There is no offensive discharge or abdominal tenderness.

data_table.Speculum: Clear liquor pool; cervix 1 cm dilated
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.6, FHR 140 reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Offer expectant management for up to 96 hours before considering induction of labour
Start oral amoxicillin, admit for 24 hours of observation, and reassess for induction tomorrow morning
Perform an immediate emergency caesarean because rupture of membranes with GBS is an operative indication
Withhold antibiotics until active labour is established and reassess GBS risk at that time
Commence intrapartum intravenous benzylpenicillin and induce labour with oxytocin infusion now

subtopic_detail: Planning birth in the pregnancy after a shoulder dystocia
stem: A 31-year-old woman attends at 20 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first birth was complicated by an impacted anterior shoulder and she asks how this one will be planned.

data_table.First birth: Birth weight 4.3 kg, arm weakness that resolved by four months
data_table.This pregnancy: Singleton, no diabetes on screening so far, body mass index 27 kg/m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about mode of birth?

options.text: Discuss the recurrence risk and support either a vaginal birth or caesarean
Recommend a planned caesarean section, since recurrence is close to certain
Recommend induction at 38 weeks, which removes the risk of recurrence
Recommend a vaginal birth, since this does not happen twice to one woman
Defer the discussion until a growth scan at 36 weeks gives an estimate

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia after failed McRoberts
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar managing a shoulder dystocia in a 34-year-old G3P2. Two minutes have elapsed since head delivery. McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure have been applied by two experienced midwives for 60 seconds without release of the anterior shoulder.

An episiotomy is now in place. The consultant is en route from home. The mother has an epidural providing effective perineal anaesthesia and paediatrics have been called to attend. Her previous two babies were 3800 g and 4100 g and delivered vaginally without difficulty.

Maternal vital signs remain stable. The fetus was estimated at 4300 g at 39 weeks with no known congenital anomalies. The team is preparing for the next step.

data_table.Manoeuvres so far: McRoberts plus suprapubic pressure for 60 seconds
data_table.Team: Two midwives, obstetric registrar, paediatrics called; consultant en route

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Perform internal rotational manoeuvre (Rubin II or Wood's screw) via the vagina
Perform symphysiotomy at the bedside using a scalpel with local anaesthetic infiltration
Attempt Zavanelli cephalic replacement and transfer to theatre for caesarean delivery
Apply firm downward and lateral traction on the fetal head with McRoberts positioning
Apply strong fundal pressure while the midwife maintains suprapubic pressure over the abdomen

subtopic_detail: TTTS recognition and referral
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29-year-old G1 with a known monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 20 weeks. She is asymptomatic but has come for a routine fortnightly surveillance scan.

Ultrasound today reports twin A with amniotic fluid deepest vertical pocket of 1.6 cm and a small stuck bladder, and twin B with deepest vertical pocket of 8.5 cm and a large bladder. Estimated fetal weights are on the 35th centile for twin A and the 60th centile for twin B. Umbilical artery Doppler indices are within normal limits for both twins.

Fetal cardiac views for both twins appear structurally normal. There is no cervical shortening. Maternal vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Twin A: DVP 1.6 cm; small stuck bladder; EFW 35th centile
data_table.Twin B: DVP 8.5 cm; large bladder; EFW 60th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue fortnightly ultrasound surveillance and reassess in two weeks
Deliver by emergency caesarean now because of established twin-twin transfusion syndrome
Urgent referral to a fetal medicine unit for consideration of fetoscopic laser ablation
Perform amnioreduction only, without fetoscopy, and continue expectant management thereafter
Commence indometacin to reduce fetal urine output and improve the amniotic fluid disparity

subtopic_detail: Timing and mode of delivery
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar counselling a 32-year-old G1 with an uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 36 weeks. Growth on serial scans has been concordant with both twins on the 50th centile and normal Doppler indices.

Twin A is cephalic; twin B is cephalic. Cervical length has been stable and there is no history of preterm labour, hypertension, or diabetes. She has been well throughout and asks about the timing and mode of delivery.

Her vital signs are within normal limits and her booking BMI is 26 kg/m2. She has no contraindications to vaginal birth.

data_table.Presentation: Twin A cephalic; twin B cephalic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.text: Plan delivery at 37+0 to 37+6 weeks with vaginal birth as the mode of delivery
Plan delivery at 38+0 to 38+6 weeks with vaginal birth as the mode of delivery
Plan delivery at 36+0 to 36+6 weeks by elective caesarean section for maternal safety reasons
Plan delivery at 34+0 to 34+6 weeks by elective caesarean section with antenatal corticosteroid cover
Continue expectant management to 40 weeks with weekly CTG and biophysical profile monitoring

subtopic_detail: Ovulation confirmation
stem:
You are the GP consulting a 30-year-old woman who has been trying to conceive with her male partner for 15 months without success. She has regular 28 day menstrual cycles with a five day flow and mid cycle mucous change she can identify.

She has never been pregnant. She has no history of pelvic infection, prior abdominal surgery, or endometriosis. Her BMI is 23 kg/m2 and thyroid function is normal.

Her partner is 32 years old and has had one previous biological child in a former relationship. Baseline pelvic ultrasound today is normal and her rubella and varicella serology confirm immunity. She asks what she should do next to work out whether she is ovulating.

data_table.Cycle: Regular 28 day cycles; five day flow; mid cycle mucous change
data_table.Duration: 15 months of unprotected intercourse without conception

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm ovulation?

options.text: Basal body temperature charting for three consecutive menstrual cycles at home
Serum anti Mullerian hormone measured on any day of the cycle to assess ovulation
Serial transvaginal ultrasound follicle tracking from day 10 to detect follicular collapse
Urinary luteinising hormone testing kits used daily from cycle day 8 to detect the LH surge
Serum progesterone measured seven days before the expected next menstrual period

subtopic_detail: Tubal patency assessment
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 33-year-old woman investigated for 14 months of unexplained subfertility. Mid luteal progesterone was 42 nmol/L on two cycles. Baseline pelvic ultrasound today shows a normal uterus, no adnexal masses, and antral follicle counts of 8 and 9.

She has no history of pelvic infection, endometriosis, or ectopic pregnancy. She is not iodine allergic. Her partner's semen analysis showed 22 million/mL concentration with 45 percent progressive motility and 5 percent normal morphology by WHO 2021 criteria.

She asks whether she needs to have a hysterosalpingogram or whether a less invasive test would work. Her body mass index is 24 kg/m2 and she is not currently taking any contraception.

data_table.Prior investigations: Mid luteal progesterone 42 nmol/L on two cycles; normal pelvic USS
data_table.History: No pelvic infection, endometriosis, or ectopic pregnancy
data_table.Partner semen analysis (WHO 2021): 22 million/mL; 45 percent progressive motility; 5 percent normal morphology

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Hysterosalpingogram with fluoroscopic imaging using iodinated contrast in radiology
Hysterosalpingo contrast sonography (HyCoSy) with saline and air microbubbles
Diagnostic laparoscopy with methylene blue chromopertubation performed under general anaesthesia
Serum chlamydia antibody titre alone as a non-invasive proxy marker of tubal disease risk
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis with dynamic contrast to visualise the fallopian tubes

subtopic_detail: Quick start with recent progestogen exposure
stem:
You are the GP consulting a 25-year-old woman who took ulipristal acetate 30 mg 20 hours ago after a burst condom. Her last menstrual period started 15 days ago and cycles are regular at 30 days. Her body mass index is 24 kg/m2 and she has no contraindications to hormonal contraception.

She wants to start ongoing hormonal contraception today at this appointment, and specifically asks whether she can begin the combined oral contraceptive pill straight away or whether she needs to wait. She has never used hormonal contraception before and has no personal or family history of VTE, migraine with aura, or breast cancer.

She is otherwise well. Vital signs are within normal limits.

data_table.Cycle position: Day 15 of a regular 30 day cycle

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about starting hormonal contraception?

options.text: Start the combined oral contraceptive pill immediately today and use barrier cover for the next seven days
Start the combined oral contraceptive pill at the beginning of her next menstrual period with no cover needed
Delay starting the combined oral contraceptive pill for five days, then quick start with seven days barrier cover
Take a second dose of ulipristal in five days to cover her cycle until the next menstrual period begins
Insert an etonogestrel subdermal implant today and provide no barrier cover as the implant works within 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Refractory hyperemesis with hyponatraemia and confusion
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 24-year-old G1 at 11 weeks admitted three days ago for hyperemesis. She has been vomiting persistently despite regular doxylamine-pyridoxine, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, and ondansetron. She has now had five litres of intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride with added potassium over the last 48 hours.

Overnight her partner reports she has become confused and unsteady on her feet. On examination she has horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze and ataxia when asked to walk. There is no papilloedema, no focal weakness, and her Glasgow Coma Scale is 14.

Repeat sodium is now 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), and magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.0). Blood glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. Urine osmolality is high relative to serum osmolality. Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 108/64, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8.

data_table.Neurology: Horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze; ataxia; confusion; GCS 14
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.0); glucose 5.8 mmol/L
data_table.Fluid history: Five litres 0.9 percent NaCl with potassium over 48 hours
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 108/64, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temp 36.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous thiamine 500 mg three times daily and cautiously correct sodium under electrolyte specialist advice
Give 100 mL of 3 percent hypertonic saline over 10 minutes to rapidly correct the sodium level
Start intravenous glucose 10 percent as a bolus and infusion to correct hypoglycaemia before any thiamine
Arrange urgent CT brain to exclude intracranial pathology before commencing any specific treatment
Commence intravenous methylprednisolone as a corticosteroid rescue for refractory hyperemesis

subtopic_detail: Premature ovarian insufficiency HRT dose
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman referred with six months of amenorrhoea, hot flushes, and vaginal dryness. She has no family history of early menopause and no personal history of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or pelvic surgery.

Investigations show follicle stimulating hormone 42 IU/L (postmenopausal above 30) on two samples six weeks apart, oestradiol under 100 pmol/L, and thyroid function normal. Karyotype and fragile X premutation screen have been sent by the referring GP.

She has not yet completed her family. Her BMI is 23 kg/m2, blood pressure is 118/74, and she has no history of VTE, migraine, or breast cancer. Bone mineral density scan is pending.

data_table.History: Six months amenorrhoea; vasomotor symptoms; vaginal dryness
data_table.Investigations: FSH 42 IU/L twice six weeks apart; oestradiol under 100 pmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial hormone therapy?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill with continuous or cyclical use until the average natural menopause age
Standard postmenopausal transdermal oestradiol 25 mcg patch with micronised progesterone
No hormone replacement; symptoms will resolve spontaneously as the body adjusts to the new hormonal state
Tibolone 2.5 mg orally daily as a synthetic single tablet regimen without additional progestogen
Referral for donor oocyte in vitro fertilisation without any hormonal replacement in the interim

subtopic_detail: First-line investigation of a swollen calf in pregnancy
stem:
A 28-year-old woman at 26 weeks in her second pregnancy comes to the day assessment unit with two days of left calf pain that is worse when she walks to the letterbox. She has had no chest tightness, breathlessness or cough.

On examination the left calf measures 3 cm greater in circumference than the right at 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity, and there is tenderness along the medial calf with mild pitting over the ankle. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius; fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Plasma D-dimer, proceeding to leg imaging only if the reported level is raised
Contrast venography of the left leg performed with abdominal shielding in place
Compression duplex ultrasound of the left leg veins performed the same day
Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram of the chest using a reduced-dose protocol
Magnetic resonance venography of the pelvic veins and both femoral segments

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a low D-dimer in suspected pregnancy deep vein thrombosis
stem:
A 34-year-old woman at 31 weeks presents to the emergency department with three days of right thigh and calf aching and a feeling that the leg is tight. She is a school teacher and spent last week largely off her feet after a minor ankle sprain on the other side.

The right leg is diffusely swollen to the groin with tenderness along the medial thigh; the ankle sprain on the left has settled. A D-dimer was collected at triage before you saw her and has returned at 0.42 mg/L fibrinogen equivalent units (reference less than 0.50). She has no bleeding history and takes no anticoagulant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 94/min, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius; fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 116 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy); platelets 224 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 52 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Start therapeutic-dose enoxaparin now and arrange leg compression ultrasound the same day
Reassure her that clot is excluded and review in a week if swelling persists
Repeat the D-dimer in 48 hours and arrange leg imaging only if raised
Arrange a ventilation perfusion lung scan before any decision about anticoagulation is made
Commence prophylactic-dose enoxaparin and review her in the antenatal clinic in seven days

subtopic_detail: Empirical anticoagulation while imaging is arranged for suspected pulmonary embolism
stem:
A 29-year-old woman at 33 weeks in her first pregnancy is brought in with sudden right-sided chest pain that catches when she breathes in, and breathlessness climbing a single flight of stairs. She has a body mass index of 33 and returned ten days ago from a flight home from Perth.

Her chest is clear on auscultation and her calves are soft and equal. An electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia only, and her chest radiograph is reported as normal. At her 28 week visit her oxygen saturation was recorded as 99 per cent on room air. She has had no fever and no cough.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116/min, BP 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius; fetal heart rate 152/min
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 112 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy); platelets 198 x10^9/L (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Withhold anticoagulation until definitive chest imaging has confirmed or excluded a clot
Give prophylactic-dose enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily and arrange chest imaging tomorrow
Give aspirin 300 mg orally now and arrange chest imaging within the next 24 hours
Give therapeutic-dose enoxaparin now and arrange definitive chest imaging the same day
Start an unfractionated heparin infusion titrated to the activated partial thromboplastin time ratio

subtopic_detail: Choosing chest imaging for suspected pulmonary embolism when the chest radiograph is normal
stem:
A 26-year-old woman at 30 weeks is being assessed for two days of pleuritic left chest pain and exertional breathlessness. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer, and has already been started on therapeutic-dose enoxaparin.

Bilateral leg compression ultrasound showed no deep vein thrombosis. Her chest radiograph is reported as normal, with clear lung fields and a normal cardiac outline. She asks you what the next test will involve.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, BP 114/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius; fetal heart rate 146/min
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, calves soft and equal, no jugular venous distension
data_table.Investigations: Bilateral leg compression ultrasound negative; chest radiograph normal; creatinine 48 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: Which imaging investigation would you arrange next?

options.text: Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram with breast shielding and a reduced contrast volume
Ventilation perfusion lung scan of the chest, beginning with the perfusion phase
Repeat bilateral leg compression ultrasound in three days with interval clinical review
Transthoracic echocardiography to look for right ventricular strain before any further imaging
Plasma D-dimer to decide whether further chest imaging is justified at this gestation

subtopic_detail: Thromboprophylaxis during an antenatal admission with dehydration and immobility
stem:
A 23-year-old woman at 10 weeks in her first pregnancy has been admitted for the second time this month because she cannot keep fluids down. She has lost 5 kg since booking and has spent most of the past four days in bed on intravenous fluids and antiemetics.

Her booking weight was 72 kg and her body mass index at booking was 26. She has no personal or family history of clot and takes no other medicines. The nausea is improving on the current regimen and the team expects her to stay a further two days.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, calves soft and equal, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Urinary ketones 3+; sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90); platelets 268 x10^9/L (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to her inpatient management?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily for the admission, then review at her next visit
Therapeutic-dose enoxaparin for the admission, then step down to a prophylactic dose on discharge
No pharmacological prophylaxis, as clot risk is not appreciably raised in the first trimester
Graduated compression stockings alone for the admission, with early mobilisation encouraged each day
Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin daily plus graduated compression stockings while she is an inpatient

subtopic_detail: Prophylaxis plan after a previous surgery-provoked venous thromboembolism
stem:
A 31-year-old woman attends her booking visit at 9 weeks in her first pregnancy. Four years ago she had a calf deep vein thrombosis six days after a knee reconstruction, treated with three months of anticoagulation and no recurrence since.

Her body mass index is 24, she is a non-smoker and works as a physiotherapist on her feet all day. Thrombophilia testing was never done and no first-degree relative has had a clot. She asks what she needs during this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Both calves soft and equal, no varicosities, healed knee surgical scar
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What thromboprophylaxis plan would you recommend?

options.text: Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin from today until six weeks after the birth of the baby
Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin from 28 weeks until the onset of labour, with nothing afterwards
No antenatal heparin, with prophylactic-dose enoxaparin for six weeks after the birth
No heparin at any stage, with graduated compression stockings worn throughout the pregnancy
Therapeutic-dose enoxaparin from today until six weeks after the birth of the baby

subtopic_detail: Timing of antenatal prophylaxis after an oestrogen-related previous clot
stem:
A 27-year-old woman comes to the early pregnancy clinic at 7 weeks having stopped her combined oral contraceptive four months ago. At the age of 22 she had an extensive femoral vein clot that began three months after starting that same contraceptive, and she completed six months of anticoagulation.

She is otherwise well with a body mass index of 23 and works as a graphic designer. No first-degree relative has had a clot, and thrombophilia testing after her event was negative. She is anxious about needle injections and asks whether anything can wait until later in pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, BP 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mild residual left thigh varicosities, both calves equal in circumference
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 246 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 56 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for pharmacological thromboprophylaxis?

options.text: Start prophylactic-dose enoxaparin now and continue until six weeks after the birth
Start prophylactic-dose enoxaparin at 28 weeks and continue until six weeks after the birth
Start prophylactic-dose enoxaparin at the onset of labour and continue for six weeks afterwards
Give low-dose aspirin now and add prophylactic-dose enoxaparin after the birth of the baby
Repeat the thrombophilia screen now and start prophylactic-dose enoxaparin only if it is positive

subtopic_detail: Thromboprophylaxis when the postnatal platelet count is low
stem:
A 33-year-old woman is day 1 after an emergency caesarean at 34 weeks for severe pre-eclampsia. Her booking weight was 84 kg. She is receiving magnesium sulfate, is catheterised and has not yet been out of bed.

Her blood pressure is now controlled on oral labetalol and her liver enzymes are falling. The morning bloods show a platelet count of 58 x10^9/L, down from 96 x10^9/L before the birth, with no oozing from the wound or drip sites. The team asks you to write up her venous thromboembolism prevention.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, BP 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdominal wound dry, uterus firm, calves soft and equal, no petechiae
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 58 x10^9/L (150-400); haemoglobin 94 g/L (115-165); alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (5-30); creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90); international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.8-1.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate venous thromboembolism prevention plan today?

options.text: Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin daily plus graduated compression stockings, starting this morning on the ward
Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin at half the usual dose daily, with platelets rechecked tomorrow
Transfuse one adult platelet unit, then commence prophylactic-dose enoxaparin later the same day
Intermittent pneumatic compression alone, with the platelet count reassessed each day
No prophylaxis while she remains on magnesium sulfate and strict fluid restriction

subtopic_detail: Thromboprophylaxis for lower limb immobilisation in the third trimester
stem:
A 30-year-old woman at 30 weeks in her second pregnancy attends the antenatal clinic two days after slipping at home. The orthopaedic team has applied a below-knee cast for an undisplaced fibular fracture and has asked her to remain non-weight-bearing on crutches for six weeks.

Her booking weight was 68 kg, she has no previous clot and no first-degree relative with clot. The pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated with normal growth on ultrasound last week. She has been sleeping downstairs on the couch since the injury because she cannot manage the stairs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius; fetal heart rate 144/min
data_table.Examination: Right below-knee cast in situ with warm toes and normal capillary refill, left calf soft
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400); haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her thrombotic risk?

options.text: Graduated compression stocking on the uncasted leg with advice to elevate both legs daily
Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin daily for as long as the cast and crutches are needed
Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin daily commencing at 36 weeks and continuing until the birth
Serial compression ultrasound of the uncasted leg every two weeks until cast removal
Aspirin 100 mg orally daily until she is weight-bearing again, then review in clinic

subtopic_detail: Fluctuant perineal swelling with fever after a repaired second-degree tear
stem:
A 24-year-old woman returns to the maternity assessment unit on day 5 after a normal vaginal birth with a repaired second-degree tear. She says the stitches have gone from sore to burning, she cannot sit down, and she noticed a bad smell on her pad this morning.

On examination the perineum is swollen and red over a 4 cm area lateral to the repair, with a tense fluctuant area at the centre and some of the suture line gaping. Her breasts are soft and her lochia is not offensive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, BP 110/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 92 mg/L (less than 5); haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and warm salt baths, with clinic review in 48 hours
Warm salt baths, simple analgesia and daily midwifery wound review until the swelling settles
Immediate secondary repair of the dehisced wound edges under regional anaesthesia in theatre
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis and perineum before deciding on any intervention
Incision and drainage in theatre with wound swabs taken and intravenous antibiotics

subtopic_detail: Spreading redness around a caesarean wound without a collection
stem:
A 29-year-old woman is seen on day 6 after an elective caesarean because the skin around her scar has become red and sore over the past day. She is eating normally, feeding her baby and walking to the shops.

The uterus is well contracted and non-tender and her lochia is light. Careful palpation of the wound finds it warm and tender but with no fluctuance and no discharge. She has needed nothing stronger than paracetamol for the pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Erythema extending 4 cm above the incision, warm and tender to touch
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 46 mg/L (less than 5); bedside wound ultrasound shows no collection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily, marking the erythema border for review
Intravenous cefazolin 2 g eight-hourly with admission for close observation of the wound margin
Open the lower third of the wound on the ward, with oral antibiotics afterwards
Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily with simple analgesia and review in the clinic next week
Simple analgesia and wound observation alone, with advice to return if she develops any fever

subtopic_detail: Breast infection with systemic features and haemodynamic change
stem:
A 32-year-old woman presents at 3 weeks postnatal with a painful right breast that began yesterday. Overnight she had two episodes of shaking that woke her partner, and this morning she felt faint standing up to feed.

The upper outer quadrant of the right breast is red, firm and very tender over an 8 cm wedge with no discrete lump and no fluctuance. She has vomited twice and has not been able to keep fluids down since waking. Her baby is feeding well from the left breast and has no thrush.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124/min, BP 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 164 mg/L (less than 5); lactate 3.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0); creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral dicloxacillin 500 mg four times daily with feeding continued and review tomorrow
Cold packs, effective milk removal and ibuprofen, with antibiotics only if unimproved
Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin with fluid resuscitation and continued milk removal
Urgent breast ultrasound with needle aspiration of the affected quadrant before antibiotics
Stop feeding from the right breast and give oral cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly

subtopic_detail: Duration of treatment after a pulmonary embolism diagnosed in pregnancy
stem:
A 35-year-old woman had a segmental pulmonary embolism confirmed at 29 weeks and has been on therapeutic-dose enoxaparin since. She is now 36 weeks, her symptoms have resolved and the pregnancy is otherwise uncomplicated.

She has no previous clot, her thrombophilia status is unknown and she plans to breastfeed. At today's visit she asks how long she will need to keep taking injections after the baby is born, and whether she can change to tablets.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, BP 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius; fetal heart rate 140/min
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, calves soft and equal, symphysis fundal height appropriate for dates
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 208 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 60 micromol/L (45-90); haemoglobin 114 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about the duration and choice of her anticoagulation?

options.text: Stop anticoagulation once she has given birth, as the provoking factor will have resolved
Continue treatment dose until birth, then reduce to a prophylactic dose for ten days only
Change to rivaroxaban now so that she is established on tablets before she begins feeding
Continue treatment dose until birth, then change to aspirin 100 mg daily for three months
Continue treatment dose for at least six weeks postnatally and three months in total

subtopic_detail: Large breast collection with overlying skin compromise
stem:
A 30-year-old woman is reviewed at 5 weeks postnatal, having completed seven days of oral flucloxacillin for a right breast infection. The pain settled briefly and then returned, and she now describes the breast as feeling tight and heavy.

Examination shows a 5 cm firm tender mass in the lower outer quadrant with a shiny, thinned and dusky 2 cm patch of overlying skin that blanches poorly. Ultrasound reports a 52 mm multiloculated collection with thick internal debris extending to within 2 mm of the skin surface. She remains afebrile and is feeding from the left breast.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 58 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the collection?

options.text: Repeat ultrasound-guided needle aspiration every 48 hours with a further week of oral antibiotics
Surgical incision and drainage with division of loculi and tissue sent for culture
Change to oral trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole for a further ten days and review in clinic
Stop breastfeeding entirely and use cabergoline to suppress lactation before any further treatment
Urgent triple assessment with core biopsy and mammography before any drainage is undertaken

subtopic_detail: Maternal fever in labour with prolonged rupture of membranes
stem:
A 27-year-old woman at 39 weeks is in labour on the birth suite. Her membranes ruptured 22 hours ago and she has had six vaginal examinations since admission. She is 6 cm dilated with regular contractions and an epidural in situ.

Over the past hour her temperature has risen from 37.1 to 38.5 degrees Celsius and her pulse has climbed to 118 per minute.
