The cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 172 beats per minute with reduced variability and no decelerations. Her uterus is tender between contractions and the liquor draining onto the pad has an offensive smell.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.5 degrees Celsius; fetal heart rate baseline 172/min
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 21.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 118 mg/L (less than 5); lactate 1.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous paracetamol and cooling measures, with reassessment of the cardiotocograph in one hour
Intravenous benzylpenicillin alone as group B streptococcal prophylaxis, continuing expectant care
Immediate caesarean section under general anaesthesia irrespective of her progress in labour
Blood cultures then broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, with a plan to expedite birth
Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and continued hourly observations until the second stage begins

subtopic_detail: Chest imaging choice when the radiograph is abnormal and breast dose matters
stem:
A 34-year-old woman at 32 weeks has had four days of right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness on minimal exertion, with a dry cough. Bilateral leg compression ultrasound was negative this morning and she has been started on therapeutic-dose enoxaparin.

Her mother and her older sister were both diagnosed with breast cancer in their forties, and she has read that chest scans deliver radiation to the breast. Her chest radiograph shows a wedge-shaped opacity in the right lower zone with a small pleural effusion. She has remained afebrile with a normal white cell count and a C-reactive protein of 6 mg/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, BP 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius; fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Reduced air entry at the right base, calves soft and equal, no jugular venous distension
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5); creatinine 54 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: Which imaging investigation would you arrange next?

options.text: Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram, counselling her about the dose to breast tissue
Ventilation perfusion lung scan, since it delivers a much lower dose to breast tissue
Repeat bilateral leg compression ultrasound in three days, continuing the current treatment
Empirical antibiotics with a repeat chest radiograph in 48 hours to assess for resolution
Magnetic resonance pulmonary angiography, avoiding ionising radiation to the breast and fetus

subtopic_detail: Neuraxial block timing after a prophylactic dose of low molecular weight heparin
stem:
A 31-year-old woman at 39 weeks is on the morning list for an elective caesarean for breech presentation. She has been taking prophylactic-dose enoxaparin since the first trimester after a previous clot, and her last injection was at 10 pm last night.

It is now 6 am and she is first on the list. Her platelet count is 214 x10^9/L, her creatinine is 58 micromol/L and she takes no other anticoagulant or antiplatelet medicine. The anaesthetic registrar asks for your view before the woman is brought around.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius; fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Examination: Breech presentation confirmed, uterus soft, no contractions, back examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 214 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90); international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.8-1.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for her anaesthesia?

options.text: Proceed with a spinal block now, since eight hours is adequate after a prophylactic dose
Proceed now under general anaesthesia so that the operating list is not delayed today
Delay the block until at least 12 hours have passed since her last prophylactic dose
Give intravenous protamine sulfate to reverse the heparin and perform the spinal in one hour
Measure an anti-Xa concentration now and perform the spinal if the level is below 0.2 IU/mL

subtopic_detail: Managing treatment-dose heparin around a planned birth
stem:
A 33-year-old woman at 37 weeks has been on treatment-dose enoxaparin twice daily since a femoral vein clot was diagnosed at 24 weeks. An induction of labour has been booked for 39 weeks and she is well, with no bleeding and a normally grown baby.

She asks whether she will be able to have an epidural, saying that she managed poorly without one in her first labour. Her last dose today was at 8 am and she has been shown how to self-inject. The plan for her birth is being written in the antenatal clinic today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius; fetal heart rate 146/min
data_table.Examination: Cephalic presentation, symphysis fundal height 37 cm, calves soft and equal
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 236 x10^9/L (150-400); haemoglobin 116 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy); creatinine 55 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What plan for her anticoagulation around the birth would you document today?

options.text: Continue both daily doses up to admission, accepting that epidural analgesia may be unavailable
Omit the treatment dose for 24 hours before the planned induction, then reassess on admission
Omit the treatment dose for 12 hours before the planned induction, then reassess on admission
Change to warfarin at 38 weeks so that her anticoagulation can be reversed at the birth
Stop anticoagulation entirely from 38 weeks and restart at a prophylactic dose after the birth

subtopic_detail: Heavy bleeding with fever twelve days after birth and echogenic material on scan
stem:
A 26-year-old woman presents on day 12 after a normal vaginal birth with bleeding that has become heavier than her first days at home, soaking one pad every two hours since yesterday. She has felt shivery and her lower abdomen aches.

On examination the uterus is 14 weeks size, soft and tender, and the cervical os admits a fingertip with dark blood and an offensive odour. Pelvic ultrasound shows heterogeneous echogenic material measuring 24 mm within the cavity with vascularity on colour Doppler. She is not bleeding heavily enough in the department to soak a pad while you assess her.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106/min, BP 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.3 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-165); white cell count 17.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 108 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate surgical evacuation of the uterus in theatre, with antibiotics started afterwards
Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and outpatient review with a repeat scan in one week
Intramuscular ergometrine with tranexamic acid and discharge once the bleeding has settled
Uterine artery embolisation arranged urgently, with antibiotics given once the bleeding stops
Admit for intravenous antibiotics, with evacuation only if she fails to settle

subtopic_detail: Negative compression ultrasound with persisting clinical suspicion
stem:
A 32-year-old woman at 27 weeks was started on therapeutic-dose enoxaparin yesterday for three days of left thigh pain and swelling. Compression ultrasound of the femoral and popliteal segments has been reported as showing fully compressible veins with normal flow.

Today the left leg remains 4 cm larger in mid-thigh circumference than the right and she cannot fully bear weight on it. There is no calf erythema, no skin break and she is afebrile. The medical registrar asks whether the enoxaparin can now be stopped.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius; fetal heart rate 144/min
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5); creatinine 51 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the enoxaparin, as a negative compression ultrasound excludes deep vein thrombosis
Stop the enoxaparin and send a D-dimer, restarting treatment only if the level is raised
Stop the enoxaparin and arrange a computed tomography venogram of the pelvis this week
Continue the enoxaparin and repeat the compression ultrasound within the next three days
Continue the enoxaparin and treat empirically for six months without any further leg imaging

subtopic_detail: Collapse with rash two days after repair of a high vaginal tear
stem:
A 25-year-old woman is reviewed on the postnatal ward two days after a vacuum birth complicated by a high vaginal tear that was repaired in theatre. She has vomited three times this morning, had two loose motions, and feels dizzy when she sits up.

She is flushed with a diffuse red blanching rash over her trunk and limbs and her conjunctivae are injected. Her abdomen is soft with a well contracted non-tender uterus, and her breasts and caesarean-free abdomen are unremarkable. The theatre record notes that a vaginal pack was inserted at the end of the repair, and there is no entry in the notes recording its removal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, BP 84/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 21.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 186 mg/L (less than 5); lactate 4.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0); creatinine 148 micromol/L (45-90); platelets 88 x10^9/L (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics, with the vaginal examination deferred
Vaginal examination and pack removal, with fluid resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics
Intravenous hydrocortisone and antihistamine, with observation for progression of the rash
Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis before any vaginal examination is done
Intravenous fluconazole with antibiotic cover, pending blood and high vaginal swab results

subtopic_detail: Persisting fever on adequate antibiotics after caesarean with a vascular filling defect
stem:
A 29-year-old woman is day 7 after an emergency caesarean and has been on intravenous ampicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole for 72 hours for a uterine infection. Her abdominal pain has improved and her lochia is no longer offensive, but she continues to spike to 38.8 degrees Celsius twice daily.

Her wound is clean and dry, her chest is clear, her calves are soft and equal and her urine culture is negative. Blood cultures taken before antibiotics grew nothing. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast reports no collection and no retained products, but describes an enlarged right ovarian vein containing a low-attenuation filling defect extending toward the inferior vena cava.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5); blood and urine cultures negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to her management?

options.text: Add therapeutic anticoagulation to the current course of intravenous antibiotic therapy
Change to intravenous meropenem and add vancomycin to cover resistant hospital organisms
Proceed to laparotomy for washout and possible hysterectomy given the failure to defervesce
Add intravenous fluconazole for possible candidaemia after a week of broad-spectrum therapy
Cease antibiotics and repeat the computed tomography in 48 hours to reassess

subtopic_detail: Thromboprophylaxis the day after a transfused major postpartum haemorrhage
stem:
A 37-year-old woman is day 1 after an emergency caesarean at full dilatation. She lost 1900 mL, received three units of red cells and one gram of tranexamic acid, and had a balloon tamponade device removed at 12 hours with no further loss.

Her booking weight was 78 kg and her body mass index at booking was 29. Graduated compression stockings have been in place since theatre. Since the balloon came out her uterus has stayed firm, her pad loss has been minimal and her abdominal drain has drained 30 mL over eight hours. She has not yet been out of bed and is asking when she can start walking.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 94/min, BP 112/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 82 g/L (115-165); platelets 142 x10^9/L (150-400); fibrinogen 2.9 g/L (2.0-4.5); international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.8-1.2); creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate venous thromboembolism prevention plan?

options.text: Withhold heparin until her haemoglobin rises above 100 g/L, using stockings meanwhile
Withhold heparin for seven days after major haemorrhage, using mechanical measures alone
Start prophylactic-dose enoxaparin today and continue the mechanical measures as well
Start treatment-dose enoxaparin now, given the number of thrombotic risk factors accrued
Give aspirin 100 mg daily until she is mobile, then convert to enoxaparin

subtopic_detail: Selecting the enoxaparin dose band after caesarean when weight has changed
stem:
A 34-year-old woman is on the ward the morning after an emergency caesarean at 39 weeks for failure to progress. She is well, her wound is dry, her uterus is firm and her pad loss is light, and you are asked to prescribe her thromboprophylaxis before the ward round moves on.

Her first antenatal visit at 11 weeks recorded a weight of 88 kg. She gained weight steadily through the pregnancy and her weight on the ward scales this morning, after 3 litres of intraoperative and postoperative fluid, is 104 kg with pitting oedema to mid-shin. She is on no other anticoagulant and has had no bleeding since theatre.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86/min, BP 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 218 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90); haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: Which prophylactic enoxaparin regimen would you prescribe?

options.text: Enoxaparin 20 mg subcutaneously daily, reflecting her low bleeding risk after an uncomplicated operation
Enoxaparin 60 mg subcutaneously daily, calculated from the weight recorded on the ward scales today
Enoxaparin 80 mg subcutaneously daily, calculated from her weight plus total pregnancy weight gain
Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously twice daily, reflecting her caesarean birth and her body mass index
Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily, calculated from the weight recorded at her booking visit

subtopic_detail: Perineal pain out of proportion with a normal temperature two days after birth
stem:
A 28-year-old woman is called to your attention on day 2 after a forceps birth with a repaired third-degree tear. She has needed escalating oxycodone overnight and is now asking for more, saying the pain is nothing like the soreness she remembers from her first birth. She is drowsy and slow to answer questions.

The perineum looks moderately swollen with a dusky area of discolouration extending toward the right labium majus and a small amount of thin grey discharge from the repair. Tenderness extends well beyond the visible discolouration onto the right inner thigh, and a patch of skin over the labium is numb to light touch. Her temperature is 36.1 degrees Celsius and she has had no rigors.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, BP 86/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 24.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 268 mg/L (less than 5); lactate 4.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0); creatinine 156 micromol/L (45-90); sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous antibiotics with fluid resuscitation and reassessment of the perineum in six hours
Bedside incision and drainage of the perineal wound with swabs and oral antibiotics
Magnetic resonance imaging of the perineum before referral for a surgical opinion
Immediate theatre for exploration and debridement, with urgent resuscitation and antibiotics
Intravenous flucloxacillin with a wound swab and stronger analgesia, reviewed on rounds

subtopic_detail: Primary amenorrhoea with hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism and short stature requiring karyotype
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 16-year-old girl who has never had a period. Her mother is 168 cm tall and had menarche at 12 years.

She is doing well at school, exercises twice a week, eats a varied diet and her weight has been stable. She has no headaches and no visual symptoms, and reports a normal sense of smell.

data_table.Examination: Height 148 cm which is below the 1st centile, body mass index 22 kg/m2, Tanner stage 1 breast development, Tanner stage 3 pubic hair, normal external genitalia, no clitoromegaly, blood pressure equal in both arms
data_table.Investigations: FSH 68 IU/L (follicular 3 to 9), LH 24 IU/L (follicular 2 to 10), oestradiol 42 pmol/L (follicular 110 to 400), prolactin 310 mIU/L (less than 500), TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), beta hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with contrast
Pelvic ultrasound to assess uterine and ovarian morphology
Karyotype analysis performed on a peripheral blood sample
Repeat the gonadotrophins and oestradiol in three months
Measure serum anti Mullerian hormone and antral follicle count

subtopic_detail: Discrete mobile breast lump in a woman under 35 requiring ultrasound led triple assessment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 24-year-old woman who found a lump in her right breast in the shower 6 weeks ago. It has not changed in size since, and she does not think it varies with her cycle.

She has no nipple discharge, no skin change and no breast pain. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill, has never been pregnant, and no one in her family has had breast or ovarian cancer.

data_table.Examination: Discrete 22 mm smooth firm mobile lump in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, no skin dimpling, tethering or peau d'orange, nipple normal with no discharge on expression, no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, left breast normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her and review the lump after her next menstrual period
Arrange bilateral mammography and review her with the report
Refer her directly for surgical excision of the lump with histology
Arrange breast ultrasound with core biopsy if imaging is not benign
Stop the oral contraceptive pill and reassess the lump in 3 months

subtopic_detail: Overactive bladder without stress incontinence managed with conservative therapy before pharmacotherapy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 58-year-old woman who describes a sudden overwhelming need to pass urine that she sometimes cannot defer, with leakage on the way to the toilet about three times a week. She voids around 11 times a day and wakes twice at night.

She does not leak when she coughs, sneezes or lifts her grandchildren. She drinks four cups of coffee and two cups of tea daily. She had two normal vaginal births and went through menopause at 51 years.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2, no pelvic organ prolapse beyond the hymen on Valsalva, no leakage demonstrated on cough stress test, vulval and vaginal mucosa well oestrogenised, voluntary pelvic floor contraction present and sustained for 6 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for blood, nitrites and leucocytes, midstream urine culture no growth, post-void residual volume 35 mL on bladder scan, fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.0 to 5.4)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence oxybutynin 5 mg orally twice daily and review in 6 weeks
Refer for urodynamic studies before deciding on further treatment
Refer to a gynaecologist for consideration of a midurethral sling
Prescribe vaginal oestrogen cream three nights weekly and reassess
Start bladder training with a fluid and caffeine reduction program

subtopic_detail: Persistent offensive vaginal discharge in a young woman with negative sexually transmitted infection testing
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 19-year-old woman with 5 weeks of vaginal discharge that she describes as brown and foul smelling, staining her underwear daily. It has not responded to a course of oral metronidazole or to an antifungal pessary.

A self-collected swab 3 weeks ago was negative for chlamydia, gonorrhoea and trichomonas. She has no fever, no pelvic pain and no dyspareunia. Her periods are regular and she has never been pregnant.

data_table.Examination: Vulva normal, abdomen soft with no tenderness, no cervical motion tenderness and no adnexal mass on bimanual examination, uterus anteverted and normal size
data_table.Investigations: Repeat vaginal swab negative for chlamydia, gonorrhoea and trichomonas, urine dipstick negative, beta hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe a 7 day course of oral doxycycline and review after treatment
Perform a speculum examination and remove any object that is found
Arrange a transvaginal ultrasound to assess the uterus and adnexae
Take a high vaginal swab for culture and treat according to the result
Perform a cervical screening test and await the laboratory report

subtopic_detail: Hirsutism with regular ovulatory cycles and mildly raised testosterone requiring 17 hydroxyprogesterone
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 17-year-old girl who has been waxing her upper lip and chin since she was 14 and now shaves her lower abdomen twice a week. She finds it distressing and wants to know why it is happening.

Her periods started at 12 years and come every 28 to 30 days lasting 5 days. Her voice has not changed, she has noticed no change in muscle bulk and no hair loss. Her father and paternal grandfather are of Lebanese background.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, terminal hair over the upper lip, chin, periareolar area and lower abdomen, no clitoromegaly, no temporal hair recession, no acanthosis nigricans, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Total testosterone 2.8 nmol/L (0.3 to 1.9), sex hormone binding globulin 48 nmol/L (26 to 110), DHEAS 6.1 micromol/L (1.0 to 9.0), prolactin 290 mIU/L (less than 500), beta hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Pelvic ultrasound to count antral follicles and measure ovarian volume
Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test with morning cortisol
Computed tomography of the adrenal glands and pelvis with contrast
Early morning follicular phase 17 hydroxyprogesterone measurement
Repeat total testosterone with free androgen index in three months

subtopic_detail: Secondary amenorrhoea with galactorrhoea and prolactin above 4000 requiring pituitary imaging
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 27-year-old woman whose periods stopped 8 months ago after years of regular cycles. She has also noticed a milky discharge from both nipples when she showers.

She has never been pregnant, uses condoms for contraception, takes no regular medication and no over the counter preparations. She has gained no weight, feels the cold no differently, and has had no headaches.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, bilateral expressible milky nipple discharge, no breast mass or lymphadenopathy, visual fields full to confrontation, no acne or hirsutism
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 4820 mIU/L (less than 500), beta hCG negative, TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 14 pmol/L (9 to 25), FSH 3.1 IU/L (follicular 3 to 9), oestradiol 96 pmol/L (follicular 110 to 400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa
Request a macroprolactin assay before proceeding to any imaging
Commence cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly and repeat prolactin
Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to restore withdrawal bleeds
Repeat the prolactin as a fasting cannulated sample in two weeks

subtopic_detail: Antithyroid drug selection in the first trimester for a woman already established on carbimazole
stem:
You are the obstetric physician registrar seeing a 30-year-old woman at 7 weeks in her first pregnancy. She was diagnosed with Graves disease 18 months ago and takes carbimazole 15 mg daily, which she has continued since her positive pregnancy test three weeks ago.

She reports no palpitations, tremor or heat intolerance and has gained no weight. She has not yet had a discussion about her medication in pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Small smooth goitre, no bruit, no lid lag or proptosis, fine tremor absent, reflexes normal
data_table.Investigations: TSH 0.06 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 17 pmol/L (9 to 25), free T3 5.2 pmol/L (3.0 to 5.5), TSH receptor antibody 6.8 IU/L (less than 1.8), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her antithyroid medication?

options.text: Continue carbimazole 15 mg daily and recheck thyroid function monthly
Stop all antithyroid medication and monitor thyroid function 4 weekly
Switch to propylthiouracil now and review thyroid function in 4 weeks
Add propranolol 10 mg three times daily to her current carbimazole
Refer for radioactive iodine ablation to be given after 12 weeks

subtopic_detail: Established valproate therapy discovered in the second trimester after the teratogenic window has passed
stem:
You are the obstetric physician registrar seeing a 26-year-old woman at 22 weeks in an unplanned first pregnancy. She takes sodium valproate 800 mg twice daily for generalised tonic clonic epilepsy and has been seizure free for 4 years.

She did not know she was pregnant until 14 weeks and has not seen her neurologist since. She drives to work and cares for her grandmother three afternoons a week. She stopped her folic acid two years ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, symphysis fundal height 22 cm, fetal movements reported as normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and urea and electrolytes within normal limits, 20 week morphology ultrasound not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her antiseizure medication?

options.text: Stop sodium valproate today and start lamotrigine 25 mg twice daily
Halve the valproate dose now and review her in the clinic in 4 weeks
Stop valproate and commence levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily today
Continue the current dose and arrange urgent neurology and scan review
Add folic acid 5 mg daily and make no change to her antiseizure dose

subtopic_detail: Polyhydramnios at 32 weeks with a normal glucose tolerance test and appropriate fetal growth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33-year-old woman at 32 weeks in her third pregnancy, referred because her abdomen has been measuring large for dates and she feels uncomfortably tight.

Her oral glucose tolerance test at 28 weeks was normal. Her blood group is O positive with a negative antibody screen. Her two previous pregnancies were uncomplicated and both babies weighed around 3.4 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 39 cm, uterus tense with fetal parts difficult to palpate, no uterine tenderness or activity, cervix long and closed on speculum examination
data_table.Ultrasound: Deepest vertical pool 10.4 cm, estimated fetal weight on the 55th centile, umbilical artery Doppler indices normal, no fetal ascites or skin oedema, placenta posterior and clear of the os

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the oral glucose tolerance test and check the HbA1c level
Arrange therapeutic amnioreduction to reduce the preterm birth risk
Arrange a detailed ultrasound of fetal anatomy and the stomach bubble
Plan induction of labour at 37 weeks to avoid membrane rupture risk
Measure the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity this week

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen where the endometrial thickness threshold does not apply
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 63-year-old woman who has had three episodes of light vaginal bleeding over the past two months. Her last menstrual period was 12 years ago.

She completed surgery and radiotherapy for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer 5 years ago and has taken tamoxifen 20 mg daily since. She takes no other hormonal preparation and has never used menopausal hormone therapy.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg/m2, vulva and vagina atrophic with no visible lesion, cervix smooth with no polyp or contact bleeding, uterus normal size and mobile, adnexae impalpable
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound reports endometrial thickness 7 mm with a heterogeneous appearance and subendometrial cystic spaces, both ovaries normal, cervical screening test negative for oncogenic HPV 8 months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that a thickness below 8 mm excludes endometrial cancer
Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in 3 months to assess for change
Perform a Pipelle endometrial biopsy in the clinic and stop there
Stop tamoxifen and switch her to an aromatase inhibitor, then review
Arrange hysteroscopy with directed biopsy regardless of the thickness

subtopic_detail: Haemoptysis with irregular bleeding months after a term birth as metastatic gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 34-year-old woman with three weeks of breathlessness on climbing stairs and several episodes of coughing up bright red blood. She gave birth to a healthy baby at term 5 months ago.

She stopped breastfeeding at 3 months and has had irregular vaginal bleeding since about 6 weeks postpartum, which she attributed to her periods returning. She is a non smoker and has had no recent travel or immobility.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation, no calf swelling or tenderness, uterus not palpable abdominally, small amount of dark blood at the cervical os on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115 to 155), white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), platelets 246 x10^9/L (150 to 400), chest radiograph shows four rounded opacities up to 25 mm in both lung fields

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Measure the serum beta hCG and refer to a trophoblastic disease centre
Arrange a computed tomography pulmonary angiogram and anticoagulate
Refer for bronchoscopy and biopsy of the largest pulmonary opacity
Treat as community-acquired pneumonia with oral amoxicillin and review
Arrange a computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation choice in early pregnancy for a mechanical mitral valve prosthesis on low dose warfarin
stem:
You are the obstetric physician registrar seeing a 32-year-old woman at 6 weeks in her first pregnancy. She had a mechanical bileaflet mitral valve replacement 4 years ago for rheumatic valve disease and takes warfarin 4 mg daily with a target international normalised ratio of 3.0.

Her INR has been in range at every check for the past year. She has read online that warfarin harms babies and has already missed last night's dose. She has no bleeding, no breathlessness and no palpitations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Crisp mechanical first heart sound with no murmur, chest clear, no peripheral oedema, no signs of embolism
data_table.Investigations: INR 2.4 today, full blood count and creatinine within normal limits, transthoracic echocardiogram 4 months ago showed normal prosthetic gradients and preserved left ventricular function, beta hCG consistent with dates

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan for the first trimester?

options.text: Switch to therapeutic enoxaparin now and resume warfarin at 12 weeks
Continue warfarin at the current dose with weekly INR measurement
Switch to therapeutic enoxaparin for the whole of the pregnancy
Continue warfarin and add aspirin 100 mg daily until she delivers
Switch to unfractionated heparin infusion and admit for monitoring

subtopic_detail: Cyclical pelvic pain with urinary retention in an adolescent with normal breast development and no menarche
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 14-year-old girl brought in by her mother because she has not passed urine since yesterday morning and her lower tummy is sore and swollen.

She has never had a period. For the past six months she has had cramping lower abdominal pain lasting three or four days that comes back about every four weeks and has been getting worse each time. Her breasts began developing at eleven and she has had underarm and pubic hair for two years.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 4 breast and pubic hair development, tender suprapubic mass palpable to the umbilicus and dull to percussion, inspection of the introitus shows a tense bulging bluish membrane, no abdominal guarding or rebound
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, bladder scan shows a residual volume of 780 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Pass an indwelling catheter and arrange outpatient gynaecology review
Refer for surgical incision of the obstructing membrane in theatre
Request a karyotype and measure the serum testosterone concentration
Give a progestogen course and observe for a withdrawal bleed afterwards
Start a combined oral contraceptive to suppress her cyclical symptoms

subtopic_detail: Burning nipple pain between feeds with biphasic colour change of the nipple triggered by cold
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a woman who is five weeks postpartum with her first baby. She describes a deep burning pain in both nipples that starts as the baby comes off the breast and lasts about twenty minutes, and says the nipple turns white, then dusky, then bright red and throbbing before the pain eases.

It is worst when she feeds in the lounge room in the early morning and barely happens at all after a warm shower. She has used a topical antifungal cream for three weeks on advice from a pharmacist with no change. She has no fever, and the baby is gaining weight well and feeds for twenty minutes before releasing the breast himself.

data_table.Examination: Nipples intact with no fissures, no shiny or flaking areolar skin, no palpable breast lump and no wedge shaped erythema, baby's tongue and buccal mucosa clear with no white plaques, latch observed to be deep with a rounded nipple on release
data_table.Investigations: Nipple swab shows no growth of Candida species

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence a two week course of oral fluconazole for deep breast candidiasis
Apply a topical corticosteroid ointment to both nipples after every feed
Refer the baby for division of a posterior tongue tie under local anaesthesia
Advise applying dry warmth immediately after feeds and avoiding cold exposure
Arrange expression and bottle feeding of breast milk until the pain resolves

subtopic_detail: Pain over the pubic symphysis and posterior pelvis in the third trimester with a positive provocation test
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared antenatal care for a woman at 28 weeks in her second pregnancy. She reports pain at the front of her pelvis that grinds when she rolls over in bed, climbs stairs or stands on one leg to dress, and says she waddles by the end of the day.

The pain is also felt across the back of her pelvis just below the dimples at the base of her spine. She has had no vaginal bleeding or loss of fluid, no tightenings, and the baby is moving normally. She had similar but milder symptoms in her first pregnancy which settled after the birth.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 145 per minute
data_table.Examination: Tenderness over the pubic symphysis and both sacroiliac joints, posterior pelvic pain provocation test positive bilaterally, straight leg raise negative, no renal angle tenderness, power and reflexes in both legs within normal limits, symphysiofundal height 28 cm
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for protein, nitrites, leucocytes and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for a pelvic support belt and an exercise program
Advise strict bed rest until the symptoms settle and review in two weeks
Prescribe a regular oral opioid analgesic for the remainder of the pregnancy
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joints
Plan a caesarean section at 39 weeks to protect the pelvis during labour

subtopic_detail: Nocturnal hand numbness in the third trimester in a radial distribution with preserved power and bulk
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a woman at 32 weeks in the antenatal clinic who says both her hands go numb and buzzing at night and wake her, and that she shakes them over the side of the bed until the feeling comes back.

The numbness affects her thumb, index and middle fingers and spares her little finger. She drops her coffee cup occasionally in the mornings but can do up buttons and open jars normally. She has no neck pain and no pain radiating down her arms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 per minute, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148 per minute
data_table.Examination: Sensory blunting over the palmar surface of the thumb, index and middle fingers bilaterally, Phalen test reproduces symptoms within 40 seconds, Tinel sign positive at the wrist, abductor pollicis brevis power and bulk within normal limits, reflexes symmetrical, no oedema beyond mild ankle swelling
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, thyroid stimulating hormone and fasting glucose all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies before deciding on any treatment
Inject corticosteroid into the carpal tunnel at the wrist crease bilaterally
Refer to a hand surgeon for consideration of carpal tunnel decompression
Prescribe a reducing course of oral prednisolone over the next fortnight
Supply wrist splints holding the wrist in neutral to be worn overnight

subtopic_detail: Painless smooth mobile breast lump in a lactating woman with no fever and no overlying inflammation
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old woman who is four months postpartum and still fully breastfeeding. She found a lump in the outer part of her left breast about three weeks ago and says it has slowly got bigger but does not hurt.

She has had no fever or flu like symptoms, and the lump has not changed with feeding or expressing. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer.

data_table.Examination: Smooth mobile non-tender 3 cm lump in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, no overlying erythema or warmth, no skin dimpling or nipple change, no axillary lymphadenopathy, right breast normal
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe oral flucloxacillin and review the breast in forty eight hours
Advise continued feeding from that side and reassess the lump in six weeks
Arrange a breast ultrasound scan with aspiration of the lesion if indicated
Request bilateral mammography with tomosynthesis at the local imaging centre
Advise that she wean before any imaging so that the breast can be assessed

subtopic_detail: Worsening pelvic infection after four days of oral treatment with a complex multiloculated adnexal collection
stem: A 28-year-old woman has five days of lower abdominal pain and offensive vaginal discharge. Oral doxycycline and metronidazole were started four days ago. She has worsened, with rigors overnight, and cannot keep tablets down.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 /min; BP 102/60 mmHg; T 38.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Marked cervical motion tenderness with a tender right adnexal fullness
data_table.Investigations: Pregnancy test negative, white cell count 17.2 x10^9/L, CRP 184 mg/L; ultrasound shows a 6 cm multiloculated right adnexal collection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the oral antibiotics for ten days with clinic review
Admit for intravenous antibiotics with early gynaecological review
Add oral fluconazole and repeat the ultrasound in two weeks
Laparoscopy today to remove the affected tube and ovary
Analgesia and ward observation for a ruptured ovarian cyst

subtopic_detail: Severe localised pain over a known fibroid at mid gestation with a mild leucocytosis and a soft uterus between
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar assessing a woman at 24 weeks in her first pregnancy who has had two days of constant severe pain in the right side of her abdomen. She points to one spot above and to the right of her umbilicus and says the pain is worse when anything presses on it.

A fibroid measuring 8 cm was documented on her first trimester scan. She has had no vaginal bleeding or loss of fluid, no urinary symptoms, and no vomiting or change in her bowels. The baby has been moving normally.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98 per minute, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 150 per minute
data_table.Examination: Marked localised tenderness over a firm mass in the right upper uterus, uterus soft and non-tender elsewhere with no tightenings palpable, no renal angle tenderness, no rebound or guarding in the right iliac fossa, cervix long and closed on speculum with no discharge
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (6.0-16.0 in pregnancy), C reactive protein 32 mg/L (less than 5), midstream urine shows no growth, ultrasound shows an 8 cm fibroid with heterogeneous echotexture and central cystic change, normal liquor volume, normal fetal growth, cardiotocograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Take her to theatre for laparotomy and myomectomy of the painful fibroid
Arrange urgent surgical review for appendicectomy through a right sided incision
Commence intravenous antibiotics for presumed intrauterine infection
Commence nifedipine tocolysis and give intramuscular betamethasone
Admit for analgesia including a short course of a non-steroidal anti inflammatory

subtopic_detail: Fluctuant swelling at the posterior introitus in a woman past forty presenting for drainage
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 52-year-old woman with four days of increasing pain and swelling on the left side of the vaginal opening, now bad enough that she cannot sit down or walk comfortably.

She went through menopause at 50 and has had no previous vulval problems, no vulval itch and no postmenopausal bleeding. She is otherwise well, takes no regular medication and has never smoked.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 per minute, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tender fluctuant 5 cm swelling at the posterior aspect of the left labium majus displacing the introitus medially, overlying skin erythematous and intact with no induration of surrounding tissue, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, no white atrophic vulval skin
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and C reactive protein pending, urine dipstick negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Drain the cavity and send a biopsy of the gland wall for histology
Perform simple incision and drainage with a scalpel and pack the cavity
Insert a balloon tipped catheter into the cavity and leave it for four weeks
Treat with oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and warm baths for five days
Arrange elective excision of the whole gland once the inflammation has settled

subtopic_detail: Absent periods with cyclical pain after repeated uterine instrumentation and no withdrawal bleed on progestogen
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 32-year-old woman who has not had a period for eight months. Her last pregnancy ended in a vaginal birth complicated by heavy bleeding, and she had two operations to remove retained tissue from the womb in the following fortnight.

She stopped breastfeeding four months ago and describes cramping lower abdominal pain for two or three days each month with no bleeding at all. She is not using contraception and would like another pregnancy. She has had no hot flushes, no galactorrhoea and no change in weight, appetite or energy.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, no acne or hirsutism, breasts with no expressible discharge, uterus anteverted normal size and non-tender, no adnexal masses, visual fields normal to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, follicle stimulating hormone 6.2 IU/L, luteinising hormone 5.8 IU/L, oestradiol 340 pmol/L, prolactin and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, no withdrawal bleeding after a ten day course of oral medroxyprogesterone acetate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the progestogen challenge at a higher dose over fourteen days
Measure the anti Mullerian hormone concentration to assess ovarian reserve
Commence a combined oral contraceptive to re establish a regular bleeding pattern
Arrange hysteroscopy to assess the cavity and divide any adhesions found
Arrange a transvaginal ultrasound scan to measure the endometrial thickness

subtopic_detail: Birth planning after a previous repaired third degree perineal tear with normal continence and normal anorectal testing
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a woman at 34 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first baby weighed 3.6 kg and was born with a vacuum after a long second stage, and she sustained a tear involving the anal sphincter that was repaired in theatre.

She has no leakage of wind or stool, no faecal urgency and no soiling, and says her bowel control is the same as it was before her first pregnancy. Estimated fetal weight on a growth scan last week was on the 55th centile. She has read online that she must have a caesarean and wants to know what you advise.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 per minute, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 142 per minute
data_table.Examination: Symphysiofundal height 34 cm, cephalic presentation, perineum with a healed midline scar and no defect palpable on digital assessment, resting and squeeze anal tone subjectively normal
data_table.Investigations: Endoanal ultrasound shows an intact external and internal anal sphincter, anorectal manometry resting and squeeze pressures within normal limits, St Mark's incontinence score zero

lead_in: What would you first recommend regarding her mode of birth?

options.text: Recommend an elective caesarean section at 39 weeks to protect the sphincter
Recommend a planned vaginal birth and discuss the small risk of recurrent injury
Recommend a vaginal birth with a routine mediolateral episiotomy at delivery
Offer either route without a recommendation and leave the decision entirely to her
Refer to a colorectal surgeon for secondary sphincter repair before she gives birth

subtopic_detail: Entry pain limited to the vestibule reproduced by cotton bud testing with normal skin and negative swabs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26-year-old woman who has had eighteen months of burning pain at the entrance to the vagina that occurs only with penetration and with tampon insertion. She has no pain walking, sitting or cycling, and none at any other time.

She has completed three courses of antifungal treatment prescribed over the past year without benefit, and has had no discharge, itch or odour throughout. She is in a supportive relationship, has no history of sexual assault, and finds the situation increasingly distressing.

data_table.Examination: Vulval skin normal in colour and texture with no erythema, fissuring, whitening or architectural change, cotton bud testing reproduces sharp pain at the posterior vestibule at the 5 and 7 o'clock positions and is painless on the labia majora and perineum, pelvic floor tone normal on digital examination with no guarding and no involuntary contraction on approach
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal and endocervical swabs negative for Candida species, bacterial vaginosis, chlamydia and gonorrhoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a longer course of oral fluconazole for resistant vulvovaginal candidiasis
Apply a topical oestrogen cream to the vestibule nightly for eight weeks
Refer to a gynaecologist for surgical excision of the painful vestibular tissue
Commence a low dose tricyclic antidepressant taken at night for neuropathic pain
Refer for pelvic floor physiotherapy alongside education and psychosexual support

subtopic_detail: Adnexal gestational sac alongside a live intrauterine pregnancy after embryo transfer with free pelvic fluid
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar called to the emergency department to see a 32-year-old woman at 7 weeks by dates who conceived through in vitro fertilisation with the transfer of two embryos. She has four hours of right sided lower abdominal pain and has passed a small amount of dark blood vaginally.

She describes the pain as constant and increasing, with a new ache at the tip of her right shoulder. She has vomited twice.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 per minute, blood pressure 98/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale and uncomfortable, abdomen tender in the right iliac fossa with guarding, cervical os closed with a small amount of dark blood in the vault
data_table.Investigations: Serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin 48000 IU/L, haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), transvaginal ultrasound shows an intrauterine gestational sac with a fetal pole and cardiac activity at 7 weeks, a separate right adnexal sac containing a yolk sac and a fetal pole, and echogenic free fluid extending to the hepatorenal recess

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Proceed to laparoscopy with removal of the affected fallopian tube
Give a single intramuscular dose of methotrexate calculated by body surface area
Proceed to laparoscopy with opening of the tube and removal of the trophoblast
Admit for observation with serial beta human chorionic gonadotrophin measurement
Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in forty eight hours with the fertility unit

subtopic_detail: Woman requesting to end an unintended pregnancy at eight weeks by ultrasound who wishes to avoid a procedure and has reliable transport
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24-year-old woman who has decided to end an unintended pregnancy. She is certain of her decision, has read about her options, and says she would prefer to avoid an operation and an anaesthetic if that is possible.

She lives 20 minutes from a regional hospital with a gynaecology service, has a supportive partner at home, and has no bleeding disorder and no intrauterine device in place. She is not breastfeeding and takes no regular medication.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no adnexal mass or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound shows a single intrauterine gestational sac with a crown rump length corresponding to 8 weeks and 1 day, no adnexal abnormality, blood group O RhD positive, haemoglobin 131 g/L (115 to 155)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for suction curettage on the next available gynaecology operating list
Arrange misoprostol alone with a repeat dose if bleeding has not started
Arrange methotrexate followed by misoprostol two to three days afterwards
Arrange an anti D injection before any treatment is commenced at this gestation
Arrange mifepristone then misoprostol with confirmation that expulsion is complete

subtopic_detail: Persistent raised area on chronically pale thickened vulval skin that has not settled despite six months of adherent potent topical steroid
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 68-year-old woman with a six year history of vulval itch treated with a potent topical steroid ointment. Her itch has settled everywhere except one spot on the right side, where she says there is a hard raised patch that has slowly grown over four months and now catches on her underwear and sometimes bleeds a little.

She brings her ointment and her pharmacy record confirms she has been collecting it regularly and applying it as instructed.

data_table.Examination: Pale thickened atrophic skin with loss of the labia minora and narrowing of the introitus, and on the right labium majus a firm raised plaque 15 mm across with an irregular surface and a small area of surface breakdown, no discharge, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, cervix and vagina normal on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Change to a different potent steroid ointment and review her in three months
Prescribe topical tacrolimus ointment to the resistant area twice daily for eight weeks
Take a vulvovaginal swab for culture and treat according to the organism grown
Perform a punch biopsy of the lesion and refer according to the histology
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis and groins before any biopsy

subtopic_detail: Incidental thin walled single chamber ovarian cyst found on imaging for another reason in a woman five years past her last period
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 57-year-old woman whose abdominal ultrasound, requested to investigate right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal, incidentally showed an ovarian cyst. Her last period was five years ago and she has had no vaginal bleeding since.

She has no abdominal distension, no early satiety, no change in bowel habit and no unintentional weight loss. There is no family history of breast, ovarian or bowel cancer.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no mass, no ascites, no inguinal or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, bimanual examination unremarkable with no adnexal mass palpable
data_table.Investigations: Dedicated transvaginal ultrasound shows a right ovarian cyst 38 mm in diameter, unilocular, thin smooth walled, anechoic, with no solid component, no papillary projection, no internal vascularity and no free fluid, left ovary not visualised and atrophic, CA125 11 kU/L (less than 35)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a gynaecological oncologist for assessment at a specialist centre
Refer for laparoscopic oophorectomy to obtain a histological diagnosis
Arrange computed tomography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging
Discharge her with advice to return only if abdominal symptoms develop
Repeat the ultrasound and CA125 in four months to confirm the cyst is stable

subtopic_detail: Woman in her mid seventies with a femoral neck bone density well below threshold and no previous fracture attending for the result
stem:
You are the general practitioner giving a 74-year-old woman the result of a bone density scan you arranged because of her age and a recent loss of height. She has never broken a bone, walks each morning, and takes no medication other than an antihypertensive.

She drinks two standard drinks most days and has never smoked. Her mother had a hip fracture at 80.

data_table.Examination: Height 3 cm less than her recorded height eight years ago, mild thoracic kyphosis, no spinal tenderness, steady gait, able to rise from a chair without using her arms
data_table.Investigations: Dual energy x ray absorptiometry femoral neck T score minus 2.7 and lumbar spine T score minus 2.4, corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.20 to 2.60), phosphate 1.10 mmol/L (0.80 to 1.50), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 62 nmol/L (greater than 50), estimated glomerular filtration rate 74 mL/min/1.73m2 (greater than 60), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise weight bearing exercise and repeat the bone density scan in two years
Start an oral bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D intake reviewed
Start menopausal hormone therapy at the lowest effective dose for bone protection
Start teriparatide by daily injection and arrange specialist endocrine review
Start high dose vitamin D and calcium supplements as sole pharmacological therapy

subtopic_detail: Third trimester itch of the palms and soles at night with raised bile acids in the intermediate range and normal liver architecture
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 31-year-old woman at 34 weeks in her first pregnancy who describes relentless itch of her palms and the soles of her feet that keeps her awake from about two in the morning. There is no rash other than scratch marks.

Her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated with normal growth on ultrasound and normal fetal movements. She has no headache, no visual disturbance and no epigastric pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 145 beats per minute
data_table.Examination: Linear excoriations over both forearms and shins, no primary rash, no jaundice, no right upper quadrant tenderness, symphysis fundal height 34 cm, cardiotocograph normal
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bile acids 45 micromol/L (less than 19), alanine aminotransferase 78 U/L (less than 35), bilirubin 12 micromol/L (less than 20), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150 to 400), international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.8 to 1.2), protein creatinine ratio 12 mg/mmol (less than 30), hepatitis serology negative, liver ultrasound shows no biliary dilatation or gallstones

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Arrange delivery within 48 hours because of the risk of sudden fetal death
Commence twice weekly cardiotocography as the principal tool to prevent stillbirth
Commence ursodeoxycholic acid as the intervention that reduces perinatal death
Monitor bile acids serially and plan birth at 38 to 39 weeks after discussion
Commence oral prednisolone and repeat the liver enzymes in one week

subtopic_detail: Woman in her mid thirties with four months without periods, night sweats and two raised gonadotrophin measurements six weeks apart
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 36-year-old woman whose periods stopped four months ago after two years of gradually lengthening cycles. She wakes drenched two or three nights a week, finds sex uncomfortable because of dryness, and has become tearful and irritable in a way she says is not like her.

She has never been pregnant and had hoped to start a family in the next few years. She has no history of chemotherapy, pelvic surgery or autoimmune disease.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg/m2, no goitre, no hirsutism, no galactorrhoea, vulval and vaginal mucosa appear thin and pale, uterus normal size, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, follicle stimulating hormone 48 IU/L and repeat six weeks later 52 IU/L (3.5 to 12.5 follicular), oestradiol 62 pmol/L (110 to 400 follicular), prolactin 310 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.4 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), karyotype 46 XX, fragile X premutation not detected, adrenal and thyroid antibodies negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a non hormonal agent for vasomotor symptoms and review in six months
Prescribe systemic hormone therapy to continue until the usual age of menopause
Advise that pregnancy is no longer possible and that contraception is unnecessary
Arrange a bone density scan and defer treatment until the result is available
Prescribe vaginal oestrogen alone and add systemic treatment only if flushes persist

subtopic_detail: Breastfeeding woman six weeks after birth with persistent low mood, a high screening score and passive thoughts of being better off gone but no plan
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old woman at six weeks postpartum. The child health nurse referred her after a routine screening questionnaire, and when you explore it she describes six weeks of flat mood every day, no enjoyment in anything including her baby, waking at four each morning unable to return to sleep, and eating almost nothing.

She says she feels her family would manage better without her but has no thoughts of acting on that and no plan, and that she has never felt this way before. She is not hearing or seeing anything unusual and holds no unusual beliefs about the baby.

data_table.Examination: Slowed speech with restricted affect, oriented and attentive with no perceptual disturbance, no delusional beliefs, attends to and responds appropriately to her baby, weight 4 kg below her prepregnancy weight
data_table.Investigations: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 19 with item 10 scored 1, haemoglobin 124 g/L (115 to 155), ferritin 62 micrograms/L (30 to 300), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange emergency mental health assessment for admission to a mother and baby unit
Advise stopping breastfeeding so that antidepressant treatment can be commenced
Arrange practical support and review her in four weeks without starting treatment
Start sertraline with psychological therapy and arrange early structured review
Repeat the screening questionnaire in two weeks and decide on treatment then

subtopic_detail: Newly diagnosed maternal thyrotoxicosis with a suppressed thyrotrophin and raised receptor antibodies in the first trimester
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 27-year-old woman at 8 weeks in her first pregnancy who was referred with a three month history of palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor and weight loss despite a good appetite. Her symptoms began before she conceived and have continued since.

She vomits occasionally in the mornings but keeps food down and has lost no further weight in the past fortnight. She has a fine tremor of the outstretched hands and says her eyes have felt gritty and look more prominent in photographs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Smooth symmetrically enlarged thyroid with a bruit, fine tremor of the outstretched hands, warm moist palms, lid retraction with proptosis on both sides, no pretibial changes, uterus not palpable abdominally
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free thyroxine 34 pmol/L (10 to 20), free triiodothyronine 11.2 pmol/L (3.5 to 6.5), thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibody strongly positive, ultrasound confirms a single intrauterine pregnancy with a crown rump length consistent with 8 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Carbimazole at a dose titrated to keep free thyroxine in the upper normal range
Radioactive iodine ablation followed by thyroxine replacement after treatment
Propylthiouracil at a dose titrated to keep free thyroxine in the upper normal range
Supportive treatment with antiemetics and repeat thyroid function in four weeks
Thyroidectomy in the first trimester once she is medically prepared for surgery

subtopic_detail: Woman who has completed her family requesting a permanent method and declining long acting reversible alternatives after counselling
stem:
You are the gynaecologist seeing a 39-year-old woman, para 3, who has been referred requesting a permanent contraceptive procedure. She has discussed long-acting reversible options with her general practitioner, has used an intrauterine system previously and disliked it, and is clear that she wants something she never has to think about again.

Her periods are regular and not heavy, her cervical screening is up to date and negative, and she has no pelvic pain. Her mother died of ovarian cancer at 61 and no genetic testing has been undertaken in the family. Her partner has declined vasectomy after discussion between them.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 28 kg/m2, abdomen soft with two previous low transverse scars, uterus normal size and mobile, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, pelvic ultrasound shows a normal uterus with an endometrial thickness of 6 mm and normal ovaries

lead_in: What would you recommend as the procedure of choice?

options.text: Laparoscopic application of clips to occlude both fallopian tubes
Laparoscopic bilateral oophorectomy with hormone therapy until the age of fifty
Laparoscopic bilateral salpingectomy with referral for family cancer assessment
Hysteroscopic placement of intratubal inserts as a procedure avoiding abdominal entry
Insertion of a further levonorgestrel intrauterine system after a trial of counselling

subtopic_detail: Woman in her mid forties with heavy regular periods unresponsive to six months of medical treatment and a structurally normal pelvic ultrasound
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 46-year-old woman whose periods have been heavy for two years. She has flooded through double protection on her worst days and taken six months of treatment that you prescribed, first an antifibrinolytic with a non-steroidal and then a progestogen, with no improvement in the volume of loss.

Her cycles remain regular at 27 days with no bleeding between periods and no bleeding after intercourse. She has a body mass index of 34 kg/m2 and takes metformin for polycystic ovary syndrome diagnosed in her twenties.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable mass, uterus normal size and mobile on bimanual examination, cervix appears normal on speculum examination with no visible lesion or contact bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115 to 155), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30 to 300), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.2 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), coagulation screen normal, cervical screening test negative four months ago, transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal uterus, an endometrial thickness of 9 mm with a regular outline and no focal lesion, and normal ovaries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for endometrial ablation as definitive treatment for her heavy bleeding
Commence intravenous iron and repeat the full blood count in three months
Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in the early proliferative phase of her cycle
Arrange endometrial sampling before any further treatment is offered
Refer for hysterectomy given the failure of two lines of medical treatment

subtopic_detail: Second episode of bleeding years after the last period in a woman whose endometrium measures under the reassurance threshold on both scans
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 64-year-old woman with a second episode of vaginal bleeding. Her last period was twelve years ago. The first episode was four months ago, when a transvaginal ultrasound showed an endometrial thickness of 3 mm and she was reassured and discharged from the clinic.

She has bled again for two days this week, describing it as watery and pink on wiping. She takes no hormone therapy and no tamoxifen, and she has never been on anticoagulation.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 31 kg/m2, atrophic vulval and vaginal epithelium with no visible laceration or lesion, cervix appears normal with no polyp and no contact bleeding, uterus small and mobile, no adnexal mass, rectal examination unremarkable with no blood on the glove
data_table.Investigations: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 3 mm with a regular outline, a small amount of fluid within the cavity, and normal ovaries, cervical screening test negative two years ago, midstream urine culture no growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her on the basis of the thin endometrium and review only if bleeding recurs
Prescribe vaginal oestrogen for atrophic bleeding and review her in three months
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to look for an occult uterine lesion
Arrange an outpatient blind endometrial biopsy and manage according to the result
Arrange hysteroscopy with directed biopsy under direct vision of the whole cavity

subtopic_detail: Woman with well controlled generalised seizures on an established anticonvulsant attending to plan a first pregnancy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 28-year-old woman who tells you she and her partner want to start trying for a baby in the next few months. She has generalised tonic clonic seizures that have been fully controlled for four years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, having had breakthrough seizures on two previous agents.

She drives to work, has not had a seizure since starting this medication, and is terrified of losing her licence. She takes no other medication and no supplements.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 25 kg/m2, neurological examination unremarkable, no tremor, no gum hypertrophy
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, full blood count and liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently to a neurologist to plan a change of agent before she conceives
Continue the current agent at the lowest effective dose and add high dose folic acid
Stop the anticonvulsant now given four years of seizure freedom and review in a month
Advise her to conceive on the current agent and change it as soon as she is pregnant
Reduce the current agent to half the dose now and start folic acid one month before conception

subtopic_detail: Older woman with urgency and nocturia unimproved by bladder training who is already taking a cholinesterase inhibitor for memory problems
stem: A 78-year-old woman has 18 months of urgency, eight voids by day and three by night, with occasional leakage on the way to the toilet. Three months of supervised bladder training has not helped. She has no leakage on coughing. She takes donepezil for mild cognitive impairment, amlodipine and atorvastatin.

data_table.Examination: Atrophic vaginal epithelium, no prolapse, cough stress test negative, post-void residual 35 mL
data_table.Investigations: Midstream urine no growth

lead_in: Which treatment would you add?

options.text: Oxybutynin, titrated to symptom response
Mirabegron, with blood pressure checked after starting
Desmopressin at night, with sodium checked in week one
Refer for intradetrusor botulinum toxin injection
Refer for a midurethral sling after urodynamics

subtopic_detail: Symptomatic anterior vaginal wall descent to the hymen in an 82 year old declined for anaesthesia because of severe respiratory disease
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing an 82-year-old woman who describes a dragging feeling and a bulge she can feel at the entrance to the vagina by the end of each day. It is worse after she has been gardening and eases when she lies down.

She has severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease on home oxygen and was assessed by the anaesthetic clinic last month as unsuitable for a general or regional anaesthetic. She has completed three months of supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist without improvement. She is sexually inactive, has had no bleeding, and her last cervical screening test was normal two years ago. Examination shows anterior wall descent reaching the hymen on straining with well oestrogenised tissue.

data_table.Examination: Anterior vaginal wall descending to the level of the hymen on Valsalva, cervix descending to 2 cm above the hymen, no posterior compartment defect, vaginal epithelium moist and rugated with no ulceration, no adnexal mass, post-void residual volume 40 mL on bladder scan
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for nitrites and leucocytes, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Fit a ring pessary in the clinic and review her in the clinic within six weeks
Refer for vaginal hysterectomy with anterior repair on the next elective list
Prescribe a further six months of supervised pelvic floor muscle training now
Prescribe vaginal oestrogen cream alone and review her symptoms in three months
Refer for colpocleisis under local infiltration on the next available theatre list

subtopic_detail: Frequent prolonged unscheduled bleeding five months after insertion of a progestogen implant in a woman who wants to keep the device
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24-year-old woman who had a contraceptive implant placed in her upper arm five months ago. She has bled on more days than not since, with episodes lasting eight to ten days, and she has had enough of it but says she does not want to go back to remembering a daily tablet.

She has no pain, no postcoital bleeding and no discharge, and she is in a new relationship since the implant was inserted. Her cervical screening test last year was negative for human papillomavirus. A urine pregnancy test today is negative and a self collected swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea is negative. Speculum and bimanual examination are normal and the implant is palpable in the correct plane.

data_table.Examination: Implant palpable subdermally in the medial upper left arm, cervix healthy with no contact bleeding, uterus anteverted and normal size, adnexae non-tender with no mass
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, self collected vaginal swab negative for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, haemoglobin 129 g/L (115-155), ferritin 38 micrograms per litre (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her bleeding?

options.text: Remove the implant today and arrange insertion of a hormonal intrauterine device
Reassure her that the pattern will settle and review her again in three months
Offer a three month course of a combined oral contraceptive alongside the implant
Prescribe tranexamic acid to be taken continuously for the next three months
Arrange a pelvic ultrasound and an endometrial biopsy before any other treatment

subtopic_detail: Sixteen year old requesting the three monthly progestogen injection whose mother has raised concerns about bone strength
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 16-year-old who has come in with her mother asking for the contraceptive injection because her friend uses it and she does not want anything she has to think about. She has regular periods, no medical problems and takes no medication.

Her mother has read that the injection weakens bones and wants to know whether her daughter should have a bone density scan first. She eats normally, plays netball twice a week and has never had a fracture. She is competent to consent and has discussed the decision with you alone as well as with her mother present. Her body mass index is 22 kg per square metre, her blood pressure is normal and she does not smoke.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg per square metre, no features of an eating disorder, secondary sexual characteristics fully developed, general examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice and management?

options.text: Decline the injection because of her age and offer the combined pill as an alternative
Arrange a dual energy X-ray absorptiometry scan before the first injection is given
Give the injection now and plan to stop the method after two years of continuous use
Give the injection now, with advice on calcium, vitamin D and weight bearing exercise
Give the injection now and add a daily oestrogen tablet to protect her bone density

subtopic_detail: Painful glazed erosions at the vestibule with a lacy white border and oral changes in a woman failing topical steroid
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58-year-old woman with eighteen months of vulval soreness and burning that makes intercourse impossible. She describes rawness rather than itch and says the skin feels like it is peeling.

Her general practitioner has treated her for thrush three times and then prescribed a potent topical corticosteroid ointment for eight weeks, which helped a little but never cleared it. She has also had sore gums for the past year and her dentist has commented on white streaks inside her cheeks. She has hypothyroidism on thyroxine. Examination shows glazed red erosions at the vestibule with a fine white lacy margin, loss of the labia minora, and narrowing of the introitus.

data_table.Examination: Glazed erythematous erosions around the vestibule with a reticulate white border, resorption of the labia minora, introital narrowing admitting one finger with discomfort, no thickened white plaques over the perianal skin, buccal mucosa with bilateral white lacy striae, vaginal walls erythematous with a serous discharge
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal swab negative for candida and bacterial vaginosis, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?
