options.text: Take a vulval biopsy from the centre of an erosion and stop all topical treatment
Prescribe a further course of oral fluconazole and repeat the vaginal swab afterwards
Prescribe topical vaginal oestrogen alone and review her symptoms in three months
Refer for examination under anaesthesia with surgical division of the narrowed introitus
Take a vulval biopsy from the edge of an erosion and continue ultrapotent steroid

subtopic_detail: Monthly lower abdominal pain for six months with no menarche and a bluish bulging membrane at the introitus in a fully developed adolescent
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 14-year-old girl referred by her general practitioner with six months of lower abdominal pain that comes for three or four days each month and then goes completely. She has never had a period.

Her breasts developed at 11 and she has full pubic and axillary hair. She has grown 9 cm in the last two years. Over the last fortnight she has also been going to the toilet more often and feeling that she cannot empty her bladder properly. Abdominal examination finds a smooth suprapubic mass rising to just below the umbilicus. Inspection of the introitus shows a tense bluish membrane that bulges when she strains.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, smooth non-tender suprapubic mass palpable to 4 cm below the umbilicus, tense bluish membrane bulging at the introitus on Valsalva with no visible vaginal opening, normal external genitalia otherwise, no inguinal masses
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, post-void bladder scan 180 mL, pelvic ultrasound showing a distended vagina filled with echogenic fluid and a normal uterus and both ovaries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Arrange needle aspiration of the collection in the clinic under local anaesthesia
Start a combined oral contraceptive continuously to suppress further bleeding now
Arrange surgical incision and drainage of the obstructed outflow tract in theatre
Arrange a karyotype and measure gonadotrophins before any procedure is undertaken
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before any decision on treatment

subtopic_detail: Milky discharge from both breasts with six months of absent periods and a mildly raised prolactin in a woman recently started on an antiemetic
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old woman who has noticed a milky fluid coming from both nipples when she showers, and who has not had a period for six months. She has never been pregnant.

She has had nausea from gastroparesis for the last eight months and her gastroenterologist started her on domperidone seven months ago, which she takes three times a day. She has no headache and no change in her vision, and she has not gained weight or become constipated. A urine pregnancy test today is negative. Her serum prolactin taken this morning after a rushed walk from the car park is 1180 milliunits per litre.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral expressible milky nipple discharge, breasts otherwise normal with no mass, visual fields full to confrontation, no acromegalic features, no goitre, no striae or proximal weakness
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1180 milliunits per litre (less than 500), urine pregnancy test negative, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.4 milliunits per litre (0.4-4.0), follicle stimulating hormone 4.1 international units per litre, luteinising hormone 3.6 international units per litre, oestradiol 180 picomoles per litre

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with contrast this week
Start cabergoline twice weekly and review her prolactin level again in eight weeks
Start a combined oral contraceptive to restore her periods and review in three months
Discuss stopping the antiemetic with her gastroenterologist and repeat the prolactin
Arrange a macroprolactin assay and consider the result sufficient if it is positive

subtopic_detail: Leakage only on coughing and running eight months after a second vaginal birth with a normal bladder diary and no urgency
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 33-year-old woman eight months after the vaginal birth of her second child. She leaks a small amount of urine when she coughs, sneezes or runs after her toddler, and has stopped going to her exercise class because of it.

She never leaks on the way to the toilet and does not get a sudden overwhelming need to go. She empties her bladder five times a day and does not wake at night for it. Her bladder diary shows a normal fluid intake of 1.8 litres and voided volumes between 250 and 400 mL. She has completed her family and is not breastfeeding. Examination shows a well healed perineum and she can hold a voluntary pelvic floor contraction for three seconds.

data_table.Examination: Well healed second degree perineal repair, no vaginal wall descent on Valsalva, voluntary pelvic floor contraction palpable but weak and held for 3 seconds, leakage of a small volume of urine observed on cough with a comfortably full bladder, post-void residual volume 25 mL on bladder scan
data_table.Investigations: Midstream urine negative on culture, urine dipstick negative for blood nitrites and glucose

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Refer for a supervised pelvic floor muscle training program of at least three months
Refer to a urogynaecologist for a midurethral sling on the next available elective list
Start an antimuscarinic and arrange a bladder training program with fluid advice
Arrange urodynamic studies before committing her to any particular treatment pathway
Prescribe topical vaginal oestrogen and review her symptoms again in three months

subtopic_detail: Three second trimester losses at 16 to 19 weeks with painless cervical dilatation twice and a normal antiphospholipid and karyotype screen
stem: A 32-year-old woman has had three pregnancies lost at 16, 18 and 19 weeks, twice with membranes bulging through an open cervix without contractions or bleeding.

data_table.Examination: Cervix closed and 3 cm long; uterus of normal size
data_table.Investigations: Antiphospholipid antibodies negative on two occasions twelve weeks apart; thyroid function, HbA1c and parental karyotypes normal; transvaginal ultrasound shows a 12 mm midline cavity indentation with a flat external fundal contour

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Hysteroscopic resection of the midline tissue on the next theatre list
Three dimensional ultrasound to define the cavity and fundal contour
Elective cervical cerclage at 12 weeks in her next pregnancy
Low dose aspirin with prophylactic low molecular weight heparin
Vaginal progesterone from 16 weeks with cervical length monitoring

subtopic_detail: Sixteen year old with no menstruation, full breast development, sparse pubic hair and a short blind ending vagina with bilateral groin swellings
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 16-year-old who has never menstruated. Her breasts developed at 12 and she has grown to 176 cm, taller than both parents.

She has almost no pubic or axillary hair, which she says has never bothered her. She has never had cyclical abdominal pain of any kind. She has a firm mobile swelling in each groin that her mother assumed were hernias. On examination the external genitalia are female and the vagina is 4 cm long and ends blindly. A pelvic ultrasound performed this morning reports no uterus and no ovaries, with soft tissue structures in both inguinal canals.

data_table.Examination: Height 176 cm, Tanner stage 5 breast development, Tanner stage 1 to 2 pubic and axillary hair, normal female external genitalia, vagina 4 cm long ending blindly with no cervix visible, firm mobile 3 cm swelling in each inguinal canal, no acne or clitoromegaly
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound with no uterus and no ovaries identified and soft tissue structures in both inguinal canals, testosterone 18 nanomoles per litre (female range 0.5-2.6), luteinising hormone 14 international units per litre, follicle stimulating hormone 5 international units per litre, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: Which investigation will confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis and both inguinal canals with contrast
Measurement of serum anti Mullerian hormone with inhibin B on a morning sample
Karyotype analysis on a peripheral blood sample sent to a cytogenetics laboratory
Measurement of serum 17 hydroxyprogesterone with a short synacthen stimulation test
Diagnostic laparoscopy with biopsy of the structures found in both inguinal canals

subtopic_detail: Four months of bloating and early satiety in a postmenopausal woman with a solid adnexal mass with papillary projections and ascites
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62-year-old woman who has felt bloated for four months and now fills up after a few mouthfuls. She has lost 4 kg without trying and has been to the toilet more often to pass urine.

She went through menopause at 51 and has had no vaginal bleeding. She was treated for irritable bowel symptoms for the last three months without improvement. Her mother died of ovarian cancer at 58 and a maternal aunt had breast cancer at 44. Abdominal examination finds shifting dullness and a firm mass arising from the pelvis. The ultrasound she had yesterday describes a 9 cm solid mass with papillary projections and internal blood flow, with free fluid in the abdomen.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen distended with shifting dullness, firm irregular mass arising from the pelvis reaching 5 cm above the symphysis, no hepatomegaly, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, no vaginal bleeding on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal and abdominal ultrasound showing a 9 cm solid adnexal mass with papillary projections and internal vascularity plus moderate ascites, CA125 640 units per millilitre (less than 35), haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), albumin 33 g/L (35-50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer directly to a gynaecological oncology centre for staging and multidisciplinary care
Refer to the general gynaecology list for laparoscopic removal of the adnexal mass
Refer to the interventional suite for diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis this week
Refer for colonoscopy and gastroscopy to exclude a gastrointestinal primary tumour first
Refer for genetic counselling and germline testing before any surgical decision is taken

subtopic_detail: Right sided abdominal pain with fever at 24 weeks where the appendix is not visualised on ultrasound and the white cell count sits in the physiological pregnancy range
stem: A 26-year-old woman at 24 weeks in her first pregnancy has 18 hours of pain that began periumbilically and settled in the right abdomen above the umbilicus. She has vomited twice.

data_table.Examination: Tender in the right abdomen 4 cm above the umbilicus with guarding, no rebound
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.8 x10^9/L (pregnancy range 6.0-16.0), CRP 68 mg/L; transabdominal ultrasound did not visualise the appendix, with normal kidneys and ovaries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast
Repeat transabdominal ultrasound in twelve hours with serial examination
Intravenous antibiotics with observation and surgical reassessment later
Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen without gadolinium
Diagnostic laparoscopy on the emergency list without further imaging

subtopic_detail: Contraceptive choice for a woman with focal epilepsy on carbamazepine who has already conceived once on a combined pill and does not want pregnancy for five years
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29-year-old woman with focal epilepsy that has been seizure free for three years on carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily. She conceived unexpectedly two years ago while taking a combined oral contraceptive every day and had a termination.

She has two children, does not want another pregnancy for at least five years, and is adamant she will not rely on remembering anything daily. She has heavy but regular periods and a haemoglobin of 112 g/L. Her blood pressure is normal, she does not smoke and she has no history of thrombosis. Her neurologist has documented that carbamazepine is the only agent that has controlled her seizures and wants it continued.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg per square metre, cardiovascular and abdominal examination normal, pelvic examination normal with a mobile anteverted uterus
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 112 g/L (115-155), ferritin 16 micrograms per litre (30-200), urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: Which contraceptive method should you recommend first?

options.text: A subdermal etonogestrel implant inserted at the next available clinic appointment
A combined oral contraceptive containing 50 micrograms of ethinylestradiol daily
A progestogen only pill taken continuously with condoms used as a second method
A three monthly depot medroxyprogesterone injection with a shortened dosing interval
A levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system inserted at the next available appointment

subtopic_detail: A seven centimetre multiloculated adnexal collection still febrile after forty eight hours of intravenous antibiotics for pelvic infection
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman admitted two days ago with lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia and cervical motion tenderness. She has been on intravenous ceftriaxone, azithromycin and metronidazole since admission.

Her pain has not settled, she continues to spike temperatures and she looks tired but is not confused. Her abdomen is tender in both iliac fossae with voluntary guarding but no rebound and no board like rigidity. A serum pregnancy test taken on admission was negative. A repeat transvaginal ultrasound today reports a 7 cm multiloculated collection incorporating the left tube and ovary, with no free fluid elsewhere in the abdomen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tenderness in both iliac fossae with voluntary guarding, no rebound tenderness and no rigidity, bowel sounds present, cervical motion tenderness on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), C reactive protein 214 mg/L rising from 168 on admission (less than 5), serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin negative, transvaginal ultrasound reports a 7 cm multiloculated left tubo-ovarian collection with no free intraperitoneal fluid, blood cultures no growth to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Change to oral doxycycline and metronidazole and plan discharge tomorrow
Continue the current antibiotics and reassess after a further seven days
Proceed to total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
Arrange image guided drainage of the collection and continue antibiotics
Add intravenous vancomycin and reassess after a further seventy two hours

subtopic_detail: Heavy painful periods with a globally enlarged tender uterus and junctional zone thickening on magnetic resonance imaging at forty one
stem:
You are the gynaecologist seeing a 41-year-old woman with four years of progressively heavier and more painful periods. She describes flooding through a pad in an hour on her worst days and cramping that starts several days before bleeding begins and continues throughout.

Her two children were born by normal vaginal delivery and she does not wish to conceive again. On examination the uterus is bulky, globular and tender, estimated at a 10 week size, with no adnexal masses. An endometrial biopsy taken last month showed proliferative endometrium with no hyperplasia and no atypia. Magnetic resonance imaging reports a diffusely thickened junctional zone of 15 mm with no discrete myometrial lesion and a normal endometrial thickness.

data_table.Examination: Bulky globular tender uterus of approximately 10 week size, mobile with no adnexal masses, cervix appears normal with a recent negative cervical screening test
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115 to 155), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (30 to 200), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, endometrial biopsy shows proliferative endometrium without hyperplasia or atypia, magnetic resonance imaging reports a diffusely thickened junctional zone of 15 mm with no discrete myometrial lesion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system and review in six months
Start combined oral contraception continuously and review her in six months
Refer for hysteroscopic resection of the lesion and review postoperatively
Start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist alone and review in six months
Refer for uterine artery embolisation and review in the interventional clinic

subtopic_detail: Burning pain reproduced by cotton bud touch at the vestibule with normal vulval skin and negative swabs in a twenty six year old
stem: A 26-year-old woman has eighteen months of burning discomfort at the vaginal entrance that occurs only on touch, including tampons and intercourse. Several over the counter antifungal courses have not helped.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulval architecture, no white plaques or fissuring; cotton bud touch at the vestibule reproduces the pain sharply but is painless on the labia majora; levator ani hypertonic
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab normal flora with no candida; chlamydia and gonorrhoea testing negative; vaginal pH 4.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: A course of topical clobetasol with review in eight weeks
Weekly oral fluconazole for six months, then review
Referral for vestibulectomy and surgical outpatient review
Pelvic floor physiotherapy with a topical local anaesthetic
Topical oestrogen cream nightly with review in eight weeks

subtopic_detail: Frothy discharge with motile flagellates on wet mount at ten weeks gestation with a vaginal pH of 5.5
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24-year-old woman at ten weeks in her first pregnancy who reports three weeks of a heavy, frothy, yellow-green discharge with soreness and an offensive smell. She has recently moved to your town from a remote area of the Northern Territory.

She has used a clotrimazole pessary without improvement. On speculum examination there is a copious frothy discharge and the cervix has a punctate red appearance. The vaginal pH is 5.5. Wet mount microscopy shows motile flagellated organisms and no hyphae or spores, and nucleic acid amplification testing is negative for chlamydia and gonorrhoea. She has one regular sexual partner.

data_table.Examination: Copious frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge, punctate erythema of the ectocervix, no cervical motion tenderness, uterus consistent with dates, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH 5.5, wet mount microscopy shows motile flagellated organisms with no hyphae or spores, nucleic acid amplification testing negative for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, syphilis and blood borne virus serology negative, urine culture no growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Oral fluconazole 150 mg as a single dose with treatment of her partner
Oral metronidazole 2 g as a single dose with treatment of her partner
Defer treatment until the second trimester and treat her partner now
Topical clotrimazole for six nights with treatment of her regular partner
Intramuscular ceftriaxone 500 mg with treatment of her regular partner

subtopic_detail: Type three female genital cutting identified at the booking visit in a primigravida at fourteen weeks who wants a vaginal birth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar at a booking visit for a 26-year-old primigravida at 14 weeks who arrived in Australia four years ago. She tells you through a professional interpreter that she was cut as a child, that passing urine takes a long time and that she has recurrent urinary infections.

She says she would like to give birth vaginally and asks what will happen. On examination the labia are fused with a narrowed posterior opening admitting one fingertip, the clitoris and labia minora are not identifiable, and the urethral meatus cannot be visualised. There is no scar tenderness and no keloid. Her pregnancy is otherwise uncomplicated and the dating ultrasound is consistent with her dates.

data_table.Examination: Fused labia with a narrowed vaginal opening admitting one fingertip, clitoris and labia minora not identifiable, urethral meatus not visualised, no keloid or scar tenderness, uterine size consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Dating ultrasound consistent with menstrual dates, booking bloods within normal limits, midstream urine culture grows Escherichia coli sensitive to nitrofurantoin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for her genital tract?

options.text: Plan deinfibulation during established labour in the first stage
Plan an elective caesarean section at thirty nine weeks gestation
Offer deinfibulation in the second trimester after counselling
Defer discussion of delivery options until the third trimester
Plan reinfibulation after the birth if she requests it at delivery

subtopic_detail: Failure of lactation with fatigue and dizziness six weeks after a postpartum haemorrhage requiring six units of red cells
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 32-year-old woman six weeks after the birth of her first baby. Her delivery was complicated by a postpartum haemorrhage of 3200 mL requiring six units of red cells and a period of hypotension before she was stabilised.

She says her milk never came in properly and she stopped trying to breastfeed at two weeks. She feels exhausted, cold and light headed when she stands up quickly, and she has not had a period. She scores 4 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale and says her mood is fine but her body is not. Her lying blood pressure is 102/64 mmHg falling to 84/52 mmHg on standing, and her ferritin has normalised since the transfusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg lying and 84/52 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale with dry skin, no goitre, breasts soft and non engorged, no axillary hair regrowth since delivery, uterus involuted, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115 to 155), ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30 to 200), sodium 131 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score 4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure thyroid stimulating hormone alone and review in four weeks
Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in four weeks
Measure ferritin and start oral iron, then review her in four weeks
Measure early morning cortisol, free thyroxine and prolactin together
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary before any bloods

subtopic_detail: Severe limb and back pain at twenty six weeks in a woman with haemoglobin SS disease whose oxygen saturation and chest examination are normal
stem: A 29-year-old at 26 weeks in her second pregnancy has haemoglobin SS disease. Since yesterday she has had severe pain in both thighs and her lower back, worse than she manages at home with paracetamol. She has no fever or breathlessness.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 /min, BP 118/70 mmHg, SpO2 98% in air, T 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Distressed by pain, chest clear with equal air entry
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 79 g/L at her recorded baseline, reticulocytes appropriately raised, CRP 8 mg/L, cardiotocograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her pain?

options.text: Admit for intravenous morphine with hydration
Admit for intramuscular pethidine with hydration
Admit for oral paracetamol alone with hydration
Admit for urgent exchange transfusion and hydration
Discharge on oral oxycodone with hydration advice

subtopic_detail: An anti-Kell antibody titre of 1 in 16 at twenty weeks with a partner heterozygous for the Kell antigen
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman at 20 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her antibody screen at booking detected anti-Kell, and the repeat titre today is 1 in 16.

She received two units of red cells after a retained placenta in her first pregnancy, and that baby was well with no jaundice. Her blood group is O RhD positive, so anti-D is not relevant to her care. Genotyping shows her partner is heterozygous for the Kell antigen, and cell free fetal DNA testing reports the fetus as Kell antigen positive. The anatomy ultrasound today is structurally normal with no ascites, no skin oedema and a normal amniotic fluid volume.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 20 cm consistent with dates, fetal movements reported as normal, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Maternal blood group O RhD positive, antibody screen positive for anti-Kell with a titre of 1 in 16, paternal genotype heterozygous for the Kell antigen, cell free fetal DNA reports the fetus as Kell antigen positive, anatomy ultrasound structurally normal with no ascites or skin oedema and normal amniotic fluid volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for fetal surveillance?

options.text: Repeat the antibody titre monthly and intervene when it reaches 1 in 32
Arrange serial amniocentesis for amniotic fluid bilirubin from 24 weeks
Give anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 and 34 weeks and continue routine care
Plan delivery at 37 weeks with no additional antenatal surveillance
Refer for serial middle cerebral artery Doppler velocity surveillance

subtopic_detail: Immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G negative parvovirus serology at sixteen weeks in a childcare worker exposed to slapped cheek rash
stem:
You are the obstetrician seeing a 30-year-old childcare worker at 16 weeks in her second pregnancy. Three weeks ago several children in her room developed a bright red rash on both cheeks, and a fortnight ago she had two days of aching joints in her hands and a mild fever that she put down to a virus.

She feels well now and reports normal fetal movements for her gestation. She asks whether the outbreak at work could harm the baby. Her serology taken this week reports immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G negative for parvovirus B19, with rubella immunoglobulin G immune and cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin G positive from booking. An ultrasound today shows a structurally normal fetus with no ascites, no pericardial effusion, no skin oedema and normal amniotic fluid.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height consistent with dates, no rash or joint swelling currently, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Parvovirus B19 immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G negative, rubella immunoglobulin G immune, cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin G positive from booking bloods, full blood count within normal limits, ultrasound shows a structurally normal fetus with no ascites, no pericardial effusion, no skin oedema and normal amniotic fluid volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure her and continue routine antenatal care without extra surveillance
Offer termination of pregnancy because of the risk of fetal abnormality
Arrange weekly ultrasound for fetal anaemia and hydrops for twelve weeks
Give intravenous immunoglobulin to the mother and continue routine care
Arrange amniocentesis for viral nucleic acid testing and then reassess

subtopic_detail: Fever with diarrhoea and backache at thirty weeks after eating soft cheese and pre prepared salad with a negative urine dipstick
stem: A 33-year-old woman at 30 weeks has two days of fever, muscle aches, headache and loose stools. She ate a soft cheese platter and a pre prepared supermarket salad five days ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 116 /min; BP 106/62 mmHg; T 38.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Flushed and unwell; chest clear; uterus soft and non-tender; urine dipstick negative
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.6 x10^9/L, CRP 96 mg/L; cardiotocograph baseline 165 /min with reduced variability, new from previous traces

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Blood cultures and oral azithromycin pending the results
Blood cultures and empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin
Blood cultures and oral cefalexin pending the culture result
Stool culture with antibiotics withheld pending the result
Blood cultures and empirical intravenous ceftriaxone today

subtopic_detail: Hirsutism and oligomenorrhoea with an early follicular 17 hydroxyprogesterone of 9 nmol/L in a twenty three year old
stem: A 23-year-old woman has had slowly progressive coarse dark hair on the upper lip, chin and lower abdomen since she was 15, with periods every six to ten weeks. Her voice is unchanged.

data_table.Examination: BMI 22 kg/m2, Ferriman-Gallwey score 14; no acanthosis nigricans or striae; normal clitoral size, no temporal balding
data_table.Investigations: Early follicular 17 hydroxyprogesterone 9 nmol/L at 0800 (less than 6), mildly raised testosterone and DHEAS, normal prolactin and TSH

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start the combined oral contraceptive pill and review in six months
Start metformin with lifestyle support and review in six months
Pelvic ultrasound to count antral follicles and then reassess
Adrenocorticotrophic hormone stimulation test before any treatment
Twenty four hour urinary free cortisol and then reassess her

subtopic_detail: Screening for gestational diabetes at twenty six weeks two years after sleeve gastrectomy in a woman with post prandial dizziness
stem:
You are the obstetrician seeing a 34-year-old woman at 26 weeks in her first pregnancy. She had a sleeve gastrectomy two years ago and her weight has been stable for the past year at a body mass index of 29 kg per square metre.

She tells you that if she eats anything sweet on an empty stomach she feels hot, shaky and light headed about twenty minutes later, and then washed out an hour or so after that. She takes the multivitamin, iron and vitamin B12 supplements prescribed by the bariatric service. Her booking glycated haemoglobin was 5.2 per cent, her fetal growth is on the 45th centile and her amniotic fluid volume is normal. She has been booked for a glucose tolerance test tomorrow morning and asks whether she should attend.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29 kg per square metre, symphysis fundal height 26 cm consistent with dates, well healed laparoscopic port sites
data_table.Investigations: Booking glycated haemoglobin 5.2 per cent (less than 6.5), haemoglobin 118 g/L (115 to 155), ferritin 42 micrograms/L (30 to 200), vitamin B12 within normal limits, growth ultrasound at the 45th centile with normal amniotic fluid volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to screening her for gestational diabetes?

options.text: Arrange one week of fasting and post prandial capillary glucose monitoring
Proceed with the standard 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks
Measure glycated haemoglobin alone and repeat the measurement at 32 weeks
Measure a random plasma glucose alone and repeat the test at 32 weeks
Omit screening because bariatric surgery removes the risk of diabetes

subtopic_detail: Toxoplasma seroconversion detected at eleven weeks on repeat serology with low avidity immunoglobulin G
stem:
You are the obstetrician seeing a 29-year-old woman at 11 weeks in her first pregnancy. She had serology taken privately before conception that was negative for toxoplasma immunoglobulin G, and a repeat panel taken last week because of a two week illness with tender neck glands and fatigue.

She keeps two cats and has been emptying the litter tray herself, and she gardens without gloves. The repeat serology is immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G positive with a low avidity index, and the reference laboratory reports this as consistent with infection acquired within the last three months. She feels well now. Ultrasound today shows a structurally normal fetus with a crown rump length consistent with dates.

data_table.Examination: Small mobile non-tender posterior cervical lymph nodes, no rash, no hepatosplenomegaly, uterus consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Preconception toxoplasma immunoglobulin G negative, current toxoplasma immunoglobulin M positive and immunoglobulin G positive with a low avidity index, full blood count within normal limits, ultrasound reports a structurally normal fetus with crown rump length consistent with dates

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Start oral azithromycin and arrange monthly ultrasound until delivery
Start pyrimethamine with sulfadiazine and folinic acid immediately now
Offer termination of pregnancy given the risk of congenital infection
Reassure and continue routine care since maternal infection is benign
Start spiramycin and arrange amniocentesis for nucleic acid testing

subtopic_detail: Bleeding after intercourse in a woman whose most recent primary screening test for human papillomavirus was negative, with a fleshy growth visible at the cervical os
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34-year-old woman who has had spotting after intercourse on most occasions for the past four months, and occasionally a small amount of brown loss between periods. Her cycles are otherwise regular and not heavy.

She has had two vaginal births, uses condoms for contraception and has never smoked. Her cervical screening test 14 months ago was reported as human papillomavirus not detected. On speculum examination there is a smooth fleshy pedunculated lesion about 12 mm across protruding from the external os, and touching it with a swab reproduces a small amount of bleeding. The cervix is otherwise smooth, the vaginal walls look healthy and there is no abnormal discharge. Bimanual examination shows a normal sized mobile non-tender uterus with no adnexal mass.

data_table.Examination: Smooth pedunculated 12 mm lesion protruding from the external cervical os that bleeds on contact, remainder of the cervix smooth with no friability, healthy vaginal walls, uterus normal size mobile and non-tender, no adnexal mass or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test 14 months ago reported human papillomavirus not detected, urine pregnancy test negative today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Repeat the primary human papillomavirus screening test today
Prescribe tranexamic acid and review her again in three months
Remove the lesion and send it for histological examination
Take endocervical swabs and treat for pelvic inflammatory disease
Arrange transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial sampling first

subtopic_detail: Antenatal serology at twelve weeks showing no protective antibody against rubella in a woman with no record of childhood immunisation
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing the results of the first antenatal visit for a 27-year-old woman at 12 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy. She arrived in Australia as a teenager and has no immunisation records from her country of birth.

She is well, has no rash and reports no recent contact with anyone unwell. Her booking bloods show rubella IgG below the protective threshold with rubella IgM not detected, and her varicella IgG is protective. Hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology are all negative, her blood group is O positive with no atypical antibodies, and her full blood count is within normal limits. She asks what should be done about the rubella result.

data_table.Investigations: Rubella IgG below the protective threshold with rubella IgM not detected, varicella IgG protective, hepatitis B surface antigen negative, hepatitis C antibody negative, syphilis serology negative, human immunodeficiency virus serology negative, blood group O positive with antibody screen negative, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her rubella status?

options.text: Reassure her, as the absent IgM excludes any risk to this pregnancy
Give measles, mumps and rubella vaccine at her next antenatal visit
Give rubella immunoglobulin now and repeat her serology in four weeks
Advise avoiding contact with unwell children and vaccinate after birth
Repeat the rubella IgG in the third trimester before making any plan

subtopic_detail: Choosing between maternal immunisation in late pregnancy and a monoclonal antibody for the newborn to protect an infant born in the middle of winter
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in an antenatal clinic in June seeing a 31-year-old woman at 30 weeks gestation in her second pregnancy. Her first child was admitted at 7 weeks of age with bronchiolitis and needed two days of oxygen, and she wants to know what can be done to protect this baby.

This pregnancy has been uncomplicated with normal growth on her 28 week scan and a normal glucose tolerance test. She has already received her pertussis containing vaccine at 22 weeks and her influenza vaccine in April. She has no allergies and takes only pregnancy multivitamins. She plans a vaginal birth at term at her local hospital and intends to breastfeed.

data_table.Investigations: Growth scan at 28 weeks with estimated fetal weight on the 55th centile and normal liquor volume, oral glucose tolerance test within normal limits, pertussis containing vaccine given at 22 weeks, influenza vaccine given in April

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about protecting her baby from respiratory syncytial virus?

options.text: No protection is available until the infant reaches six months of age
Offer the maternal vaccine now, or the infant antibody after birth
Defer any decision until the baby shows signs of a respiratory illness
Give the maternal vaccine immediately after the birth of the baby
Rely on exclusive breastfeeding and avoiding contact with older children

subtopic_detail: Burning nipple pain that lasts after every feed with shiny flaking skin on both areolae and white patches inside the baby's mouth
stem: A 29-year-old woman is 5 weeks postpartum. Both nipples burn partway through each feed and for 20 to 30 minutes afterwards. The pain began a week ago, after settling at two weeks.

data_table.Examination: Nipples and areolae shiny, pink and finely flaking, no cracks; latch good on review three days ago; no lump, wedge erythema or fever
data_table.Infant: Adherent white plaques on the buccal mucosa and tongue that do not wipe away

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral flucloxacillin and arrange a breast ultrasound this week
Refer for further attachment review and supply nipple shields
Advise expressing and cup feeding until the pain has settled
Refer her urgently for a punch biopsy of the affected areolar skin
Treat mother and baby together and continue breastfeeding

subtopic_detail: A perineal repair on day seven after birth with gaping edges, surrounding redness and offensive discharge but no collection on examination
stem: A 26-year-old woman is seen on day 7 after a normal birth with a repaired second degree tear. Perineal pain has increased since day 4, with offensive discharge and a sense that the wound has separated.

data_table.Examination: Repair gaping over 2 cm with surrounding erythema and induration, thin offensive discharge, no fluctuant collection or crepitus; lochia not offensive
data_table.Investigations: WCC 13.8 x10^9/L, CRP 62 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Remove the remaining sutures and arrange daily nurse packing
Reassure her that separation at this stage heals without treatment
Take her to theatre today for immediate resuturing of the perineum
Start oral antibiotics with wound care and review in two days
Pelvic ultrasound and intravenous antibiotics for presumed endometritis

subtopic_detail: A dilated fluid filled tube on the left seen on scan before a first cycle of in vitro fertilisation in a woman with past chlamydial infection
stem: A 33-year-old woman with three years of primary infertility is starting her first cycle of in vitro fertilisation. She had chlamydial pelvic infection in her twenties.

data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: 4 cm elongated fluid filled structure with incomplete septations in the left adnexa, separate from a normal left ovary; cavity and right adnexa normal. Hysterosalpingogram: free right spill, dilated non-filling left tube

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before embryo transfer?

options.text: Remove the affected tube laparoscopically before proceeding to transfer
Proceed with transfer and reassess the left adnexa afterwards
Aspirate the fluid transvaginally at the time of oocyte collection
Give a course of doxycycline and repeat her ultrasound in six weeks
Attempt to reopen the distal end of the tube to restore its patency

subtopic_detail: A gestational sac sitting within the lower anterior uterine wall at the site of two previous operative scars with thin overlying myometrium
stem: A 36-year-old woman at 7 weeks has light vaginal bleeding and mild suprapubic discomfort. She has had two caesarean sections and is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with mild suprapubic tenderness, closed cervical os
data_table.Investigations: Beta hCG 9400 IU/L
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: Empty cavity and cervical canal; sac with fetal pole and cardiac activity within the lower anterior myometrium at the scar; myometrium between sac and bladder 2 mm; peritrophoblastic flow; normal ovaries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange suction curettage of the cavity on the emergency list
Give a single intramuscular dose of methotrexate with weekly levels
Refer to a specialist unit for planned treatment in theatre
Observe with serial scans, since many such pregnancies relocate
Perform laparoscopic salpingectomy and send the tube for histology

subtopic_detail: Bleeding years after the last period with a thickened endometrium and a solid ovarian mass whose inhibin B is markedly raised
stem: A 58-year-old woman whose periods stopped at 51 has had painless vaginal bleeding on and off for three months. She has taken no hormone therapy and no tamoxifen.

data_table.Examination: Firm mobile mass arising from the left side of the pelvis
data_table.Investigations: Endometrial thickness 16 mm and a 7 cm solid left ovarian mass with internal vascularity; pipelle shows simple hyperplasia without atypia; CA125 38 kU/L (less than 35); inhibin B markedly raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Hysteroscopy and repeat endometrial sampling before deciding
Colonoscopy and gastroscopy to find a primary bowel tumour
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system and rescan in six months
Interval imaging of the ovarian mass in three months' time
Refer for gynaecological oncology review and surgical staging

subtopic_detail: Three mid pregnancy losses in a woman whose uterus shows a fundal indentation dividing the cavity with a normal external contour
stem: A 30-year-old woman is referred after three losses at 17, 19 and 16 weeks, each preceded by painless cervical dilatation over a few hours. She has no living children.

data_table.Investigations: Three dimensional transvaginal ultrasound: smooth convex external fundal contour with an internal fundal indentation extending more than half way to the internal os, dividing the cavity; normal ovaries; antiphospholipid antibodies negative on two occasions twelve weeks apart; thyroid function, HbA1c and parental karyotypes normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Hysteroscopic division of the dividing tissue before conceiving
Elective cervical suture at twelve weeks in her next pregnancy
Low dose aspirin with low molecular weight heparin once pregnant
Abdominal reconstruction to unify the two uterine horns
Supportive early pregnancy care with serial scans, no intervention

subtopic_detail: A deepest pool of fifteen millimetres at thirty nine weeks with growth on the fiftieth centile, normal artery waveforms and no membrane rupture
stem: A 28-year-old woman at 39+2 weeks in her first pregnancy is referred with a symphysis fundal height 3 cm below expected. Fetal movements are normal and she denies leaking fluid.

data_table.Examination: Cephalic presentation; no pooling on speculum, none on coughing; cervix closed
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: estimated fetal weight on the 50th centile, deepest amniotic fluid pool 15 mm, normal umbilical artery and middle cerebral artery Dopplers; cardiotocograph normal with accelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Twice weekly cardiotocography and rescan in one week
Induction of labour with continuous monitoring in labour
Maternal oral hydration and repeat the scan in 48 hours
Caesarean section today because of the reduced liquor
Routine midwifery care with review at 41 weeks

subtopic_detail: Solid masses on both ovaries with ascites in a woman whose gastric biopsy shows cells containing mucin that displaces the nucleus
stem: A 44-year-old woman has four months of bloating, early satiety and 6 kg weight loss, and a year of epigastric discomfort treated as reflux.

data_table.Examination: Shifting dullness, firm mass in each iliac fossa
data_table.Computed tomography: Bilateral solid ovarian masses 9 cm and 8 cm, moderate ascites, diffuse gastric wall thickening with perigastric nodes
data_table.Investigations: CA125 210 kU/L (less than 35), carcinoembryonic antigen raised
data_table.Gastroscopy: Rigid infiltrated gastric body; biopsy poorly cohesive adenocarcinoma with mucin displacing the nucleus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange image guided biopsy of an ovarian mass before treatment
Perform therapeutic paracentesis and review her again in four weeks
Proceed to primary debulking surgery with abdominal hysterectomy
Refer to the upper gastrointestinal multidisciplinary team for systemic therapy
Start carboplatin and paclitaxel for epithelial ovarian cancer

subtopic_detail: No periods by sixteen with well developed breasts but almost no pubic or underarm hair, a short blind vagina and no uterus on scan
stem: A 16-year-old has never had a period and has no cyclical pain. She is 174 cm, above her mid-parental centile. Breasts are Tanner stage 4; pubic and axillary hair are Tanner stage 1.

data_table.Examination: Normal female external genitalia, blind ending vagina 4 cm with no cervix, soft swellings in both inguinal canals
data_table.Investigations: Imaging reports absent uterus and upper vagina and no pelvic ovaries; testosterone in the normal adult male range, luteinising hormone mildly raised, renal tract normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange surgical creation of a vaginal canal this year
Request renal tract imaging and spinal radiographs
Refer to a specialist multidisciplinary service after karyotype
Arrange laparoscopic removal of both inguinal gonads
Start cyclical oestrogen and progestogen for menstruation

subtopic_detail: Monthly lower abdominal pain and difficulty passing urine in a fourteen year old who has never menstruated
stem: A 14-year-old girl has six months of lower abdominal pain for three days every four weeks and has never menstruated. For two days she has passed small volumes of urine frequently, and today none at all.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5, tender suprapubic mass below the umbilicus, bulging bluish membrane at the introitus
data_table.Investigations: Bladder scan 620 mL, pregnancy test negative, ultrasound shows a fluid filled vagina above a normal uterus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Insert a catheter and refer for surgical incision of the membrane
Aspirate the collection with a wide bore needle for culture
Start a continuous combined oral contraceptive and review in three months
Arrange karyotype and serum testosterone before deciding management
Arrange pelvic magnetic resonance imaging before any intervention

subtopic_detail: Fever with myalgia and diarrhoea at twenty eight weeks after eating soft cheese and pre-prepared salad
stem: A 31-year-old woman at 28 weeks in her first pregnancy has three days of fever, myalgia and loose stools, with no cough, dysuria or rash. Five days ago she ate soft cheese and pre-prepared coleslaw.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 104 /min, T 38.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 158 /min
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non-tender, chest clear, cardiotocograph normal
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.2 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 62 mg/L, midstream urine clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Send stool for culture and review if she is still febrile in 48 hours
Take blood cultures and start intravenous benzylpenicillin with gentamicin
Start oral azithromycin and arrange a shielded chest radiograph
Give intramuscular ceftriaxone and arrange outpatient review tomorrow
Give intramuscular betamethasone and admit without antimicrobial therapy

subtopic_detail: Pain over the pubic symphysis and posterior pelvis limiting walking at twenty six weeks in an otherwise well pregnancy
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 26 weeks in her second pregnancy has six weeks of pain across the front of the pelvis and both buttocks, worst turning in bed and climbing stairs. She now waddles and takes paracetamol most days.

data_table.Examination: Tender over the pubic symphysis and both sacroiliac joints, pain on active straight leg raise, full painless hip movement, normal power and reflexes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Advise rest from work and avoid weight bearing until delivery
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the spine and sacroiliac joints
Refer to a pelvic health physiotherapist for exercises and a belt
Prescribe a short course of a non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug
Book an elective caesarean at 39 weeks for her pelvic symptoms

subtopic_detail: Severe nipple pain with shallow attachment on day nine postpartum where feeding has not yet been formally assessed
stem: A 27-year-old nine days after her first vaginal birth has stabbing pain each time the baby attaches, easing part way through the feed. Her sister says the baby has a tongue tie. There is no breast lump or fever.

data_table.Examination: Wedge shaped compression line on both nipples with a fissure at the left base; tongue elevates to the mid mouth and extends past the lower gum
data_table.Investigations: Weight 3420 g, birthweight 3390 g, eight wet nappies daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer the baby for frenotomy on the visible membrane
Arrange a lactation consultant assessment of attachment and transfer
Prescribe miconazole gel and antifungal cream for both nipples
Advise expressing and bottle feeding for two weeks to heal
Commence domperidone and offer formula top ups after feeds

subtopic_detail: Intrauterine device visible below the gestational sac on ultrasound at seven weeks in a continuing pregnancy
stem:
You are the doctor in an early pregnancy assessment clinic seeing a 33-year-old woman with a positive pregnancy test who has a copper intrauterine device in place, inserted two years ago. She has two children and wishes to continue this pregnancy.

She has had light spotting for two days but no pain, fever or discharge. She could not feel her threads when she checked last month and did not seek review at the time.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, speculum examination showing a closed cervix with threads visible at the external os and a small amount of old blood in the vagina, uterus consistent with dates on bimanual examination, no adnexal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound showing a single intrauterine gestational sac with a fetal pole and cardiac activity at 7 weeks 1 day, the intrauterine device lying in the lower uterine cavity below the gestational sac, no adnexal mass, no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Give a prophylactic course of oral doxycycline and defer any decision about the device until the second trimester scan
Leave the device in place and arrange serial ultrasound surveillance for chorioamnionitis through the second trimester
Arrange hysteroscopic retrieval of the device under general anaesthesia on the next available elective operating list
Remove the device now by gentle traction on the visible threads, having counselled her about the small risk of miscarriage
Refer her for uterine artery Doppler assessment at twelve weeks and manage the pregnancy as high risk without intervention

subtopic_detail: A tense tender vulval swelling with fluctuance at the posterior introitus in a woman with a second episode in two years
stem: A 28-year-old woman has three days of increasing pain at the right vaginal introitus, now too severe to sit. A similar swelling on the same side two years ago was incised and recurred within four months.

data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant 4 cm swelling at the right posterior introitus, skin thinned at one point, no surrounding induration, cervix healthy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Excision of the gland under general anaesthesia with histology
Incision and drainage under local anaesthesia with gauze packing
Oral amoxicillin with clavulanic acid for seven days and review
Marsupialisation on the next elective list, with analgesia meanwhile
Incision under local anaesthesia with a balloon catheter left for four weeks

subtopic_detail: Right sided abdominal pain with vomiting at twenty six weeks where ultrasound of the appendix is non diagnostic
stem: A 30-year-old woman at 26 weeks has 18 hours of central abdominal pain that has moved to the right side, with nausea and vomiting.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 106 /min, BP 114/70 mmHg, T 37.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Guarding in the right flank at the umbilical level, uterus non-tender
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.8 x10^9/L (5.5-15.0 in pregnancy), neutrophils 14.1 x10^9/L, CRP 88 mg/L; ultrasound appendix not visualised, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen without gadolinium
Admit for fluids, serial examination and repeat markers in 12 hours
Intravenous antibiotics with non operative management and repeat ultrasound
Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast
Intramuscular betamethasone and transfer to a tertiary centre before imaging

subtopic_detail: Continuous urinary leakage beginning three days after a prolonged obstructed labour with a stillbirth
stem: A 24-year-old woman gave birth three weeks ago overseas after three days of obstructed labour; the baby was stillborn. Since day four she has leaked urine continuously, day and night, with no preceding urge.

data_table.Examination: Clear fluid pooling in the vagina; 1 cm area of tissue loss in the anterior vaginal wall below the bladder neck; excoriated inner thighs
data_table.Investigations: Methylene blue in the bladder stains a vaginal swab blue; creatinine 74 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for surgical repair on this week's gynaecology operating list
Indwelling catheter for free drainage and urogynaecology referral
Anticholinergic therapy with urodynamic studies in the coming weeks
Oral trimethoprim for seven days, reviewing once the infection clears
Pelvic floor muscle training with physiotherapy review in three months

subtopic_detail: Planning intrapartum care at booking for a woman with type three female genital cutting in her first pregnancy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar at a booking visit for a 26-year-old woman at 13 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy, who came to Australia as a child. Through a professional interpreter she says she was cut as a girl in her country of birth and that passing urine takes several minutes.

She has intercourse with difficulty and has never had a cervical screening test. She asks what will happen when the baby is born and says her mother expects her to be closed again afterwards.

data_table.Examination: Fused labial tissue forming a horizontal bridge across the introitus with a posterior opening of approximately 8 mm, clitoral tissue not visible, no vulval ulceration or discharge, no inclusion cyst palpable, abdominal examination consistent with 13 weeks gestation
data_table.Investigations: Booking bloods unremarkable with haemoglobin 118 g/L (110 to 140), dating ultrasound consistent with 13 weeks gestation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for her care?

options.text: Book an elective caesarean section at 39 weeks as the safest mode of birth and counsel her accordingly at this visit
Plan deinfibulation in the first stage of labour under epidural analgesia, with no antenatal genital procedure offered
Offer antenatal deinfibulation in the second trimester and document that reinfibulation will not be performed after the birth
Make a mandatory report to the state child protection service about the procedure she underwent as a child overseas
Defer any genital examination or discussion until 36 weeks so that she can settle into antenatal care with her midwife

subtopic_detail: Inability to void 14 hours after an instrumental birth with a palpable bladder and a large residual volume
stem: A 32-year-old woman gave birth 14 hours ago by forceps with an epidural and a repaired second degree tear. She has not passed urine since and cannot tell when she needs to go.

data_table.Examination: Bladder palpable midway to the umbilicus; perineal repair intact with oedema; lower limb power and sensation recovered
data_table.Investigations: Bladder scan residual volume 780 mL; urine dipstick negative for nitrites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound and urology review before draining the bladder
Single in and out catheterisation now, rescanning her in 6 hours
Oral bethanechol to stimulate the detrusor, reassessing after two doses
Oral cefalexin for presumed infection with a repeat scan in 4 hours
Indwelling catheter for 24 to 48 hours then a formal trial of void

subtopic_detail: An asymptomatic simple ovarian cyst of eight centimetres found at the dating scan in the first trimester
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28-year-old woman at 12 weeks gestation whose dating ultrasound reported an ovarian cyst. She has no pain and had no symptoms before the scan, and the pregnancy was conceived spontaneously.

She has heard that the cyst could twist and asks whether it should be taken out before it causes trouble. She has no personal or family history of ovarian or breast cancer.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender with no palpable mass, uterus not palpable abdominally, no ascites, no supraclavicular or inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound showing a single intrauterine pregnancy at 12 weeks 2 days, a right ovarian cyst of 8.2 cm that is unilocular and anechoic with thin smooth walls, no solid components, no papillary projections and no internal vascularity on colour Doppler, left ovary normal, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange laparoscopic cystectomy in the second trimester to eliminate the risk of torsion later in the pregnancy
Measure serum cancer antigen 125 now and refer her to gynaecological oncology if the level is above the standard cut off
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis without contrast to characterise the cyst before deciding on management
Plan conservative management with a repeat ultrasound in the second trimester and advice about symptoms of torsion
Arrange ultrasound guided aspiration of the cyst in the clinic and send the aspirated fluid for cytological examination

subtopic_detail: Escalating perineal pain with a tense unilateral vulval swelling four hours after a vaginal birth and a falling haemoglobin
stem: A 26-year-old woman gave birth four hours ago by vacuum extraction with a mediolateral episiotomy. She is asking for more analgesia despite paracetamol, a suppository and oxycodone. Vaginal loss has been light.

data_table.Examination: Tense tender purple 8 cm swelling of the right labium majus; episiotomy repair intact with no bleeding; uterus firm and central
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 82 g/L, from 121 g/L on admission; INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ice pack, intravenous morphine and reassessment in two hours
Intramuscular ergometrine 500 microgram and an oxytocin infusion
Transfuse two units of packed red cells and repeat the blood count
Urgent computed tomography angiogram and consider embolisation
Theatre for evacuation of the haematoma and ligation of bleeding vessels

subtopic_detail: New atrial fibrillation with pulmonary oedema at thirty weeks in a woman with previously undiagnosed rheumatic mitral stenosis
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 30 weeks in her first pregnancy cannot lie flat. She had rheumatic fever as a child overseas and has been breathless for three weeks. Tonight her heart raced and she became acutely short of breath.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 156 /min irregularly irregular, BP 102/66 mmHg, RR 32 /min, SpO2 90% in air
data_table.Examination: Crackles to the mid zones, raised jugular venous pressure, opening snap with apical diastolic murmur
data_table.Investigations: ECG atrial fibrillation; radiograph interstitial oedema; echocardiogram mitral valve area 1.0 cm2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Intravenous metoprolol, furosemide and therapeutic enoxaparin
Intravenous digoxin loading, then reassess her respiratory status
Emergency caesarean section under general anaesthesia
Synchronised cardioversion under sedation with fetal monitoring
Intravenous fluid bolus to improve diastolic filling

subtopic_detail: Intensely itchy raised lesions arising within the abdominal stretch marks at 36 weeks with the navel spared
stem: A 34-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 36 weeks has five days of an intensely itchy rash that began in the stretch marks on her lower abdomen and has spread to her thighs and buttocks.

data_table.Examination: Urticated papules and plaques arising within the abdominal striae, with a clear rim of uninvolved skin around the umbilicus; no bullae
data_table.Investigations: Liver function tests normal, serum bile acids 4 micromol/L (less than 10)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid with repeat bile acids and liver tests in a week
Induction of labour at 37 weeks because symptoms will not settle
Skin biopsy with immunofluorescence and systemic corticosteroids meanwhile
A potent topical corticosteroid ointment with emollients
A topical antifungal cream with antenatal review in two weeks

subtopic_detail: Disabling headache on the second postnatal day that is present on sitting up and gone within minutes of lying flat
stem: Two days after a vaginal birth with an epidural, a 29-year-old woman has a severe headache that starts within a minute of sitting up and goes when she lies flat. The anaesthetic record documents a dural puncture at insertion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82 /min, BP 118/72 mmHg, T 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No neck stiffness or papilloedema, cranial nerves intact, no focal weakness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Bed rest, paracetamol, oral caffeine and fluids, review in two days
Urgent computed tomography of the brain with venography today
Intravenous magnesium sulfate with antihypertensive therapy
Diagnostic lumbar puncture to measure the opening pressure
Refer to the anaesthetic team for an epidural blood patch

subtopic_detail: Constant localised pain over a known uterine fibroid at 26 weeks with a low grade temperature and a quiet cervix
stem: A 33-year-old at 26 weeks has two days of constant right sided abdominal pain and has felt hot and shivery. An 8 cm fibroid was documented on her 20 week scan. Fetal movements are normal.

data_table.Examination: Tenderness localised over a firm mass in the uterus, cervix long and closed
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.4 x10^9/L, CRP 28 mg/L, urine clear; ultrasound 8 cm fibroid with cystic change and reduced vascularity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for myomectomy before the inflammatory response worsens
Corticosteroids and nifedipine tocolysis for established preterm labour
Intravenous ampicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole for chorioamnionitis
Admit for paracetamol, a short opioid course and hydration
Diagnostic laparoscopy, since appendicitis cannot be excluded

subtopic_detail: Daily non prescribed oxycodone use disclosed at booking by a woman at 14 weeks who wants to stop straight away
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in an antenatal clinic booking a 26-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation in her second pregnancy. She discloses that she has been taking around 100 mg of non prescribed oxycodone daily for the past two years and that she injects nothing.

She tells you she is determined to be completely off everything before the baby arrives and asks you to help her stop this week. She has no medical comorbidities, her booking bloods including hepatitis and human immunodeficiency virus serology are pending, and her first child lives with her and her partner.

data_table.Examination: No stigmata of intravenous drug use, no needle marks, chest clear, abdomen soft with a uterus palpable just above the symphysis pubis, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound confirming a single live intrauterine pregnancy consistent with 14 weeks gestation, full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 42 micrograms/L (30 to 200)

lead_in: What would you first recommend to her?

options.text: Make an immediate child protection notification about the unborn baby and the older child before discussing treatment options with her
Admit her for a supervised rapid inpatient detoxification over the coming week while the pregnancy is still in the second trimester
Commence oral naltrexone once she has stopped opioids for several days in order to block any further effect from opioid use
Support her plan to cease abruptly this week with symptomatic medication only and review her in the antenatal clinic in two weeks
Refer her urgently to a specialist drug and alcohol service for stabilisation on opioid agonist treatment alongside her antenatal care

subtopic_detail: Third episode of severe right upper abdominal pain after fatty food at 18 weeks with gallstones and normal liver tests
stem: A 30-year-old woman at 18 weeks has recovered from her third episode of severe right upper quadrant pain. Each began an hour or two after a fatty meal, lasted about four hours and faded completely.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender between episodes, Murphy sign negative, not jaundiced
data_table.Investigations: Liver function tests normal, lipase 32 U/L, white cell count 9.8 x10^9/L, C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L
data_table.Ultrasound: Multiple mobile gallstones, normal gallbladder wall thickness, common bile duct 4 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Low fat diet and analgesia, deferring surgery until six weeks after birth
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with sphincterotomy to clear the duct
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this second trimester after counselling
Oral ursodeoxycholic acid to dissolve the gallstones and prevent recurrence
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography before deciding management

subtopic_detail: Absent periods at sixteen with normal breasts, very sparse pubic hair and no uterus seen on pelvic ultrasound
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 16-year-old girl referred because she has never had a period. Her mother reports that her breasts developed normally from about the age of eleven.

She is well, plays netball at a competitive level, has never been underweight and reports no headaches or visual symptoms. She has never been sexually active and has had no cyclical abdominal pain.

data_table.Examination: Height 175 cm, weight 64 kg, Tanner stage 5 breast development, Tanner stage 1 to 2 pubic and axillary hair, no clitoromegaly, no acne or facial hair, external genitalia otherwise normal in appearance, no palpable abdominal or inguinal masses, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound reporting no uterus identified with no structures in either adnexa clearly identified as ovaries, follicle stimulating hormone 6.2 IU/L (2 to 10 follicular), prolactin within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to define the Mullerian anatomy and search for any obstructed uterine remnant
Administer a progestogen challenge and interpret whether a withdrawal bleed occurs before ordering any further hormonal investigations
Measure a serum testosterone level and request a karyotype, and arrange review in a service with adolescent gynaecology experience
Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to induce regular withdrawal bleeding and review her symptoms in the clinic in three months
Reassure her that constitutional delay is likely given her athletic training and review her again in six months if periods have not started

subtopic_detail: Fever with hypotension and offensive bleeding three days into a first trimester loss with an open cervical os
stem: A 24-year-old woman at 10 weeks has had heavy bleeding for three days and, for twelve hours, rigors, offensive loss and constant lower abdominal pain. She is drowsy after 2 L of crystalloid.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 /min, BP 86/48 mmHg, RR 28 /min, T 39.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Exquisitely tender uterus, purulent discharge, products of conception at an open cervical os
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.6 mmol/L, WCC 22.8 x10^9/L, platelets 96 x10^9/L, INR 1.4, creatinine 138 micromol/L

lead_in: Cultures are taken and antibiotics started. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent hysterectomy as the definitive source control procedure
Reassessment for evacuation after forty eight hours of antibiotics
Misoprostol to complete the miscarriage without surgery
Urgent suction evacuation of the uterus in theatre now
Transfer to a tertiary centre before any procedure

subtopic_detail: Empty uterus on transvaginal scan with a beta human chorionic gonadotrophin that rises by only twelve per cent in 48 hours
stem: A 27-year-old woman with six weeks of amenorrhoea has two days of light spotting and mild cramping. She has no shoulder tip pain and lives close to the hospital.

data_table.Examination: Mild suprapubic tenderness, no adnexal mass, closed cervical os
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterus, endometrium 9 mm, no adnexal mass, no free fluid. Beta-hCG 1450 IU/L, then 1624 IU/L 48 hours later

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate today with beta-hCG on days 4 and 7
Repeat transvaginal ultrasound and beta-hCG in 48 hours with return advice
Diagnostic laparoscopy today to locate and treat the pregnancy surgically
Uterine evacuation with histology to look for chorionic villi in the specimen
Routine antenatal booking, as the pregnancy is too early to see

subtopic_detail: Gestational sac implanted within the anterior lower segment scar of two previous caesareans with cardiac activity present
stem: A 32-year-old woman with two previous caesarean sections attends at 7 weeks for a dating scan. She has no bleeding or pain and asks whether the pregnancy can continue.

data_table.Ultrasound: Empty cavity and cervical canal with the sac in the anterior lower segment at the previous scar; 2 mm myometrium between sac and bladder; cardiac activity present; prominent peritrophoblastic flow

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Suction curettage on the next available list, with tissue for histology
Expectant management with weekly beta-hCG and repeat scans
Refer to a tertiary unit for intragestational injection or resection
Single intramuscular methotrexate as an outpatient with day 4 and 7 levels
Counsel that hysterectomy is the safest option and arrange it in due course

subtopic_detail: Rapidly enlarging solid adnexal mass in a nineteen year old with a raised lactate dehydrogenase and normal alpha fetoprotein
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 19-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner with three weeks of increasing abdominal swelling and a dragging discomfort in her lower abdomen. She has noticed her jeans no longer do up.

Her periods have been regular and she has never been pregnant. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. She asks directly whether she will still be able to have children.

data_table.Examination: Firm non-tender mass arising from the pelvis and palpable to the level of the umbilicus, no ascites clinically detectable, no inguinal or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, no signs of virilisation
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis showing a 12 cm solid right adnexal mass with no ascites, no omental deposits, no peritoneal nodularity and no enlarged retroperitoneal nodes, lactate dehydrogenase 820 U/L (120 to 250), alpha fetoprotein 3 micrograms/L (less than 10), beta human chorionic gonadotrophin less than 2 IU/L, CA125 62 U/mL (less than 35)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange an image guided core biopsy of the mass to obtain a tissue diagnosis before committing her to any form of definitive treatment
Refer her to a gynaecological oncology unit for fertility sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with comprehensive surgical staging
Arrange laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy to shell out the lesion and preserve as much normal ovarian tissue on that side as possible
Refer her for bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with total hysterectomy and omentectomy as the standard staging operation for ovarian cancer
Commence neoadjuvant platinum based chemotherapy and plan an interval debulking operation once the mass has responded to treatment

subtopic_detail: Rapidly deteriorating fever and abdominal pain on the fourth postnatal day in a mother whose toddler has a sore throat
stem: A 31-year-old on day four after a normal vaginal birth has six hours of rigors and constant severe lower abdominal pain, far worse than her afterpains. Her three-year-old has been off school with a sore throat.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 134 /min, BP 88/50 mmHg, RR 30 /min, T 39.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Lower abdominal guarding, bulky exquisitely tender uterus, heavy offensive lochia, no crepitus
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 2.1 x10^9/L, neutrophils 1.2 x10^9/L, CRP 268 mg/L, lactate 5.2 mmol/L, platelets 88 x10^9/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent pelvic ultrasound before starting any antibiotic
Commence oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for presumed endometritis
Commence intravenous cefazolin alone, escalating in the morning
Await culture results before starting any antibiotic therapy
Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin with clindamycin and resuscitation

subtopic_detail: Death of one twin at 28 weeks in a shared placenta pregnancy where the survivor appears well on the scan
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 28 weeks in a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy attends with reduced movements. The scan shows no cardiac activity in twin one. She has no bleeding, pain or contractions. The tertiary centre is ninety minutes away.

data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non-tender, cervix long and closed
data_table.Investigations: Twin two active with normal liquor and umbilical artery Doppler, middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity 1.2 multiples of the median; coagulation profile normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Emergency caesarean section now to deliver the surviving twin
Transfer to fetal medicine for corticosteroids and Doppler surveillance
Induce labour within twenty four hours to avoid maternal coagulopathy
Intrauterine transfusion to the surviving twin later today
Continue local outpatient care with weekly cardiotocography only

subtopic_detail: Anti D decision for light bleeding at eleven weeks with a viable intrauterine pregnancy
stem: A 29-year-old woman in her second pregnancy had light fresh bleeding on wiping this morning, now stopped, with no pain.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, cervical os closed, uterus consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O negative, antibody screen negative; ultrasound shows a single viable intrauterine pregnancy at eleven weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her rhesus status?

options.text: Withhold immunoglobulin now and continue the routine antenatal and postnatal doses
Give immunoglobulin today and continue the routine antenatal and postnatal doses
Kleihauer test today, giving immunoglobulin only if fetal cells are detected
Fetal rhesus genotyping on maternal plasma, treating only if the fetus is positive
Withhold immunoglobulin antenatally and give a single dose after the birth

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus grown from a routine urine culture at sixteen weeks gestation
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared antenatal care for a 32-year-old woman in her first pregnancy. She feels entirely well and mentions no urinary symptoms.

Her routine midstream urine culture taken at booking has grown a heavy pure growth of Streptococcus agalactiae, sensitive to penicillin. She has no drug allergies. She asks whether this means anything for the birth, having read that a swab is usually taken later in pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no renal angle tenderness, uterus palpable just above the symphysis pubis, no vaginal discharge reported
data_table.Investigations: Midstream urine culture with heavy pure growth of Streptococcus agalactiae sensitive to penicillin, no white cells reported on microscopy, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155)
