lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat the bacteriuria with oral antibiotics now and give intrapartum prophylaxis only if the vaginal and rectal swab taken later proves to be positive
Leave the bacteriuria untreated because she has no symptoms, and arrange the routine vaginal and rectal swab at thirty six weeks as for any other woman
Treat now with oral antibiotics and repeat the urine culture monthly, giving intrapartum prophylaxis only if the organism is grown again later in pregnancy
Give a course of oral antibiotics now and prescribe daily suppressive antibiotics for the remainder of the pregnancy to eradicate genital tract colonisation
Treat the bacteriuria with oral antibiotics now and plan intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis in labour irrespective of any later vaginal swab result

subtopic_detail: Discrepancy of nine days between certain menstrual dates and first trimester crown rump length
stem: A 26-year-old attends her first antenatal visit. She is certain her last menstrual period was nine weeks and five days ago and tracks regular 28 day cycles.

data_table.Investigations: Dating ultrasound yesterday: single live intrauterine pregnancy, crown rump length 23 mm corresponding to eight weeks and four days, optimal midsagittal view

lead_in: How should her estimated date of birth be set?

options.text: Keep the menstrual date, since her cycles are regular
Take the midpoint of the two estimates and record that date
Repeat the ultrasound in two weeks and date from interval growth
Use the menstrual date, revising it at the morphology scan
Use the ultrasound, since the discrepancy exceeds the accepted margin

subtopic_detail: Four episodes of bacterial vaginosis in twelve months each recurring after menstruation
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who has had four episodes of malodorous thin grey discharge in the past year. Each has responded to oral metronidazole and each has returned within a week or two of her period.

She is in a stable relationship with a male partner, uses condoms inconsistently and has no dyspareunia or pelvic pain. Her cervical screening is up to date and normal. She has stopped using vaginal douches after previous advice and asks what can be done to stop the cycle of recurrence.

data_table.Examination: Homogeneous thin grey vaginal discharge coating the walls, no cervical excitation, no adnexal tenderness, vulval skin normal with no erythema or fissuring
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH above 4.5, microscopy shows clue cells with scanty lactobacilli, nucleic acid testing negative for chlamydia, gonorrhoea and trichomonas, candida not isolated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give an induction course of antibiotic treatment and advise a daily oral lactobacillus probiotic preparation taken indefinitely to restore the vaginal flora
Treat each recurrence with an oral antibiotic course as it happens and take swabs before each course to confirm the diagnosis microscopically each time
Treat with an intravaginal antifungal preparation and a topical corticosteroid, and review her when the current symptoms have settled completely
Give an induction course of antibiotic treatment followed by twice weekly intravaginal metronidazole gel as suppressive therapy for several months
Give an induction course of antibiotic treatment and prescribe a simultaneous course for her male partner to prevent reintroduction of the organisms

subtopic_detail: Imminent birth at twenty eight weeks with corticosteroids already given twelve hours earlier
stem: A 31-year-old woman at 28 weeks in her second pregnancy is in established preterm labour despite nifedipine. She received the first dose of betamethasone twelve hours ago.

data_table.Examination: Contracting three in ten minutes, cervix 8 cm dilated, vertex at the spines, membranes intact, afebrile
data_table.Investigations: Group B streptococcus swab negative last week, cardiotocograph normal

lead_in: What additional treatment should be given now?

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate, loading dose then infusion until birth
Intravenous benzylpenicillin until the baby has been born
A further course of antenatal corticosteroids given now
An additional tocolytic to complete the corticosteroid course
Intravenous antibiotics with a macrolide for subclinical infection

subtopic_detail: Twin pregnancy at twelve weeks with a single placental mass and a T sign at the membrane insertion
stem: A 27-year-old in her first pregnancy has had her dating ultrasound at twelve weeks. She asks how her care will differ from a friend expecting twins who is scanned every four weeks.

data_table.Investigations: Two live fetuses, a single placental mass, a thin dividing membrane meeting the placenta at a right angle with no intervening wedge, concordant crown rump lengths, normal nuchal translucency

lead_in: What surveillance plan should be arranged?

options.text: Defer the decision until fetal sex is determined at the morphology scan
Fortnightly ultrasound from sixteen weeks assessing liquor and bladder filling
Four weekly ultrasound from twenty four weeks assessing growth and liquor
Routine care with a morphology scan and one third trimester growth scan
Amniocentesis to confirm zygosity, then four weekly ultrasound

subtopic_detail: Intrauterine device in place with a continuing intrauterine pregnancy at seven weeks and threads visible
stem: A 30-year-old woman has a positive pregnancy test with a copper intrauterine device inserted three years ago. She wishes to continue the pregnancy and has no pain or bleeding.

data_table.Examination: Threads visible at the external os, cervix closed, uterus consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: single live intrauterine pregnancy at seven weeks with the device lying below the gestation sac

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Leave the device in place, with serial ultrasound, and remove it at birth
Leave the device until the second trimester, then remove under ultrasound
Arrange hysteroscopic removal under general anaesthesia in the second trimester
Advise that the pregnancy is not viable and refer to discuss termination
Remove the device now by gentle traction on the visible threads

subtopic_detail: Spontaneous labour at thirty seven weeks after a previous classical uterine incision
stem: A 34-year-old in her second pregnancy arrives at 37 weeks contracting every four minutes. Her first baby was born at 27 weeks by caesarean, and the operation report records a vertical incision in the upper uterine segment.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm and 80 per cent effaced, membranes intact, vertex at minus two station, abdomen not tender between contractions
data_table.Investigations: Pulse 94 /min, BP 124/76 mmHg, cardiotocograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Allow labour to continue with continuous cardiotocography
Offer epidural analgesia and review her progress in two hours
Give a tocolytic and arrange an elective caesarean later
Measure lower uterine segment thickness and decide on that
Proceed to caesarean section now, alerting the theatre team

subtopic_detail: Hepatitis B surface antigen positive at booking with a viral load above 200000 international units per millilitre
stem: A 25-year-old woman at 14 weeks in her first pregnancy has chronic hepatitis B acquired in childhood, never treated.

data_table.Examination: No stigmata of chronic liver disease; liver ultrasound normal
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis B surface antigen and e antigen positive, viral load 4 x 10^7 IU/mL, ALT 24 U/L

lead_in: The baby will receive hepatitis B immunoglobulin and vaccine within twelve hours of birth. What further step most reduces transmission?

options.text: Advise against breastfeeding to avoid postnatal transmission
Start maternal pegylated interferon now to lower the viral load
Start maternal tenofovir disoproxil in the third trimester
No treatment now, with a repeat viral load in the third trimester
Plan an elective caesarean section at term rather than vaginal birth

subtopic_detail: Maternal fever with fetal tachycardia two days after membrane rupture at thirty weeks
stem: A 33-year-old woman admitted two days ago with ruptured membranes at 30 weeks has completed betamethasone and is on oral antibiotics. Overnight she developed abdominal pain, fever and offensive liquor. A neonatal cot is available.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122 /min, BP 106/58 mmHg, RR 24 /min, T 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus tender on palpation, cervix long and closed
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L, CRP 148 mg/L; CTG baseline 178 bpm with reduced variability

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intravenous antibiotics with tocolysis, magnesium and quaternary transfer
Intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics and expedited birth
Intravenous antibiotics with expectant management, reassessing in six hours
Intravenous antibiotics and a second corticosteroid course before birth
Amniocentesis for liquor glucose, Gram stain and culture first

subtopic_detail: Positive syphilis serology at booking in a woman reporting anaphylaxis to penicillin
stem: A 22-year-old woman at 16 weeks has booking serology reactive for syphilis and has never been treated. She recalls facial swelling and difficulty breathing after amoxicillin as a teenager. She has no rash, ulcers or neurological symptoms.

data_table.Examination: No rash on trunk, palms or soles, no ulceration
data_table.Investigations: Rapid plasma reagin titre 1 in 32 on two samples, treponemal antibody positive; HIV and hepatitis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Defer treatment until birth and treat the newborn with parenteral penicillin
Penicillin desensitisation, then intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin
Oral doxycycline for the duration appropriate to the stage, with monthly titres
Oral azithromycin with monthly serological titres and detailed fetal ultrasound
Intravenous ceftriaxone in the day unit with repeat serology at delivery

subtopic_detail: Thromboprophylaxis duration after emergency caesarean in a woman with a body mass index of 39
stem: A 36-year-old woman is 36 hours after an emergency caesarean section at term following a long labour. Her booking body mass index was 39 kg/m2, she has mobilised slowly and is breastfeeding. Her mother had a pulmonary embolism after hip replacement. She has had enoxaparin since surgery.

data_table.Examination: Wound dry, uterus well contracted, calves soft, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), platelets 268 x10^9/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, blood loss at operation 700 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate thromboprophylaxis plan?

options.text: Change to oral rivaroxaban for six weeks after the birth
Stop heparin now given the postoperative blood loss and anaemia
Continue low molecular weight heparin for six weeks after the birth
Continue low molecular weight heparin until discharge from hospital
Continue low molecular weight heparin for ten days after the birth

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation choice at six weeks for a mechanical mitral valve maintained on a low daily warfarin dose
stem: A 31-year-old woman is six weeks pregnant. She has a bileaflet mechanical mitral valve replaced eight years ago and takes warfarin 2.5 mg daily, with the international normalised ratio in range at every check. She has never had a thromboembolic event.

data_table.Examination: Crisp mechanical first heart sound, no regurgitant murmur
data_table.Investigations: INR 2.8 (target 2.5-3.5); echocardiogram three months ago normal

lead_in: What anticoagulation strategy should you recommend?

options.text: Continue warfarin through the first trimester, changing to heparin before birth
Therapeutic low molecular weight heparin throughout, with anti-Xa monitoring
Prophylactic low molecular weight heparin and aspirin, then warfarin
Unfractionated heparin by infusion in hospital for the first trimester
A direct oral anticoagulant in place of warfarin for the pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Porcelain white vulval plaques with loss of the labia minora and burying of the clitoris in a postmenopausal woman
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62-year-old woman who reports two years of vulval itch that is worst at night. She has tried several over the counter antifungal creams and a barrier ointment without benefit, and has recently found intercourse painful at the entrance.

She went through menopause at fifty one and has used no hormone therapy. She has autoimmune hypothyroidism treated with thyroxine. She has had no abnormal cervical screening results and no vaginal discharge.

data_table.Examination: Porcelain white thickened plaques over both labia majora extending to the perineum in a figure of eight pattern, resorption of the labia minora, clitoral hood fused over the clitoris, several linear excoriations, introital narrowing, no discrete nodule or ulcer, vaginal mucosa normal on speculum examination
data_table.Investigations: Vulval swab shows no candida and no bacterial pathogen, urinalysis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe topical oestrogen cream nightly for two weeks then twice weekly as ongoing maintenance therapy
Prescribe a two week course of oral fluconazole and advise soap avoidance with regular emollient use
Apply hydrocortisone one per cent ointment twice daily for six weeks and then review the symptomatic response
Refer for surgical division of the fused clitoral hood and release of the introital narrowing before medical therapy
Apply a potent topical corticosteroid ointment in a reducing regimen over three months with planned clinical review

subtopic_detail: Third painful fluctuant swelling at the posterior introitus in eighteen months after two previous incision and drainage procedures
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 29-year-old woman with three days of increasing pain and swelling at the entrance to the vagina on the left. She cannot sit comfortably and has been walking with a limp.

She has had two similar episodes in the past eighteen months, each treated in the emergency department with incision and drainage under local anaesthetic, and each recurring within a few months. She is otherwise well, is afebrile, and her last cervical screening test was normal two years ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 37.3 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant swelling of 4 cm at the posterior aspect of the left labium majus displacing the introitus medially, overlying skin erythematous and pointing, no induration extending into the perineum, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, no vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: Self collected vaginal swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea sent, result pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of this episode?

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin with metronidazole for seven days and review her in the clinic after the course finishes
Perform simple incision and drainage under local anaesthetic and arrange follow up with her general practitioner
Aspirate the collection with a wide bore needle under local anaesthetic and send the aspirate for bacterial culture
Insert a balloon tipped word catheter after incision, leaving it in place for four weeks to form an epithelialised tract
Arrange excision of the gland on the next available elective theatre list and manage the pain with oral analgesia

subtopic_detail: Wedge shaped breast redness with rigors persisting after twenty four hours of effective milk removal and cold packs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old woman who is sixteen days postpartum and breastfeeding her first baby. She noticed a tender area in the right breast yesterday morning and has been feeding frequently from that side, applying cold packs afterwards and taking regular ibuprofen and paracetamol as advised by the midwife.

Overnight she developed shaking chills and aching limbs. She has a crack at the base of the right nipple which has been present for a week. The baby is feeding every three hours, has plenty of wet nappies and has regained birth weight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Wedge shaped erythema over the upper outer quadrant of the right breast, warm firm and tender with no discrete fluctuant mass, fissure at the base of the right nipple with no surrounding satellite lesions, no axillary lymphadenopathy, left breast normal
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue conservative measures with effective milk removal and analgesia, and review the following day if unchanged
Prescribe oral flucloxacillin for five to seven days and encourage continued feeding from the affected breast
Prescribe oral cefalexin and advise expressing and discarding milk from the right breast until the fever settles
Arrange urgent breast ultrasound and surgical review for drainage of a probable underlying collection
Prescribe oral fluconazole for ductal candidiasis and advise treating the baby with oral antifungal gel as well

subtopic_detail: Urine loss confined to coughing and netball with no nocturia and a normal post void residual in a woman wanting to avoid surgery
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 44-year-old woman who leaks urine when she coughs, sneezes and plays netball on Thursday nights. She has two children delivered vaginally, the second with forceps, and has noticed the problem worsening over three years.

She wears a liner most days and has stopped playing in the second half of games. She does not wake at night to pass urine, does not get a sudden compelling urge and has never leaked on the way to the toilet. She tells you she would prefer to avoid an operation if there is anything else worth trying.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2, no abdominal mass, demonstrable leak from the urethral meatus on coughing with a full bladder, pelvic floor contraction weak and poorly sustained on digital assessment, no prolapse beyond the hymen on straining, vaginal mucosa well oestrogenised
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for nitrites leucocytes glucose and blood, post-void residual 25 mL on bladder scan, three day bladder diary shows six voids daily with average volumes of 320 mL and no nocturia

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Refer for urodynamic studies to characterise the bladder before offering her any specific form of treatment
Prescribe a low dose vaginal oestrogen pessary twice weekly and review her symptoms in three months' time
Arrange supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist for at least three months
Start oral solifenacin at night and titrate the dose according to her symptom response over six weeks
Refer to a urogynaecologist for a midurethral sling, given the three year history and effect on her sport

subtopic_detail: New urgency and nocturia in a seventy six year old already taking amitriptyline and oxybutynin with a rising post void residual
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 76-year-old woman who reports a sudden compelling need to pass urine six or seven times a day and twice at night, with leakage before she reaches the toilet on perhaps two days each week.

She has hypertension, osteoarthritis and insomnia. Her daughter mentions that she has seemed more forgetful over recent months and has had two falls getting up at night. She was started on oxybutynin by a locum four months ago with no improvement, and she has taken amitriptyline for sleep for several years.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable bladder, vaginal mucosa thin and pale with loss of rugae, no prolapse beyond the hymen on straining, no perineal sensory loss, gait slow with a wide base, standardised cognitive score 24 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes, post-void residual 140 mL on bladder scan, three day bladder diary shows nine voids daily with average volumes of 160 mL, serum creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the oxybutynin dose and add a bedtime fluid restriction to address the nocturia specifically
Refer for intradetrusor botulinum toxin injection as the next escalation of her overactive bladder therapy
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to manage the leakage and prevent further night time falls at home
Cease the oxybutynin and review the amitriptyline, starting supervised bladder training with vaginal oestrogen
Arrange urgent cystoscopy and urine cytology to exclude bladder malignancy as a cause of her urgency

subtopic_detail: Vaginal bulge reaching the hymen with dragging discomfort in a woman who declines surgery while caring for her husband
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68-year-old woman who describes a feeling of something coming down in the vagina, worst by the end of the day and when she lifts her grandchildren. She has a dragging discomfort but no urinary or bowel symptoms.

She had three vaginal births and has been postmenopausal for sixteen years. She is the full time carer for her husband, who has advanced Parkinson disease, and tells you she cannot contemplate several weeks of recovery from an operation while he depends on her. She has no bleeding and her cervical screening is up to date.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29 kg/m2, anterior vaginal wall descending to the level of the hymen on Valsalva, cervix descending to within 2 cm of the hymen, posterior wall well supported, vaginal mucosa thin and pale, no ulceration of the exposed epithelium, pelvic floor contraction weak
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative, post-void residual 40 mL on bladder scan

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Refer for vaginal hysterectomy with anterior repair and explain that this offers the most durable long term result
Advise observation with reassurance, since prolapse at this level rarely progresses and causes no lasting harm
Prescribe a course of oral oestrogen with progestogen to restore vaginal tissue quality and improve the support
Refer for laser or radiofrequency vaginal tightening treatment as a non surgical alternative to a formal repair
Arrange fitting of a vaginal pessary with topical oestrogen and referral for pelvic floor muscle training

subtopic_detail: Oncogenic human papillomavirus not types sixteen or eighteen with a negative reflex liquid based cytology result
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 34-year-old woman's cervical screening result. She attended for a routine test having had a negative screening result five years earlier, and she has no abnormal bleeding, no discharge and no pain.

She has two children, uses a copper intrauterine device for contraception and has never smoked. She received the human papillomavirus vaccine as part of the school program in year eight. She is not immunosuppressed and has had no previous abnormal result.

data_table.Examination: Cervix appears normal on speculum examination with no visible lesion, no contact bleeding, intrauterine device threads visible
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test reports oncogenic human papillomavirus detected, not type sixteen or eighteen, with reflex liquid based cytology showing negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for colposcopy within eight weeks because any oncogenic human papillomavirus detection requires assessment
Repeat the human papillomavirus test in twelve months and refer for colposcopy if oncogenic types persist
Return her to routine five yearly screening, since the reflex cytology showed no intraepithelial abnormality
Repeat the screening test in six months and refer for colposcopy only if the cytology becomes abnormal as well
Offer the nonavalent human papillomavirus vaccine now to help clear the infection that has been detected

subtopic_detail: Deep dyspareunia with cervical motion tenderness and a negative pregnancy test in a woman with a recent new partner
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 23-year-old woman with five days of lower abdominal pain, deep pain with intercourse and an increased vaginal discharge. She has had a new sexual partner for two months and uses condoms inconsistently.

She describes the pain as constant and bilateral, worse on movement. Her last menstrual period was two weeks ago and was normal. She has no urinary symptoms, no vomiting and has been eating normally. She has no history of pelvic surgery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bilateral lower abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound, mucopurulent cervical discharge with contact bleeding on speculum examination, marked cervical motion tenderness with bilateral adnexal tenderness, no adnexal mass palpable
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative, urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes, endocervical swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea sent, transvaginal ultrasound shows normal ovaries with no tubo ovarian collection and no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until the endocervical swab results are available, providing analgesia and review in 48 hours
Prescribe oral trimethoprim for five days and arrange a midstream urine culture with review if symptoms persist
Admit for intravenous antibiotics and surgical review, given the fever and the degree of adnexal tenderness
Prescribe oral doxycycline alone for fourteen days and advise that her partner be tested before any treatment
Give intramuscular ceftriaxone now with oral doxycycline and metronidazole for fourteen days, and treat her partner

subtopic_detail: Cycles of forty to ninety days with a normal semen analysis and patent tubes after fourteen months of trying to conceive
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 28-year-old woman who has been trying to conceive for fourteen months. Her periods come every forty to ninety days and have done so since her teens.

She has noticed coarse hair on her chin and upper lip which she waxes fortnightly. Her weight has been stable for two years. Her partner's semen analysis was normal and a hysterosalpingogram performed last month showed both tubes patent with normal uterine contour. She has never smoked and takes folic acid daily.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 31 kg/m2, waist circumference 94 cm, terminal hairs over chin and upper lip, no acanthosis nigricans, no striae, no galactorrhoea, normal visual fields to confrontation, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), prolactin 320 mIU/L (less than 500), follicle stimulating hormone 5.8 IU/L, luteinising hormone 12.4 IU/L, total testosterone 2.8 nmol/L (0.5-1.7), day 21 progesterone 4 nmol/L on two occasions, pelvic ultrasound shows twenty four follicles in one ovary with normal endometrium

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment to help her conceive?

options.text: Prescribe letrozole for ovulation induction with cycle monitoring, alongside advice on weight and lifestyle
Prescribe metformin as a single agent and review her cycle regularity after six months of continuous treatment
Refer directly for in vitro fertilisation given the fourteen month history and the documented ovulatory failure
Prescribe a combined oral contraceptive for three months to regulate her cycles before attempting conception again
Refer for laparoscopic ovarian drilling as a durable way to restore spontaneous ovulation over several cycles

subtopic_detail: Continued bright red loss with a firmly contracted fundus after oxytocin and ergometrine following a rapid second stage
stem: A 29-year-old woman is 20 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth at term; the second stage lasted eleven minutes and the baby weighed 3980 g. She has lost 900 mL and bleeds steadily despite further oxytocin, intramuscular ergometrine, fundal rubbing and catheterisation. The placenta appeared complete.

data_table.Examination: Fundus firm two centimetres below the umbilicus, steady bright red loss
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L, platelets 218 x10^9/L, international normalised ratio 1.0, fibrinogen 4.2 g/L (2.0-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms every fifteen minutes
Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device and inflate it
Transfuse two units of red cells and repeat the blood count
Transfer to theatre for examination of the genital tract under anaesthesia
Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g and observe for thirty minutes

subtopic_detail: Blood pressure of 172/114 at thirty four weeks in a woman using salbutamol several times weekly for asthma
stem: A 31-year-old woman at 34 weeks in her first pregnancy has a headache and a blood pressure that has not settled after fifteen minutes of rest. She has asthma and uses salbutamol three or four times a week.

data_table.Examination: Mild pitting oedema, brisk reflexes without clonus, chest clear with no wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein creatinine ratio 48 mg/mmol (less than 30), platelets 186 x10^9/L, ALT 34 U/L

lead_in: Which antihypertensive is most appropriate for immediate blood pressure control?

options.text: Intravenous labetalol as a slow bolus, repeated according to response
Intravenous magnesium sulfate loading dose then maintenance infusion
Oral methyldopa, increased every second day according to the readings
Oral immediate release nifedipine, repeated after thirty minutes if needed
Intravenous furosemide to reduce the intravascular volume driving the pressure

subtopic_detail: Heavy vaginal bleeding on day twelve with an open cervical os and a tender uterus after an uncomplicated birth
stem: A 26-year-old woman is twelve days after an uncomplicated vaginal birth. Her lochia has become heavier and offensive over two days, soaking three pads this morning, with shivers overnight. The placenta was complete.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112 /min, BP 108/64 mmHg, T 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus tender, palpable to the umbilicus, cervical os admits a fingertip, offensive discharge
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.6 x10^9/L, CRP 132 mg/L; ultrasound: bulky uterus, 16 mm heterogeneous endometrial content

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate surgical evacuation of the heterogeneous material seen on scan
Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and community midwife review tomorrow
Admission for intravenous antibiotics and uterotonics, evacuating only if no improvement
Tranexamic acid and a combined oral contraceptive to reduce the bleeding
Outpatient magnetic resonance imaging to characterise the endometrial content

subtopic_detail: Unilateral calf swelling at twenty six weeks with a negative D-dimer reported against a non pregnant reference range
stem: A 33-year-old woman at 26 weeks in her second pregnancy has three days of left calf pain and swelling after a long haul flight. She has no chest pain or breathlessness.

data_table.Examination: Left calf 4 cm larger than the right 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity, tender over the deep veins, mild pitting oedema
data_table.Investigations: D-dimer 480 mcg/L (less than 500 mcg/L in the non pregnant adult)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Accept the negative D-dimer and manage this as physiological oedema
Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram before assessing the affected limb
Graduated compression stockings and leg elevation, with review in one week
Compression duplex ultrasound with therapeutic low molecular weight heparin meanwhile
Treatment dose rivaroxaban with duplex ultrasound within 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Disabling vasomotor symptoms in a woman two years into adjuvant tamoxifen after oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 51-year-old woman who is two years into a five year course of tamoxifen following surgery and radiotherapy for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer. She reports fifteen to twenty hot flushes a day and drenching night sweats that wake her three or four times.

She has stopped attending her book club and has been falling asleep at her desk. She has tried reducing caffeine and alcohol and dressing in layers without benefit. She has no history of seizures and takes no other regular medication. Her oncologist has confirmed she should complete the full course of endocrine therapy.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg/m2, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, no palpable breast or axillary abnormality on the treated or contralateral side, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count and liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for her vasomotor symptoms?

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol patches, on the basis that transdermal delivery avoids the first pass hepatic effect
Venlafaxine at a low dose, titrated according to symptom response and tolerability over several weeks
Paroxetine at a low dose each evening, which has the best published evidence among the antidepressant options
A black cohosh preparation taken daily, with liver function monitoring arranged at three monthly intervals
Tibolone taken daily, since its tissue selective action avoids stimulating breast tissue in treated women

subtopic_detail: Nocturnal palmar and plantar itching at thirty four weeks with bile acids of 108 and no rash
stem: A 36-year-old woman at 34+2 weeks has three weeks of itching, worst at night and on her palms and soles, with no rash other than excoriations.

data_table.Examination: Linear excoriations on palms and forearms; no primary rash; no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: Fasting total serum bile acids 108 micromol/L (less than 19), ALT 96 U/L, bilirubin 14 micromol/L, platelets 232 x10^9/L, INR 1.0; hepatitis serology negative; liver ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Plan birth at 35 to 36 weeks after corticosteroids, with weekly bile acids
Ursodeoxycholic acid with birth at 39 weeks to reduce stillbirth risk
Twice weekly cardiotocography and Dopplers, awaiting labour at term
Emollients and sedating antihistamines, repeating bile acids in three weeks
Immediate caesarean section today given bile acids above 100 micromol/L

subtopic_detail: Deepest vertical pocket of 9 cm in one sac and 1.4 cm in the other at twenty weeks with a visible bladder in both twins
stem: A 29-year-old at 20+1 weeks with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy is increasingly uncomfortable and says her abdomen has grown quickly. The nearest fetal medicine unit is four hours away.

data_table.Examination: Uterus tense, symphysis fundal height 28 cm, cervix closed
data_table.Investigations: Twin one deepest vertical pocket 1.4 cm, bladder visible, estimated weight 12th centile; twin two deepest vertical pocket 9 cm, full bladder, 38th centile; umbilical artery and ductus venosus Doppler normal in both

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Amnioreduction of the larger sac locally today to relieve pressure
Continue fortnightly surveillance, since both Doppler studies are normal
Refer urgently for fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses
Give corticosteroids and deliver by caesarean within 48 hours
Amniocentesis of both sacs for karyotype and infection screening

subtopic_detail: quantifying additional immunoglobulin requirement after a Kleihauer result showing a large transplacental bleed following a car accident
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 32 weeks in her first pregnancy was the restrained driver in a low speed collision two hours ago. She has no bleeding and normal fetal movements.

data_table.Examination: Seatbelt bruising; uterus soft and non-tender; cardiotocograph normal
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O negative, antibody screen negative at booking and 28 weeks after routine prophylaxis; Kleihauer shows a fetomaternal haemorrhage of 18 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her immunoglobulin requirement?

options.text: A single standard 625 international unit dose now covers the event
No further immunoglobulin, since the 28 week dose was already given
No further immunoglobulin, since the antibody screen was negative
Further immunoglobulin only if a repeat Kleihauer at 24 hours is positive
Additional immunoglobulin calculated from the Kleihauer volume, with a repeat Kleihauer

subtopic_detail: intrapartum antimicrobial choice when the colonising isolate is resistant to the usual second line agent and the allergy history is severe
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on the birth suite. A 33-year-old woman in her second pregnancy presents at 39 weeks in established labour with contractions every three minutes and a cervix 5 cm dilated. Her membranes ruptured ninety minutes ago and the liquor is clear.

Her 36 week vaginal and rectal swab grew group B streptococcus. The laboratory report notes that the isolate is resistant to clindamycin and resistant to erythromycin, and susceptible to vancomycin. Her records document that six years ago, twenty minutes after a dose of amoxicillin for sinusitis, she developed generalised urticaria, lip swelling and wheeze requiring intramuscular adrenaline in an emergency department. She has never been formally allergy tested. Her observations and the cardiotocograph are within normal limits, and she is afebrile.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits, afebrile
data_table.Examination: Cervix 5 cm dilated, vertex presenting at station minus one, clear liquor draining
data_table.Investigations: Group B streptococcus on 36 week swab, isolate resistant to clindamycin and erythromycin, susceptible to vancomycin
data_table.Allergy: Amoxicillin six years ago followed within twenty minutes by urticaria, lip swelling and wheeze treated with intramuscular adrenaline

lead_in: Which intrapartum antibiotic would you prescribe?

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin given as a weight based dose and repeated at the recommended interval
Intravenous benzylpenicillin at the standard loading dose followed by four hourly maintenance doses
Intravenous cefazolin at the standard loading dose followed by eight hourly maintenance doses
Intravenous clindamycin at the standard dose repeated eight hourly until the baby is delivered
No intrapartum antibiotic, with newborn observation for forty eight hours after an uncomplicated birth

subtopic_detail: investigation of bleeding after the menopause in a woman on an oestrogen receptor modulator where the usual thickness threshold does not apply
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in a rapid access clinic. A 63-year-old woman who completed menopause at 51 reports three episodes of light vaginal bleeding over the past six weeks. She has been taking tamoxifen for four years following surgery and radiotherapy for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer.

She uses no vaginal oestrogen and takes no anticoagulant. Her cervical screening history is up to date and her last test was negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus. Speculum examination shows a healthy cervix with no visible lesion and no atrophic changes sufficient to explain bleeding. A transvaginal ultrasound reports an endometrial thickness of 9 mm with a heterogeneous appearance and several small cystic spaces, and normal ovaries. Her body mass index is 26 kg/m2 and her observations are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Healthy cervix with no visible lesion, no significant vaginal atrophy, uterus normal size and mobile
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 9 mm with heterogeneous echotexture and small cystic spaces, normal ovaries
data_table.Medications: Tamoxifen for four years, no vaginal oestrogen, no anticoagulant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound with saline infusion sonography and act only on an abnormal result
Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy under anaesthesia to sample the cavity under direct vision
Reassurance and review in six months, since a thickness of 9 mm is expected on this medication
Blind outpatient endometrial pipelle sampling in the clinic today with results in one week
Switch from tamoxifen to an aromatase inhibitor and repeat the ultrasound in three months

subtopic_detail: next step after a screening test detects a non-16 non-18 oncogenic virus with negative reflex cytology in a woman with no symptoms
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing results with a 34-year-old woman who attended for routine cervical screening two weeks ago. She has no intermenstrual bleeding, no postcoital bleeding and no unusual discharge, and her periods are regular on a combined oral contraceptive pill.

This was her first screening test in the renewed program, and her previous cytology at age 29 was reported as negative. The current report states that oncogenic human papillomavirus was detected, that types 16 and 18 were not detected, and that reflex liquid based cytology showed a negative result with no abnormal squamous or glandular cells and a satisfactory sample. She is not pregnant, is immunocompetent, has never had a high grade abnormality and has no history of diethylstilbestrol exposure. She asks whether she needs a procedure.

data_table.Examination: Speculum examination at the time of collection documented a healthy looking cervix
data_table.Investigations: Oncogenic human papillomavirus detected, types 16 and 18 not detected, reflex cytology negative on a satisfactory sample
data_table.Background: Immunocompetent, not pregnant, no previous high grade abnormality, no symptoms

lead_in: What do you advise?

options.text: Repeat the screening test in six months, because an earlier repeat detects persistence sooner
Offer human papillomavirus vaccination now, since it will clear the currently detected infection
Repeat the screening test in twelve months, with colposcopy if the virus is still detected then
Refer for colposcopy now, because any detection of an oncogenic type warrants direct visualisation
Return to routine five yearly screening, because the reflex cytology was reported as negative

subtopic_detail: choosing a method at the six week check for a fully breastfeeding woman with a history of clot during a previous pregnancy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 31-year-old woman at her six week postnatal check. She had a spontaneous vaginal birth at term and is fully breastfeeding with no formula supplementation, and her baby is feeding every three hours through the day and once overnight.

During her previous pregnancy four years ago she developed a deep vein thrombosis in the left leg at 30 weeks gestation and was anticoagulated until six weeks after that birth. Thrombophilia screening was negative and she has had no further clot. She has no migraine, her blood pressure today is 112/70 mmHg and her body mass index is 24 kg/m2. She has not resumed periods and has not yet resumed intercourse. She tells you she definitely does not want another pregnancy within the next two years and would prefer not to think about contraception every day.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Well, uterus involuted, perineum healed, no calf tenderness or swelling
data_table.Background: Fully breastfeeding, amenorrhoeic, body mass index 24 kg/m2, no migraine
data_table.History: Pregnancy associated deep vein thrombosis four years ago, negative thrombophilia screen, no recurrence

lead_in: Which contraceptive would you recommend first?

options.text: Lactational amenorrhoea alone, which suits her feeding pattern and her wish to avoid a device
A progestogen only pill started now, which suits her thrombosis history and her breastfeeding
Condoms alone until weaning, which suits her breastfeeding and avoids all hormonal exposure
A levonorgestrel intrauterine device inserted now, which suits her thrombosis history and her preference
A combined oral contraceptive pill started now, which suits her cycle control and her preference

subtopic_detail: first line ovulation induction for a woman with irregular cycles and a raised body mass index who has been trying to conceive for fourteen months
stem: A 28-year-old woman has been trying to conceive for fourteen months. Her cycles have come every 45 to 90 days since her teens and she removes coarse chin hair weekly. Her body mass index is 33 kg/m2.

data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and prolactin normal; mid-luteal progesterone low twice; HbA1c 5.4 per cent; partner's semen analysis normal
data_table.Imaging: Pelvic ultrasound: 26 antral follicles, ovarian volume 12 mL; both tubes patent on hysterosalpingogram

lead_in: Which pharmacological treatment would you offer first?

options.text: Clomifene for five days early in the cycle, tracked by ultrasound
Metformin daily in a titrated dose, tracked by mid-luteal progesterone
Low dose step up injectable gonadotrophins, tracked by ultrasound
A combined oral contraceptive pill, tracked by cycle regularity
Letrozole for five days early in the cycle, tracked by ultrasound

subtopic_detail: emergency contraception choice five days after unprotected intercourse at mid-cycle in a woman whose weight reduces oral efficacy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 24-year-old woman who requests emergency contraception. She had unprotected intercourse five days ago, on day 12 of a regular 28 day cycle, and has had no other unprotected intercourse this cycle.

Her body mass index is 35 kg/m2 and her weight is 98 kg. She has no history of pelvic inflammatory disease, no abnormal bleeding and no current pelvic pain or discharge. A urine pregnancy test today is negative. She takes no regular medication, including no enzyme inducing drugs, and has no copper allergy. She tells you she has been meaning to sort out a longer term method for a while and would be happy to start something today if it can also cover this exposure. Her last cervical screening test was normal two years ago.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no cervical motion tenderness, no abnormal discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative
data_table.Background: Weight 98 kg, body mass index 35 kg/m2, regular 28 day cycle, no enzyme inducing medication

lead_in: Which option would you recommend?

options.text: A copper intrauterine device inserted today, which also provides her with ongoing contraception
Oral levonorgestrel 1.5 mg taken today, with a repeat dose if she vomits within three hours
Oral ulipristal acetate 30 mg taken today, with a repeat dose if she vomits within three hours
A levonorgestrel intrauterine device inserted today, which also provides her with ongoing contraception
An etonogestrel implant inserted today, which also provides her with ongoing contraception

subtopic_detail: counselling about mode of birth in a subsequent pregnancy after a third degree perineal tear with ongoing symptoms
stem: A 30-year-old is 20 weeks into her second pregnancy. Two years ago a forceps delivery caused a third degree tear through less than half the external anal sphincter, repaired in theatre. She now has faecal urgency, twice not reaching the toilet this year, and wears a pad to exercise.

data_table.Examination: Well healed perineum, reduced voluntary anal squeeze pressure
data_table.Investigations: No endoanal ultrasound or manometry performed; this pregnancy uncomplicated with a cephalic presentation

lead_in: What do you advise?

options.text: Refer for physiotherapy and defer the discussion until thirty six weeks
Arrange endoanal ultrasound and manometry, discussing caesarean if abnormal
Recommend vaginal birth, since repeat injury affects a small minority
Recommend vaginal birth with an elective mediolateral episiotomy
Recommend elective caesarean now without further investigation

subtopic_detail: discordant amniotic fluid volumes in a shared placenta twin pregnancy at twenty one weeks with normal umbilical artery Dopplers
stem: A 27-year-old woman at 21 weeks had a first trimester scan showing one placenta with a T sign and two sacs. Her abdomen has become tight over ten days and she is breathless lying flat.

data_table.Ultrasound: Twin one deepest vertical pocket 1.4 cm with no bladder seen; twin two 10.4 cm with a distended bladder; weight discordance 16 per cent
data_table.Doppler: Normal umbilical artery and ductus venosus Dopplers in both twins

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Corticosteroids and delivery of both twins within two days
Maternal serology and repeat growth scans for the smaller twin
Same day referral to a fetal therapy centre for laser ablation
Repeat the ultrasound in two weeks, as the Dopplers are normal
Serial amnioreduction from the polyhydramniotic sac with weekly review

subtopic_detail: persistent trophoblastic marker plateau after uterine evacuation of a complete molar pregnancy in a woman who wants another child
stem: A 34-year-old woman had suction evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole ten weeks ago; her pre-evacuation human chorionic gonadotrophin was 186000 IU/L. She has light irregular bleeding, no cough and no neurological symptoms, and asks when she can conceive again.

data_table.Examination: Normally sized uterus, no adnexal mass
data_table.Imaging: Pelvic ultrasound shows a 14 mm vascular myometrial area; chest radiograph normal
data_table.Bloods: Full blood count, liver and thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Perform a second uterine evacuation of the vascular myometrial area
Perform hysterectomy with preservation of both ovaries
Reassure her and advise that she may conceive once bleeding settles
Refer to a trophoblast centre for staging and chemotherapy
Continue weekly surveillance for a further four weeks

subtopic_detail: blood product selection during ongoing postpartum bleeding when the fibrinogen has fallen to a level that is normal outside pregnancy
stem: A 36-year-old woman gave birth vaginally 40 minutes ago and has lost 2500 mL. She bleeds briskly from a well contracted uterus despite oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost and tranexamic acid. The placenta is complete and no laceration was found.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128 /min, BP 88/46 mmHg, temperature 35.8 degrees C
data_table.Point of care testing: Platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400), international normalised ratio 1.3, APTT 38 seconds (25-38), fibrinogen 1.9 g/L (laboratory non-pregnant range 1.5 to 4.0)

lead_in: Which blood product should you request next?

options.text: Platelet transfusion, aiming to keep the count above 75 x10^9/L
Fresh frozen plasma at 15 mL/kg to correct the international normalised ratio
Prothrombin complex concentrate for the vitamin K dependent factors
Recombinant activated factor VII to generate a thrombin burst
Cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate, targeting a fibrinogen above 2 g/L

subtopic_detail: adjusting an established thyroxine dose at the moment pregnancy is confirmed in a woman with treated hypothyroidism
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 31-year-old woman who has just had a positive home pregnancy test. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago and she has not yet had a dating scan or any antenatal bloods.

She has taken thyroxine 100 micrograms daily for eight years for autoimmune hypothyroidism and her most recent thyroid function tests, done three months ago as part of routine annual review, showed a thyroid stimulating hormone of 2.9 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0) with a normal free thyroxine. She takes the tablet first thing each morning and has never missed a dose. She is otherwise well, takes a pregnancy multivitamin containing iodine, and asks whether anything about her tablets needs to change now.

data_table.Examination: No goitre, no tremor, weight stable
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.9 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0) with normal free thyroxine, taken three months ago
data_table.Medications: Thyroxine 100 micrograms orally each morning, pregnancy multivitamin containing iodine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about her thyroxine today?

options.text: Continue the current dose and add potassium iodide 150 micrograms daily as a separate tablet
Switch to liothyronine 20 micrograms daily to provide the active hormone directly to the fetus
Continue the current dose and check thyroid function at the routine 12 week antenatal visit
Increase the dose by about 25 to 30 per cent now and check thyroid function within two weeks
Reduce the dose by about 25 per cent now to avoid fetal thyrotoxicosis in the first trimester

subtopic_detail: timing maternal pertussis immunisation to maximise transplacental antibody transfer in a woman vaccinated in a recent previous pregnancy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar running an antenatal visit for a 29-year-old woman at 21 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first child is 18 months old and is fully immunised.

She tells you she had a whooping cough vaccine at 30 weeks in her previous pregnancy and does not think she needs another one so soon, since her father was told an adult booster lasts ten years. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated, her morphology scan yesterday was normal, and her blood pressure and urinalysis today are unremarkable. She had an influenza vaccine three weeks ago without any reaction. She has no history of Guillain Barre syndrome, no allergy to vaccine components and no immunosuppression.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height consistent with dates, fetal movements reported as normal
data_table.Investigations: Morphology scan at 20 weeks reported as normal, urinalysis negative
data_table.Immunisation history: Pertussis containing vaccine at 30 weeks of previous pregnancy 18 months ago, influenza vaccine 3 weeks ago

lead_in: What would you recommend regarding pertussis immunisation in this pregnancy?

options.text: Defer the vaccine until 34 to 36 weeks so that antibody levels peak closest to the birth
Defer the vaccine until immediately after birth, before she is discharged from hospital
Omit the vaccine in this pregnancy because a dose was given less than two years ago
Check her pertussis serology now and vaccinate only if the antibody titre is found to be low
Give a pertussis containing vaccine now, since it is recommended in every pregnancy

subtopic_detail: deciding dose and the need for quantification of feto-maternal haemorrhage after a third trimester sensitising event in a rhesus negative woman
stem: A 27-year-old woman at 31 weeks in her first pregnancy attends after a car accident in which her abdomen struck the seatbelt. She had routine prophylactic anti-D at 28 weeks.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender; no bleeding or liquor on speculum
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O negative; antibody screen negative at 28 weeks
data_table.Monitoring: Cardiotocograph reactive; no retroplacental collection on ultrasound

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her rhesus status?

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU intramuscularly with a sample to quantify fetal cells
Anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU intramuscularly with an antibody screen in four weeks
Withhold anti-D, since the 28 week prophylactic dose still covers her
Withhold anti-D, since there is no bleeding and the cardiotocograph is reactive
Quantify fetal cells first and give anti-D only if any are detected

subtopic_detail: applying the missed pill rules when two combined oral contraceptive tablets are omitted in the first week of a new packet
stem:
You are the general practice registrar taking a Monday morning telephone consultation from a 22-year-old woman who takes a combined oral contraceptive containing ethinylestradiol 30 micrograms with levonorgestrel 150 micrograms.

She started a new packet last Wednesday after her usual hormone free interval. She took Wednesday's tablet, then went away for the weekend and forgot the packet, missing both Thursday's and Friday's tablets. She restarted on Saturday morning and has taken Saturday, Sunday and today's tablets on time. She had unprotected sex on Friday night and again on Sunday night. She is not using condoms, has no vomiting or diarrhoea, and takes no other medicines including no over the counter or herbal preparations. Her last menstrual period was the withdrawal bleed that finished last Tuesday.

data_table.Pill details: Ethinylestradiol 30 micrograms with levonorgestrel 150 micrograms, monophasic 21 day formulation
data_table.Missed doses: Tablets 2 and 3 of the packet missed on Thursday and Friday, tablets 4 to 6 taken on time Saturday to Monday
data_table.Exposures: Unprotected intercourse Friday night and Sunday night
data_table.Other factors: No vomiting or diarrhoea, no interacting medicines, withdrawal bleed completed last Tuesday

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice to give her now?

options.text: Arrange a urine pregnancy test today and base any further contraceptive advice on that result
Offer emergency contraception, continue the packet, and use condoms for the next seven days
Continue the packet as normal and use condoms for seven days without emergency contraception
Stop the current packet, omit the hormone free interval, and start a fresh packet tomorrow
Take two tablets today to make up the missed doses and continue the packet as scheduled

subtopic_detail: choosing between oral and parenteral iron replacement in the third trimester when oral therapy has already been tried
stem: A 33-year-old woman at 30 weeks in her third pregnancy started oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily at 22 weeks. She stopped after ten days with constipation and cramps and has taken nothing since. She tires on stairs.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115 to 155), ferritin 6 micrograms/L (30 to 200), mean cell volume 74 fL, B12 and folate normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her anaemia?

options.text: Oral iron polymaltose with a full blood count at 36 weeks
Faecal occult blood and coeliac serology for a gastrointestinal source
Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose in the day assessment unit
Oral ferrous sulfate restarted on alternate days with vitamin C
Transfusion of two units of packed red cells with a recheck tomorrow

subtopic_detail: selecting first line management of symptomatic anterior compartment prolapse in a woman who has not completed her family
stem: A 34-year-old woman describes something coming down at the vaginal entrance, worse by the end of the day and relieved by lying flat. She had a forceps birth eighteen months ago and would like one more child. She has no incontinence and empties completely.

data_table.Examination: On Valsalva the anterior vaginal wall descends to 1 cm above the hymen; no descent of cervix or posterior wall; Modified Oxford score 2 out of 5

lead_in: What would you recommend as first line management?

options.text: Anterior colporrhaphy with caesarean birth for future pregnancy
Topical vaginal oestrogen cream on three nights each week
Urodynamic studies to characterise bladder function before treatment
Supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a physiotherapist
A ring pessary fitted today with review in three months

subtopic_detail: responding to an undifferentiated febrile illness in the second trimester where the food history changes the antibiotic choice
stem: A 35-year-old woman at 27 weeks in her second pregnancy has two days of fever, myalgia and headache with one episode of loose stools. Four days ago she ate a chicken and soft cheese salad from a delicatessen.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear, abdomen soft and non-tender, no rash
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.8 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 68 mg/L, urine dipstick negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antimicrobial management?

options.text: Take blood cultures and start intravenous ceftriaxone with azithromycin
Send stool for culture and manage with paracetamol and oral fluids
Start oral trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole and review tomorrow
Start oral valaciclovir and send cytomegalovirus and parvovirus serology
Take blood cultures and start intravenous benzylpenicillin with gentamicin

subtopic_detail: responding to modest painless bleeding with an abrupt fetal heart rate change immediately after membranes are ruptured
stem: A 30-year-old woman at 39 weeks, conceived by in vitro fertilisation, is in labour at 5 cm. Immediately after artificial rupture of membranes, clear liquor is followed by about 80 mL of fresh blood. She has no pain.

data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non-tender between contractions
data_table.Monitoring: Fetal heart rate 145 falling to a sustained 70 bpm within 90 seconds, no recovery between contractions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Immediate caesarean section, transferring to theatre now
Apt test on the vaginal blood before deciding on delivery
Subcutaneous terbutaline, left lateral position, observe the trace
Two large bore cannulas, cross match and maternal fluid resuscitation
Fetal scalp blood sample for lactate to decide on delivery

subtopic_detail: sequencing replacement against uterotonic drugs when the fundus cannot be felt after a controlled cord traction delivery of the placenta
stem: A 24-year-old primigravida is three minutes past delivery of the placenta by controlled cord traction. She is pale and sweating, has vomited once, and has severe lower abdominal pain.

data_table.Examination: No fundus palpable abdominally, with a dimple at the expected site; smooth dark red mass at the introitus with the placenta attached
data_table.Drugs given: Oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly with the anterior shoulder, nothing since

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Give ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscularly to contract the uterus
Attempt immediate manual replacement with the placenta left attached
Remove the placenta manually, then attempt replacement through the cervix
Insert an intrauterine balloon and inflate with warmed sodium chloride
Give atropine 600 micrograms intravenously for the bradycardia

subtopic_detail: managing abdominal distension with haemoconcentration in the week after oocyte retrieval and embryo transfer
stem: A 29-year-old with polycystic ovary syndrome had oocyte retrieval eight days ago, 32 oocytes collected, then a fresh embryo transfer. She has abdominal swelling, breathlessness lying flat, has gained 4 kg and has passed urine once today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 /min, BP 102/68 mmHg, SpO2 95% in air
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with shifting dullness, not peritonitic
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.51 (0.33 to 0.45), white cell count 18.2 x10^9/L, creatinine 104 micromol/L
data_table.Imaging: Ovaries 11 cm and 10 cm with moderate free fluid, flow preserved

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge with oral fluids and clinic review in three days
Intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole for pelvic sepsis
Admit for intravenous fluid, enoxaparin and guided paracentesis
Admit for intravenous furosemide and fluid restriction
Urgent laparoscopy to decompress the ovaries and drain fluid

subtopic_detail: deciding on immunoglobulin versus antiviral prophylaxis after a household chickenpox contact in a woman with uncertain immunity
stem:
You are the general practice registrar telephoned by a 26-year-old woman at 16 weeks in her first pregnancy. Her 4-year-old nephew stayed overnight at her house two days ago and developed a widespread blistering rash yesterday morning, which their family doctor has diagnosed as chickenpox.

She grew up overseas, has no vaccination records, and cannot recall ever having had chickenpox or shingles herself. She spent the evening reading to him and sharing the same living room for several hours. She feels entirely well today with no rash, no fever and no respiratory symptoms. You arrange an urgent varicella zoster immunoglobulin G serology which the laboratory telephones back this afternoon as negative. It is now 48 hours since the exposure, and the hospital pharmacy confirms that zoster immunoglobulin is in stock.

data_table.Examination: No rash anywhere, chest clear, no mucosal lesions
data_table.Investigations: Varicella zoster virus immunoglobulin G negative on urgent serology
data_table.Exposure details: Several hours of indoor face to face contact 48 hours ago with a child whose vesicular rash appeared the following morning

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral valaciclovir prophylaxis today and continue it for the next fourteen days
Arrange an urgent amniocentesis to test amniotic fluid for varicella zoster virus by polymerase chain reaction
Reassure her that immunity is likely despite the serology and arrange a repeat test in two weeks
Give zoster immunoglobulin now and advise her to report any rash or respiratory symptom immediately
Give a dose of live attenuated varicella vaccine now and a second dose in four weeks

subtopic_detail: separating two third trimester liver disorders when the blood pressure is normal and the glucose is low
stem: A 31-year-old woman at 35 weeks in her first pregnancy has five days of nausea, vomiting and right upper quadrant pain, and two days of increasing confusion. She has had no itch and her blood pressure has been normal throughout.

data_table.Examination: Jaundiced, asterixis, drowsy but rousable; uterus soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 2.4 mmol/L; INR 2.1; fibrinogen 1.4 g/L; ALT 340 U/L; bilirubin 78 micromol/L; creatinine 148 micromol/L; platelets 186 x10^9/L; haptoglobin normal, film unfragmented; protein to creatinine ratio 12 mg/mmol; paracetamol undetectable; bright liver on ultrasound

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate and intravenous labetalol, with expedited birth
Ursodeoxycholic acid and bile acid levels, with birth at 37 weeks
Intravenous N-acetylcysteine with continued expectant management
Plasma exchange, deferring birth until the INR normalises
Correct the glucose and coagulopathy, then expedite birth

subtopic_detail: Second-line uterotonic and adjunct choice in atonic postpartum haemorrhage following syntocinon failure
stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 had a spontaneous vaginal birth 20 minutes ago. The placenta was delivered intact after intramuscular oxytocin 10 units. She has well-controlled asthma.

data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy at the umbilicus, bimanual massage in progress, no tear bleeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Sublingual misoprostol 800 microgram alone with continued uterine massage
Intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram with intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g
Oxytocin infusion 40 units, ergometrine 250 microgram and tranexamic acid 1 g

Intrauterine balloon tamponade before any further uterotonic therapy

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection in threatened preterm birth before 30 weeks gestation
stem: A 28-year-old G3P1 woman at 28+4 weeks has contractions every 3 minutes. Membranes have ruptured and the cervix is 3 cm dilated. Birth is expected within 24 hours.

data_table.Given so far: Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly 90 minutes ago, oral nifedipine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention for neuroprotection?

options.text: Intravenous betamethasone 12 mg twelve-hourly, magnesium sulfate deferred until birth is imminent
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g over 20 minutes then 2 g/hour for 12 hours
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 6 g over 20 minutes then 2 g/hour for 24 hours
