subtopic_detail: Methotrexate versus surgical management for a tubal ectopic pregnancy under the RANZCOG bhCG threshold
stem: A 30-year-old woman at 7 weeks by dates has two days of light spotting and mild right iliac fossa discomfort. She can attend for follow-up.

data_table.Examination: Mild right iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism
data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus; 22 mm right adnexal mass with a yolk sac, no cardiac activity; trace free fluid
data_table.Bloods: beta-hCG 3800 IU/L; blood count, liver and renal function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with beta-hCG on days 4 and 7
Laparoscopic right salpingectomy, leaving the normal contralateral tube
Expectant management with weekly beta-hCG until the level falls
Laparoscopic right salpingostomy to preserve that tube's patency
Two-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 intramuscularly on day 0 and day 4

subtopic_detail: Recognition of HELLP syndrome without severe hypertension and immediate management priorities
stem: A 34-year-old G1P0 at 33+2 weeks has two days of right upper quadrant pain and nausea. Booking blood pressure was 118/72 mmHg.

data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness, urine protein 2+
data_table.Bloods: Platelets 84 x10^9/L, AST 190 U/L, LDH 780 U/L, bilirubin 32 micromol/L, schistocytes on film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Oral labetalol with expectant management, aiming for spontaneous labour after 37 weeks
Intravenous magnesium sulfate, intramuscular betamethasone, and delivery within 24 to 48 hours
Intravenous hydralazine and oral nifedipine, delivering only if blood pressure reaches 160/110
Emergency caesarean within one hour without steroid cover, after platelet transfusion
Intravenous dexamethasone with expectant management and delivery at 37 weeks

subtopic_detail: Choice of surgical procedure for tubal ectopic pregnancy when the contralateral tube is absent from prior surgery
stem: A 33-year-old G3P0 has acute left iliac fossa pain and syncope. Two years ago she had a right salpingectomy for a ruptured ectopic. She has been trying to conceive for six months.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 /min, BP 88/54 mmHg after 1 L Hartmann and 1 unit red cells
data_table.Laparoscopy: Left ampullary ectopic bleeding actively, tube intact and viable, right tube absent, uterus and ovaries healthy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical procedure?

options.text: Intratubal methotrexate with tube preservation and serial beta-hCG monitoring
Laparoscopic left salpingostomy, preserving tubal patency for conception
Laparoscopic left salpingectomy with haemostasis and pelvic washout
Laparoscopic washout only, then intramuscular methotrexate
Laparoscopic left salpingectomy with contralateral oophorectomy

subtopic_detail: Decision timing for emergency caesarean during VBAC with early features of uterine scar dehiscence
stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 at 40+1 weeks is in labour after a previous lower segment caesarean, on syntocinon augmentation. In the last 20 minutes she has had continuous suprapubic pain breaking through an effective epidural.

data_table.Cardiotocography: Baseline 150 /min, reduced variability 20 min, three late decelerations up to 90 sec
data_table.Examination: Abdomen tender between contractions; cervix 8 cm, unchanged over 2 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue augmentation and reassess after a further 30 minutes
Halve the syntocinon and reassess the trace in 20 minutes
Give subcutaneous terbutaline and reassess over 30 minutes
Stop syntocinon and proceed to emergency caesarean section
Take a fetal scalp lactate and continue if it is normal

subtopic_detail: Priorities in management of complete molar pregnancy with clinical and biochemical hyperthyroidism at diagnosis
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 13 weeks by dates has three days of heavy vaginal bleeding, a tremor and daily vomiting for a week.

data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, no goitre; uterus 18 weeks size; grape-like vesicles at a partly open cervix
data_table.Ultrasound: Snowstorm appearance, theca lutein cysts, no fetal parts
data_table.Bloods: beta-hCG 590000 IU/L, TSH below 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 32 pmol/L (10-20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Same-day total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy
Carbimazole 40 mg daily, deferring evacuation until she is euthyroid
Sublingual misoprostol 400 microgram for medical evacuation today
Radioactive iodine now, deferring any evacuation for four weeks
Propranolol 40 mg then same-day suction dilatation and evacuation

subtopic_detail: Uterine inversion diagnosis and immediate management
stem: A G3P2 at 39 weeks has just delivered a 3.9 kg baby vaginally after oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly with the anterior shoulder and cord traction. She has suddenly become light headed.

data_table.Examination: Large firm mass in the vagina with the placenta still attached; no fundus palpable abdominally

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate step?

options.text: Attempt immediate manual replacement of the uterus with the placenta attached
Remove the placenta manually first to reduce the fundal weight
Give carboprost 250 micrograms and rectal misoprostol 800 micrograms
Transfer to theatre for hysterectomy without a bedside attempt
Insert a Bakri balloon inflated to 500 mL to tamponade bleeding

subtopic_detail: Second-line uterotonic after failed oxytocin and ergometrine
stem: A 32-year-old primipara is 20 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth at 39 weeks. She has lost 1400 mL and is still bleeding briskly from a soft boggy uterus. She has no asthma and no allergies.

data_table.Uterotonics given: Oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly at birth, oxytocin 40 units in 1 L over 4 hours, ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscularly 5 minutes ago
data_table.Examination: Bladder empty, no genital tract trauma

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic?

options.text: Repeat ergometrine 250 micrograms intramuscularly as a second dose
Carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscularly, repeated every 15 minutes to 2 mg
Misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually as a single further dose
Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously over 20 minutes to relax the uterus
Recombinant activated factor VII 90 micrograms/kg intravenously

subtopic_detail: First-line pharmacotherapy when diet and metformin fail
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic seeing a 33-year-old woman at 30 weeks gestation with dietary-diagnosed gestational diabetes at 26 weeks (fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L, 2 hour 8.9 mmol/L on 75 g OGTT). She has followed the dietitian's plan for 4 weeks and metformin was uptitrated to 2 g daily 2 weeks ago. She has had no hypoglycaemia symptoms and is otherwise well; her weight gain has been within target and fetal growth is on the 45th centile.

Her 2 week home glucose diary shows fasting values consistently between 5.4 and 5.9 mmol/L (target under 5.1) with post-prandial readings on target. Vital signs and urinalysis are unremarkable and blood pressure today is 118/72 mmHg.

data_table.Gestation: 30 weeks with GDM diagnosed at 26 weeks
data_table.Current management: Dietary intervention for 4 weeks; metformin 2 g daily for 2 weeks
data_table.Home glucose diary: Fasting 5.4 to 5.9 mmol/L (target <5.1); postprandial on target

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in glycaemic management?

options.text: Continue current therapy and repeat the 75 g oral glucose tolerance test in 4 weeks
Add rapid-acting insulin lispro before each main meal targeted at post-prandial glucose control
Add bedtime intermediate-acting isophane insulin titrated to target fasting glucose under 5.1 mmol/L
Increase the metformin dose to 3 g daily divided across three meals to overcome the residual fasting elevation
Stop metformin and commence glibenclamide 2.5 mg twice daily as the primary sulfonylurea for GDM

subtopic_detail: Methotrexate versus surgical management criteria
stem: A 28-year-old G2P0 with 6 weeks and 5 days of amenorrhoea has two days of light painless bleeding. She can attend for blood tests every 3 to 4 days.

data_table.Investigations: Beta-hCG 2400 IU/L, up from 1900 IU/L 48 hours ago; creatinine, ALT and full blood count normal
data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus, right adnexal mass 22 mm, no yolk sac or cardiac activity, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to offer?

options.text: Suction curettage to obtain products for histological diagnosis
Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate with beta-hCG on days 4 and 7
Two-dose methotrexate on days 0 and 4 with no day 7 measurement
Expectant management with weekly beta-hCG and clinical review
Emergency laparoscopic salpingectomy as first-line treatment

subtopic_detail: Postpartum contraception timing with breastfeeding
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34-year-old G2P2 woman at her 6 week postnatal review. She is exclusively breastfeeding her healthy term baby every 2 to 3 hours. Her only medical history is migraine without aura for the last 5 years. Her BMI today is 27 kg/m2 and her blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg. She would like reliable contraception but wants to protect her breastmilk supply and preserve the option of another pregnancy in about 3 years.

She had an uncomplicated vaginal birth without perineal trauma. She is not currently amenorrhoeic as she had a small amount of vaginal bleeding 10 days ago. She is comfortable with an intrauterine device and has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

data_table.Postnatal history: G2P2, 6 weeks postpartum; uncomplicated vaginal birth; exclusive breastfeeding 2 to 3 hourly
data_table.Medical background: Migraine without aura; BMI 27; BP 118/76; no VTE history
data_table.Fertility plan: Desires reliable contraception now; another pregnancy in about 3 years
data_table.Bleeding pattern: Vaginal bleeding 10 days ago; not amenorrhoeic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive to recommend?

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular every 12 weeks for the next 3 years
Etonogestrel subdermal implant with combined oral contraception as backup for the first month
Rely on lactational amenorrhoea method alone as her primary contraception for the next 6 months
Combined oral contraceptive pill 30 microgram ethinylestradiol plus levonorgestrel 150 microgram daily
Insertion of the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device today with contraception effective immediately

subtopic_detail: Tocolysis choice with contraindication to first-line agent
stem: A 27-year-old G3P1 at 30+2 weeks has painful contractions every 4 minutes for 3 hours. She takes regular propranolol for migraine.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 2 cm dilated, 70 per cent effaced, station -2, membranes intact
data_table.Investigations: Cervical length 18 mm, fetal fibronectin positive; CTG reassuring
data_table.Given: Betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscularly; magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous load for neuroprotection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate tocolytic to commence?

options.text: Intravenous atosiban bolus then an infusion tapered over 48 hours
Intravenous salbutamol infusion titrated to contraction frequency
Oral indometacin 100 mg then 25 to 50 mg six hourly for 48 hours
Magnesium sulfate infusion at a higher rate for tocolysis as well
Oral nifedipine 20 mg then 10 to 20 mg every 6 to 8 hours, titrated to contractions

subtopic_detail: Antihypertensive selection during severe pre-eclampsia with contraindication to first-line
stem: A 30-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks has new severe hypertension and a frontal headache. She has moderate asthma, admitted to hospital last year, and uses a fluticasone-salmeterol preventer daily.

data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes without clonus, no visual disturbance or epigastric pain; CTG reassuring
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 128 x10^9/L, ALT 62 U/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, urine protein creatinine ratio 68 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive now?

options.text: Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate 400 microgram every 5 minutes
Oral labetalol 200 mg, repeated once after 30 minutes
Oral methyldopa 500 mg then 250 to 500 mg three times daily
Oral immediate-release nifedipine 10 mg, repeated every 30 minutes
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose alone

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia recognition and delivery timing
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 34 weeks had a sudden painless vaginal loss of about 30 mL immediately after spontaneous rupture of membranes. Her in-vitro fertilisation twin pregnancy has a bilobed placenta with a velamentous cord insertion of the leading twin.

data_table.Twin 1 cardiotocograph: Baseline 100 /min falling to 80 /min with recurrent variable decelerations
data_table.Maternal: Speculum confirms ruptured membranes with fresh red blood; cervix not dilated; HR 92 /min, BP 110/68 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continuous cardiotocography for 4 hours with expectant management
Large bore intravenous access and cross match 4 units before deciding
Category 1 caesarean section now for acute fetal compromise
Intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg with delivery deferred 24 hours
Digital vaginal examination to determine cervical dilatation first

subtopic_detail: Endometrial cancer suspicion in postmenopausal bleeding with atrophic ultrasound
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 63-year-old woman who reports a single episode of light postmenopausal per vaginum bleeding 3 days ago on a background of 12 years of amenorrhoea. She has hypertension controlled on perindopril and takes oral tamoxifen 20 mg daily for the last 18 months following breast cancer surgery. Her BMI is 32 kg/m2 and she has type 2 diabetes managed on metformin.

On examination the abdomen is soft and non-tender. Speculum shows an atrophic-appearing cervix with no visible cause for the bleed. Bimanual examination reveals a small anteverted mobile uterus and no adnexal mass. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a homogenous endometrial thickness of 3 mm with no cystic changes and no adnexal abnormality. Cervical screening is up to date and normal.

data_table.Presenting complaint: Single episode of light PMB 3 days ago; 12 years amenorrhoea
data_table.Risk factors: BMI 32; T2DM on metformin; tamoxifen 20 mg for 18 months
data_table.Examination: Atrophic cervix; small mobile uterus; no adnexal mass
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: Endometrium 3 mm homogenous; no cystic change; no adnexal abnormality
data_table.Screening: Cervical screening up to date and normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe topical oestrogen cream for 6 weeks and review if bleeding recurs
Reassure the patient and arrange follow-up if there is any further vaginal bleeding
Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in 3 months to look for interval endometrial thickening
Order a serum CA-125 and defer further investigation until the result is available
Refer for hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy despite an endometrial thickness of 3 mm

subtopic_detail: Diagnosis of gestational diabetes with 75 g OGTT
stem: A 32-year-old primigravida at 27 weeks had a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks. Her booking body mass index was 31 kg/m2, her mother has type 2 diabetes, and her booking random glucose was 8.4 mmol/L.

data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.4 mmol/L, 1 hour 9.8 mmol/L, 2 hour 8.6 mmol/L (ADIPS thresholds 5.1, 10.0, 8.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Normal result; no further glucose testing is required this pregnancy
Suggests pre-existing type 2 diabetes; request an HbA1c to confirm
Meets the criteria for gestational diabetes; refer for multidisciplinary care
Borderline result; repeat the test in 4 weeks before intervening
Normal result, but start metformin because of the family history

subtopic_detail: Uterotonic sequencing in primary postpartum haemorrhage
stem: A 34-year-old primigravida had a normal vaginal birth at 40 weeks after oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly at delivery of the anterior shoulder. Twelve minutes later she has lost 900 mL from an atonic uterus.

data_table.Examination: Atonic uterus above the umbilicus, placenta complete, bladder empty
data_table.Done so far: Bimanual massage, intravenous access, crossmatch sent, tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic?

options.text: Ergometrine 250 micrograms intravenously, repeated after 5 minutes
Carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscularly, repeated every 15 minutes
Misoprostol 800 micrograms per rectum as a single dose
Oxytocin 5 units intravenously, then 40 units in 1 L over 4 hours
Repeat oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly into the thigh

subtopic_detail: Antihypertensive threshold in severe pre-eclampsia
stem: A 28-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks with pre-eclampsia diagnosed four days ago, on labetalol 200 mg orally twice daily, has headache and epigastric pain.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 172/112 mmHg confirmed on repeat, HR 96 /min, CTG normal
data_table.Examination: Alert, brisk reflexes without clonus
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 128 x10^9/L, ALT 68 U/L
data_table.Given: Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading dose

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate blood pressure management?

options.text: Increase oral labetalol to 400 mg three times daily and recheck in 60 minutes
Intravenous nitroprusside aiming for below 130/80 mmHg within the hour
Intravenous methyldopa 250 mg with a repeat magnesium sulfate 4 g load
Emergency caesarean section before any further blood pressure treatment

subtopic_detail: Hyperemesis gravidarum inpatient management
stem: A 26-year-old primigravida at 9 weeks has vomited daily for 3 weeks and lost 4.5 kg from 68 kg. Pyridoxine and doxylamine have not helped. She has managed only sips of water for 24 hours.

data_table.Examination: Dry mouth, urinary ketones 3
data_table.Investigations: Na 132 mmol/L, K 3.1 mmol/L, urea 8.6 mmol/L, TSH and free T4 normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous sodium chloride with potassium, thiamine and ondansetron
Discharge on oral prednisolone 40 mg daily for 5 days with review tomorrow
Give intramuscular metoclopramide 10 mg and trial oral rehydration
Start 5 percent dextrose at maintenance rate with oral pyridoxine
Arrange dilation and evacuation of the pregnancy with social work referral

subtopic_detail: Timing of delivery for asymptomatic placenta praevia
stem: A 33-year-old para 1 at 34 weeks has placenta praevia, the placental edge covering the internal os by 22 mm at 32 weeks. She has had no bleeding. Her first birth was a caesarean.

data_table.Examination: No pain or bleeding, normal fetal movements, CTG normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Await spontaneous labour and aim for vaginal birth with continuous monitoring
Plan elective caesarean section at 39+0 weeks after magnetic resonance imaging
Plan elective caesarean section at 36+0 to 37+6 weeks after corticosteroids
Admit now for continuous cardiotocography until spontaneous labour begins
Perform external cephalic version at 36 weeks and await vaginal birth

subtopic_detail: Surgical choice for tubal ectopic after contralateral salpingectomy
stem: A 31-year-old nulliparous woman at 7 weeks of amenorrhoea has 3 days of right iliac fossa pain. She had a left salpingectomy 3 years ago and has been trying to conceive.

data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism, closed cervix
data_table.Investigations: Beta hCG 3200 IU/L; transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a right adnexal mass 32 x 28 mm containing a yolk sac, no cardiac activity, and free fluid in the pouch of Douglas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Methotrexate 50 mg/m2 intramuscularly with serial beta hCG follow up
Laparoscopic right salpingectomy to avoid persistent trophoblast
Expectant management with a repeat beta hCG in 48 hours
Laparoscopic right salpingostomy with serial beta hCG until zero
Laparoscopic wedge cornual resection preserving the fimbrial end

subtopic_detail: Augmentation of labour after previous caesarean
stem: A 32-year-old para 1 at 40+3 weeks is in spontaneous labour after a lower segment caesarean for breech two years ago. She consented to a trial of labour.

data_table.Examination: Contracting 2 in 10 for 40 seconds; cervix 5 cm, station -1, cephalic; membranes ruptured 2 hours ago, clear liquor
data_table.Progress: No cervical change over 2 hours; epidural in situ
data_table.Monitoring: Observations normal; CTG 140 /min with normal variability

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Insert a Foley catheter for mechanical cervical dilation, continuing cardiotocography
Give vaginal prostaglandin E2 3 mg, with continuous cardiotocography
Recommend immediate repeat caesarean section for failure to progress
Continue expectant management with intermittent auscultation for 4 hours
Commence intravenous oxytocin titrated to contractions, continuing cardiotocography

subtopic_detail: GDM diagnosis and immediate management on the 26 week OGTT
stem: A 32-year-old woman at 26+3 weeks in her second pregnancy has had her routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test.

data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT: fasting 5.4 mmol/L, 1 hour 9.6 mmol/L, 2 hour 8.7 mmol/L (ADIPS thresholds 5.1, 10.0, 8.5)
data_table.Examination: Booking BMI 27; BP 118/72 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Repeat the oral glucose tolerance test in 2 weeks before starting treatment
Start isophane insulin 10 units at night with capillary glucose monitoring
Start metformin 500 mg twice daily with capillary glucose monitoring
Refer to a dietitian and diabetes educator with capillary glucose monitoring
Continue routine antenatal care with no change to her current management

subtopic_detail: Magnesium seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia
stem: A 28-year-old primigravida at 34 plus 2 weeks has a new headache and epigastric pain, with one vomit overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 /min, BP 162/110 mmHg on repeat, FHR 140 bpm with a reactive CTG
data_table.Examination: Right upper quadrant tenderness, reflexes 3 plus with 2 beats of ankle clonus
data_table.Investigations: Urine PCR 78 mg/mmol (less than 30), platelets 88 x10^9/L, ALT 128 U/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous methyldopa 500 mg now and observe for four hours
Oral labetalol 200 mg alone, repeating the blood pressure 15-minutely
Intravenous diazepam 10 mg for prophylaxis with oral labetalol 100 mg
Intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg with observation alone
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour

subtopic_detail: Suitability for planned VBAC per RANZCOG
stem: A 33-year-old G3P2 at 36+4 weeks attends antenatal clinic. Her first birth was an emergency caesarean at 38 weeks through a lower segment transverse incision; her second was an uncomplicated vaginal birth after caesarean at 40 weeks.

data_table.Examination: BP 110/68 mmHg, cephalic on ultrasound, estimated fetal weight 50th centile
data_table.History: This pregnancy uncomplicated, no previous uterine rupture or classical caesarean

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about mode of delivery?

options.text: Planned vaginal birth, since a previous successful one raises the success rate
Elective repeat caesarean at 39 weeks, because any scar makes labour unsafe
Induction with prostaglandin E2 pessary at 39 weeks to shorten labour
Elective repeat caesarean, because her interpregnancy interval is under 24 months
Planned home birth, since her previous vaginal birth was uncomplicated

subtopic_detail: Cervical priming decision using the Bishop score
stem: A 34-year-old primigravida at 41 plus 3 weeks is admitted for post dates induction of labour. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated and there is no contraindication to vaginal birth.

data_table.Examination: Cervix posterior, 1 cm long, firm and closed; head 3 cm above the ischial spines; membranes intact
data_table.Other: BP 122/76 mmHg; reactive CTG; cephalic presentation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Artificial rupture of membranes now, then a titrated oxytocin infusion
Transcervical balloon overnight, reassessing the Bishop score in the morning
Vaginal misoprostol 25 microgram four-hourly for up to four doses
Titrated intravenous oxytocin from 2 milliunits per minute now
Caesarean section today, as induction with this cervix will fail

subtopic_detail: First line uterotonic choice in atonic PPH with hypertension excluded
stem: A 29-year-old primigravida delivered a 4.2 kg baby vaginally 20 minutes ago, with active third stage management including intramuscular oxytocin. She has lost 1200 mL and is still bleeding. She has never been hypertensive and has no bleeding disorder.

data_table.Examination: Uterus boggy above the umbilicus; placenta complete; no cervical tear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic?

options.text: Sublingual misoprostol 800 microgram
Intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram
Intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram
Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes
Intravenous adrenaline 100 microgram

subtopic_detail: Surgical management preference after prior contralateral salpingectomy
stem: A 32-year-old woman has left pelvic pain and light vaginal bleeding at 6 weeks by dates. She had a right salpingectomy three years ago for a ruptured tubal ectopic, with a macroscopically normal left tube noted. She has been trying to conceive for 12 months.

data_table.Investigations: Beta HCG 4600 IU/L, up from 4400 IU/L 48 hours earlier; transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterus, 22 mm left tubal mass with yolk sac, no cardiac activity, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with weekly beta HCG

Expectant management with beta HCG every 48 hours
Laparoscopic left salpingostomy with weekly beta HCG
Urgent laparotomy with left salpingectomy for rupture

subtopic_detail: Immediate first line manoeuvre in shoulder dystocia
stem: A 30-year-old multiparous woman at 39+6 weeks has delivered the fetal head, which has retracted against the perineum. The shoulders do not descend with routine axial traction. Her previous baby weighed 4.1 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Fetal heart rate 138 /min before delivery of the head
data_table.History: Diet-controlled gestational diabetes, estimated fetal weight 95th centile at 36 weeks
data_table.Team: Time keeper designated, paediatric team paged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate first manoeuvre?

options.text: Deliberate delivery of the posterior arm by the accoucheur
Rubin II internal rotation of the anterior shoulder
Cephalic replacement and category 1 caesarean section
Fundal pressure by an assistant with axial traction
McRoberts manoeuvre with suprapubic pressure by an assistant

subtopic_detail: Delivery of the second twin after the first with a transverse lie and cord accessible
stem: A 34-year-old primigravida with dichorionic diamniotic twins at 37+3 weeks has delivered twin 1 vaginally. She has an epidural in situ and consented antenatally to internal manoeuvres.

data_table.Ultrasound: Twin 2 transverse with the back down, membranes intact, estimated fetal weight 2.9 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step for the delivery of twin 2?

options.text: Internal podalic version to a footling breech, then breech extraction
External cephalic version, then amniotomy and oxytocin augmentation
Category 1 caesarean section for twin 2 under general anaesthesia
Artificial rupture of membranes, then observe for a longitudinal lie
Amniotomy followed by immediate ventouse assisted vaginal delivery

subtopic_detail: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis after an earlier sensitising event
stem:
You are the registrar in the antenatal clinic seeing a 27-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 28 weeks. She is blood group O RhD negative and her partner's group is unknown.

At 20 weeks she had a small painless vaginal bleed, was assessed in the day unit and received a dose of anti-D immunoglobulin at that time with a Kleihauer showing no excess fetal cells. She has had no bleeding since and reports normal fetal movements. Her antibody screen taken today is negative and her fetal morphology scan at 20 weeks was reported as normal with a posterior placenta clear of the os. She asks whether she needs anything further before delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 112/68, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6, fetal heart rate 142
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O RhD negative; antibody screen negative today; symphysis fundal height appropriate for dates

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: No further anti-D immunoglobulin, since a dose was already given for the bleed at 20 weeks
Anti-D immunoglobulin 250 international units now and repeat the same dose at 34 weeks gestation
Anti-D immunoglobulin 625 international units now and repeat the same dose at 34 weeks gestation
Anti-D immunoglobulin deferred until after delivery once the cord blood group has been determined
Kleihauer testing today with anti-D immunoglobulin given only if fetal cells are demonstrated

subtopic_detail: Bundle of care in threatened preterm birth before 30 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a level 4 regional hospital assessing a 31-year-old woman in her second pregnancy at 29 weeks and 3 days. She has had regular painful contractions every four minutes for two hours.

Speculum examination shows a closed cervix visually but digital examination finds the cervix 3 cm dilated and 80 per cent effaced. Her membranes are intact. She has had no corticosteroids in this pregnancy. She is afebrile with no uterine tenderness and her urinalysis and high vaginal swab show no evidence of infection. The cardiotocograph is reassuring with a baseline of 145 and normal variability. The neonatal unit here manages babies from 32 weeks and the tertiary centre is 90 minutes away by road.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7, fetal heart rate baseline 145
data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm dilated, 80 per cent effaced, membranes intact, vertex presenting
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph reassuring with normal variability; urinalysis and high vaginal swab show no evidence of infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intramuscular betamethasone, intravenous magnesium sulfate and transfer to the tertiary centre
Intramuscular betamethasone alone with observation in the birth suite and reassessment in six hours
Intravenous magnesium sulfate alone with transfer arranged once contractions have been suppressed
Oral nifedipine tocolysis alone with reassessment of the cervix after four hours of treatment
Intravenous benzylpenicillin for group B streptococcus prophylaxis with observation in the birth suite

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic selection in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33-year-old woman in her third pregnancy at 32 weeks and 1 day. She reports a sudden gush of clear fluid four hours ago followed by continued dampness.

Speculum examination shows a pool of clear liquor in the posterior fornix with no bleeding and a closed cervix. She has no contractions and no uterine tenderness. Her temperature is normal, her white cell count and C reactive protein are within normal limits, and the cardiotocograph is reassuring with a baseline of 138. Her group B streptococcus status is unknown and her low vaginal swab has just been sent. She had betamethasone commenced one hour ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 116/70, RR 15, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8, fetal heart rate baseline 138
data_table.Examination: Speculum: pool of clear liquor, cervix closed, no bleeding, no uterine tenderness
data_table.Investigations: White cell count and C reactive protein within normal limits; cardiotocograph reassuring; low vaginal swab pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for ten days alongside expectant inpatient management
Oral erythromycin for ten days alongside expectant inpatient management with surveillance
Intravenous benzylpenicillin now and continuing until delivery for group B streptococcus cover
No antibiotics with daily observations, and treatment commenced only if maternal fever develops
Oral metronidazole for seven days with repeat vaginal swabs performed at weekly intervals

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus prophylaxis with severe penicillin allergy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite with a 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 39 weeks and 2 days, now in established labour at 5 cm dilated with intact membranes.

Her routine 36 week low vaginal swab grew group B streptococcus. Antibiotic susceptibility testing was not requested on that isolate and the laboratory advises that the specimen is no longer available. Her allergy history records anaphylaxis to amoxicillin at age 22 requiring adrenaline and an overnight admission. She has no other allergies. Her observations and the cardiotocograph are reassuring and delivery is anticipated within the next four to six hours.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 94, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.9, fetal heart rate baseline 140
data_table.Investigations: 36 week low vaginal swab positive for group B streptococcus; susceptibility testing not performed and isolate unavailable; cardiotocograph reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin with adrenaline and resuscitation equipment available at the bedside
Intravenous cefazolin, since cross reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is uncommon
Intravenous clindamycin, which is the standard alternative agent in severe penicillin allergy
Intravenous vancomycin given as an infusion and repeated at the recommended dosing interval
Intravenous erythromycin given as an infusion and repeated at the recommended dosing interval

subtopic_detail: First line therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding with iron deficiency
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 41-year-old woman who describes flooding through a super tampon hourly on her heaviest two days and passing clots the size of a fifty cent coin. Her cycles are regular at 28 days and this pattern has been present for two years.

She has completed her family and does not want further children, and would prefer to avoid an operation. She has no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, pelvic pain or dyspareunia. Her cervical screening test six months ago was negative for human papillomavirus. Her transvaginal ultrasound reports a normal uterus with no fibroid, no polyp and an endometrial thickness of 6 mm. Her thyroid function and coagulation screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: normal uterus, no fibroid or polyp, endometrial thickness 6 mm; cervical screening test negative for human papillomavirus
data_table.Blood tests: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-165); ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-200); thyroid function and coagulation screen within normal limits

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Oral tranexamic acid taken on the heaviest days of each cycle with oral iron replacement
Oral mefenamic acid taken through the bleeding days of each cycle with oral iron replacement
Referral for endometrial ablation at the next available gynaecology outpatient appointment
A combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously without a hormone free interval and oral iron
A levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system inserted in the practice with oral iron replacement

subtopic_detail: Ovulation induction agent selection in polycystic ovary syndrome
stem:
You are the general practitioner with a special interest in women's health seeing a 27-year-old woman who has been trying to conceive for 14 months. Her cycles come every 45 to 70 days and she has hirsutism affecting her chin and upper lip.

Her body mass index is 31 kg/m2 and she has lost 4 kg over the last four months with dietitian support. Her partner's semen analysis is normal on two occasions. A hysterosalpingogram shows both tubes patent with normal uterine cavity contour. Her prolactin, thyroid function and 17 hydroxyprogesterone are within normal limits, and her pelvic ultrasound shows an antral follicle count of 28 in the right ovary. She has taken folic acid for six months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 122/76, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Antral follicle count 28 in the right ovary; hysterosalpingogram both tubes patent; partner semen analysis normal on two occasions
data_table.Blood tests: Prolactin, thyroid function and 17 hydroxyprogesterone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment to induce ovulation?

options.text: Letrozole taken for five days early in the cycle with ultrasound follicle tracking
Clomifene citrate taken for five days early in the cycle with ultrasound follicle tracking
Metformin taken twice daily as sole therapy with monitoring of cycle length over six months
Gonadotrophin injections given in a low dose step up protocol with ultrasound follicle tracking
Referral for in vitro fertilisation with a planned single embryo transfer in the first cycle

subtopic_detail: Antenatal planning for suspected placenta accreta spectrum
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a district hospital reviewing a 36-year-old woman in her fourth pregnancy at 32 weeks. She has had two previous lower segment caesarean sections and one vaginal birth.

She has had no bleeding in this pregnancy and feels well. Today's transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound reports an anterior placenta covering the internal os, loss of the retroplacental clear zone, multiple placental lacunae, and bridging vessels crossing the uterine serosa toward the bladder. The myometrial thickness overlying the placenta measures 1 mm. Her haemoglobin is 118 g/L and her blood group is A positive with a negative antibody screen. The nearest tertiary centre with an interventional radiology service is 40 minutes away.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 114/70, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6, fetal heart rate baseline 144
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: anterior placenta covering the internal os, loss of retroplacental clear zone, multiple lacunae, bridging vessels, myometrium 1 mm
data_table.Blood tests: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165); blood group A positive with negative antibody screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound at 36 weeks and plan a caesarean section here at 39 weeks gestation
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging to confirm the diagnosis before making any referral decision
Refer now to a specialist centre for planned delivery between 34 and 36 weeks with a multidisciplinary team
Plan a trial of vaginal birth given her previous successful vaginal delivery and absent bleeding
Plan a caesarean section here at 37 weeks with two units of cross matched blood available

subtopic_detail: Discordant amniotic fluid volumes in a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29-year-old woman with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 20 weeks and 4 days. Chorionicity was established at the 11 week scan by the T sign and a single placental mass.

She reports increasing abdominal tightness and breathlessness over ten days. Today's scan shows twin one with a deepest vertical pocket of 1.4 cm and a bladder that is not visualised over 40 minutes of observation, and twin two with a deepest vertical pocket of 9.2 cm and a full bladder. Both twins have normal umbilical artery Doppler waveforms with positive end diastolic flow and normal ductus venosus waveforms. Neither twin is hydropic and the estimated fetal weights differ by 14 per cent. Her cervical length is 34 mm and she is not contracting.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 108/66, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Twin one deepest vertical pocket 1.4 cm with bladder not visualised; twin two deepest vertical pocket 9.2 cm with full bladder; umbilical artery and ductus venosus Dopplers normal in both; cervical length 34 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat the ultrasound in two weeks as part of the standard monochorionic surveillance schedule
Urgent referral to a fetal medicine unit for consideration of fetoscopic laser photocoagulation
Amnioreduction of the polyhydramniotic sac with repeat drainage as maternal symptoms recur
Delivery by caesarean section after a course of antenatal corticosteroids has been completed
Selective reduction of the smaller twin by cord occlusion to protect the co twin from injury

subtopic_detail: Timing of thromboprophylaxis after neuraxial anaesthesia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 36-year-old woman two hours after an emergency caesarean section performed for failure to progress at full dilatation. Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2 and she had an unprovoked pulmonary embolism at age 28 that was treated for six months.

The caesarean was performed under a top up of her labour epidural, and the epidural catheter is still in situ for postoperative analgesia. The anaesthetist plans to remove it once she is mobile this evening, roughly six hours from now. Estimated blood loss was 700 mL, her uterus is well contracted and her lochia is normal. Her platelet count is 214 x10^9/L, her coagulation screen is within normal limits and she has no ongoing bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 116/72, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Uterus well contracted at the umbilicus, lochia normal, epidural catheter in situ and functioning
data_table.Blood tests: Platelets 214 x10^9/L (150-400); coagulation screen within normal limits; haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate thromboprophylaxis plan?

options.text: Prophylactic enoxaparin starting now and continuing for ten days after the caesarean section
Graduated compression stockings and early mobilisation with no pharmacological prophylaxis given
Low dose aspirin daily for six weeks with graduated compression stockings while an inpatient
Prophylactic enoxaparin starting four hours after epidural catheter removal and continuing six weeks
Therapeutic dose enoxaparin starting after catheter removal and continuing for three months postpartum

subtopic_detail: Antithrombotic management in obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome
stem:
You are the registrar in the recurrent miscarriage clinic seeing a 33-year-old woman who has had three consecutive first trimester losses at 8, 9 and 7 weeks, each with a fetal heart previously seen on ultrasound. She has no living children.

Her parental karyotypes are normal, her pelvic ultrasound shows a normal uterine cavity, and her thyroid function, prolactin and HbA1c are within normal limits. Lupus anticoagulant was positive on testing 14 weeks ago and again on repeat testing this week. Her anticardiolipin and beta 2 glycoprotein antibodies were negative on both occasions. She has never had a venous or arterial thrombosis, and has no rash or arthralgia. She has just had a positive home pregnancy test and her serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin today is 340 IU/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 116/70, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant positive on two occasions 14 weeks apart; anticardiolipin and beta 2 glycoprotein antibodies negative; pelvic ultrasound normal cavity; parental karyotypes normal
data_table.Blood tests: Serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin 340 IU/L; thyroid function, prolactin and HbA1c within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management for this pregnancy?

options.text: Low dose aspirin alone commenced today and continued until 36 weeks of gestation
Prednisolone with low dose aspirin commenced today and continued through the first trimester
Intravenous immunoglobulin infusions given monthly through the first and second trimesters
Vaginal progesterone pessaries nightly commenced today and continued until 16 weeks of gestation
Low dose aspirin with prophylactic dose low molecular weight heparin commenced from today

subtopic_detail: Endometrial thickness thresholds in postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58-year-old woman with two episodes of light vaginal bleeding in the past month. Her last menstrual period was seven years ago.

She completed treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer three years ago and has taken tamoxifen daily since. She takes no other hormonal preparation and uses no vaginal oestrogen. She has no postcoital bleeding and her cervical screening test last year was negative for human papillomavirus. Her body mass index is 24 kg/m2 and she has no diabetes. Her transvaginal ultrasound today reports an endometrial thickness of 3.2 mm with a heterogeneous subendometrial appearance and small cystic spaces, and normal ovaries.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 128/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 3.2 mm, heterogeneous subendometrial appearance with small cystic spaces, normal ovaries
data_table.Examination: Speculum: healthy cervix, no visible lesion, small amount of old blood in the vault

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Hysteroscopy with endometrial biopsy performed under anaesthesia at the next available list
Reassurance and review only if the bleeding recurs, since the endometrium measures under 4 mm
Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in three months with a further measurement of the endometrium
Cease tamoxifen and reassess the bleeding pattern over the following three months in clinic
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to characterise the endometrium before any tissue sampling

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus prophylaxis with severe penicillin allergy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar caring for a 29-year-old woman at 39 weeks in her first pregnancy who is in established labour with ruptured membranes two hours ago.

Her routine vaginal and rectal swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus. Her allergy record documents an episode of facial swelling, urticaria and wheeze within 20 minutes of a dose of amoxicillin as a teenager, requiring adrenaline in an emergency department. The laboratory has reported the isolate as resistant to clindamycin and susceptible to vancomycin. Her observations and the cardiotocograph are reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8, fetal heart rate 140
data_table.Examination: Cervix 5 cm dilated, membranes ruptured, clear liquor, vertex presentation
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal and rectal swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus; isolate resistant to clindamycin, susceptible to vancomycin

lead_in: Which intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is the most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin given four hourly until the baby is delivered
Intravenous cefazolin given eight hourly until the baby is delivered
Intravenous clindamycin given eight hourly until the baby is delivered
Oral azithromycin given as a single dose at the onset of established labour
Intravenous vancomycin given twelve hourly until the baby is delivered

subtopic_detail: Deterioration despite controlled blood pressure
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar caring for a 33-year-old woman at 34 weeks and 2 days in her second pregnancy, admitted three days ago with pre-eclampsia.

Her blood pressure was 168/112 on admission and is now 132/84 on oral labetalol. She completed a course of betamethasone 36 hours ago and has received magnesium sulfate since admission. She reports new right upper quadrant pain that woke her overnight and has vomited twice. Her cardiotocograph is normal with good variability and no decelerations, and umbilical artery Doppler studies show normal end diastolic flow. Her blood results from this morning are compared with those on admission below.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 132/84, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7, fetal heart rate 142
data_table.Examination: Right upper quadrant tenderness, brisk reflexes without clonus, no peripheral oedema progression
data_table.Investigations: Platelets fallen from 186 to 74 x10^9/L (150-400); alanine aminotransferase risen from 32 to 218 U/L (less than 40); lactate dehydrogenase 780 U/L (120-250); creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90); urine protein creatinine ratio 92 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue expectant management to 37 weeks with daily bloods and cardiotocography
Arrange delivery now, continuing magnesium sulfate and antihypertensive therapy
Increase the labetalol dose and repeat her blood tests again in 24 hours
Give a second course of betamethasone and plan delivery in a further 48 hours
Transfuse platelets and continue expectant management with six hourly blood tests

subtopic_detail: Menopausal hormone therapy regimen selection
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 52-year-old woman whose last menstrual period was eighteen months ago. She has fifteen to twenty hot flushes a day and wakes drenched three or four times a night, and she has stopped attending her book club because of them.

Her uterus is intact and a recent transvaginal ultrasound for a single episode of spotting showed an endometrial thickness of 3 mm. She has no personal or family history of breast cancer and no history of venous thromboembolism. Her blood pressure is well controlled on no medication and she has tried an eight week trial of a serotonin reuptake inhibitor with little benefit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 124/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, breast examination normal, no pelvic mass
data_table.Investigations: Endometrial thickness 3 mm on transvaginal ultrasound; cervical screening up to date and negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to recommend?

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol alone applied twice weekly with annual pelvic ultrasound
Cyclical oestradiol with a twelve day progestogen to produce a monthly bleed
Continuous combined transdermal oestradiol with oral micronised progesterone
Tibolone daily with review of vasomotor symptoms after three months of therapy
Vaginal oestradiol pessaries twice weekly with a non-hormonal oral adjunct

subtopic_detail: Genitourinary symptoms after hormone receptor positive breast cancer
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58-year-old woman referred with vaginal dryness and pain with penetration that has worsened over a year. She finished treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer three years ago and is in year three of anastrozole with two years remaining.

She has tried a lubricant at intercourse only, with little benefit. She has no bleeding or discharge. Examination shows pale thin vaginal walls with loss of rugae, and her most recent oncology review was clear.

data_table.Examination: Pale atrophic vaginal epithelium, loss of rugae, no lesion or ulceration, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus; vaginal swab shows no infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Vaginal oestriol cream three nights weekly after discussion with her oncologist
Systemic transdermal oestradiol with oral micronised progesterone protection
Regular vaginal moisturiser with lubricant at intercourse and pelvic floor physiotherapy
Switch anastrozole to tamoxifen to improve her vaginal symptoms during treatment
Fractional carbon dioxide laser therapy delivered as three treatments six weeks apart

subtopic_detail: Initial management of symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 56-year-old woman who describes a dragging sensation and a feeling of something coming down that is worst by the end of the day. She has three children delivered vaginally, the youngest aged 22, and has not sought treatment for this before.

She has no urinary incontinence and no bowel symptoms. On examination the anterior vaginal wall descends to 1 cm above the hymen on straining with the cervix well supported. She works as a childcare educator and has completed her family.

data_table.Examination: Anterior compartment descent to 1 cm above the hymen on Valsalva, cervix well supported, no vault descent
data_table.Investigations: Post-void residual volume 30 mL; urinalysis shows no infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for anterior colporrhaphy with the aim of restoring anterior wall support
Refer for supervised pelvic floor muscle training over at least sixteen weeks
Fit a ring pessary at this visit and arrange a review appointment in six months
Prescribe vaginal oestrogen cream as sole therapy and review in three months
Arrange magnetic resonance defaecating proctography to define the compartments involved

subtopic_detail: Lactational mastitis not responding to milk removal
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar seeing a 29-year-old woman three weeks postpartum who has had a painful red area in her left breast for 36 hours with fevers and shivers. The midwife reviewed her yesterday, corrected the attachment and advised frequent feeding from the affected side, which she has done.

She is still febrile and the red area has extended slightly. The breast is tender and firm over the upper outer quadrant with no discrete fluctuant lump and no nipple discharge. She has no penicillin allergy and her baby is feeding and gaining weight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98, BP 116/70, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Examination: Wedge shaped erythema over the left upper outer quadrant, firm and tender, no fluctuance, no axillary abscess
data_table.Investigations: Not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue effective milk removal alone and review again in a further 24 hours
Advise expressing and discarding milk from the affected breast during treatment
Arrange breast ultrasound before deciding whether antibiotic treatment is required
Start oral dicloxacillin or flucloxacillin and continue feeding from both breasts
Start oral cefalexin and advise a temporary switch to formula feeding for five days

subtopic_detail: Intermediate risk result under the renewed screening program
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing results for a 33-year-old woman who had her first cervical screening test two weeks ago after moving to Australia. She has no abnormal bleeding and no pain.

The laboratory reports oncogenic human papillomavirus detected, not types 16 or 18, with reflex liquid based cytology showing negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. She is not pregnant, uses a copper intrauterine device and is not immunosuppressed. She asks whether she needs a procedure.

data_table.Examination: Cervix appears macroscopically normal, no contact bleeding, intrauterine device threads visible
data_table.Investigations: Oncogenic human papillomavirus detected, not 16 or 18; reflex liquid based cytology negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for colposcopy now because oncogenic human papillomavirus has been detected
Repeat the human papillomavirus test in twelve months and act on that result
Return to routine five yearly screening as the cytology showed no abnormality
Repeat the screening test in six months and refer if the virus is still detected
Offer human papillomavirus vaccination now and repeat the test after the course

subtopic_detail: Ovulation induction in anovulatory polycystic ovary syndrome
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 28-year-old woman who has been trying to conceive for sixteen months. She has four to five periods a year and has had facial hirsutism since her late teens.

Her body mass index is 32 kg/m2 and she has lost 4 kg with a dietitian over four months. Her partner's semen analysis is normal and a hysterosalpingogram shows both tubes patent with a normal uterine cavity. Thyroid function and prolactin are within normal limits and she has been taking folic acid for six months.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 32 kg/m2, Ferriman-Gallwey score 12, no acanthosis nigricans, no clitoromegaly
data_table.Investigations: Anti-Mullerian hormone elevated for age; mid-luteal progesterone 4 nmol/L on two cycles (ovulatory more than 20); HbA1c 38 mmol/mol (less than 42); thyroid function and prolactin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment to achieve pregnancy?

options.text: Metformin as a single agent titrated to 1.5 g daily over four weeks
Combined oral contraception for three cycles to regulate her menstrual pattern
Letrozole for five days early in the cycle with monitoring of the response
Referral for in vitro fertilisation with a single embryo transfer policy
Laparoscopic ovarian drilling as a definitive treatment for her anovulatory cycles

subtopic_detail: Outpatient treatment of pelvic inflammatory disease
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 22-year-old woman with five days of lower abdominal pain, deep pain with intercourse and an increase in vaginal discharge. Her last menstrual period was twelve days ago and a urine pregnancy test is negative.

She has had two new partners in the past three months and uses condoms inconsistently. On bimanual examination she has cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness with no palpable mass. She is tolerating oral fluids and has no allergies, and transvaginal ultrasound shows no tubo-ovarian collection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 114/70, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.6
data_table.Examination: Cervical motion tenderness, bilateral adnexal tenderness, mucopurulent cervical discharge, no mass
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative; endocervical nucleic acid amplification testing pending; white cells 12.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); transvaginal ultrasound shows no collection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to start now?

options.text: Oral azithromycin as a single dose with repeat testing for cure in four weeks
Await the nucleic acid amplification results and treat according to the organism
Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin with surgical review arranged
Oral doxycycline for fourteen days with metronidazole for the same duration
Ceftriaxone intramuscularly with oral doxycycline and metronidazole for fourteen days

subtopic_detail: Folate dosing and antiseizure medicine review
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar seeing a 27-year-old woman who plans to conceive in the next six months. She has generalised epilepsy that has been seizure free for three years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, having previously failed lamotrigine because of a rash.

She takes no other medicines, does not smoke and has a body mass index of 23 kg/m2. She has no personal or family history of neural tube defect and her diet includes fortified breads and cereals. She asks what she should do before stopping contraception.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Arrange urgent neurology review to change medicine and start high dose folate
Continue valproate at the current dose and start folic acid 500 micrograms daily
Stop valproate immediately and start folic acid 5 mg daily from next month
Continue valproate and arrange detailed morphology scanning at nineteen weeks
Rechallenge with lamotrigine now and start folic acid 500 micrograms daily

subtopic_detail: Human chorionic gonadotrophin surveillance after molar evacuation
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman seven weeks after suction evacuation of a histologically confirmed complete hydatidiform mole. She has had no further bleeding and no abdominal pain and is using combined oral contraception.

Her serum human chorionic gonadotrophin has been measured weekly. The last four values are 3120, 2980, 3050 and 2990 IU/L. Examination shows no vaginal lesion and her chest is clear. A repeat pelvic ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a slightly heterogeneous myometrial echo pattern.

data_table.Examination: Uterus not palpable abdominally, no vaginal lesion, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Serial weekly human chorionic gonadotrophin 3120, 2980, 3050 and 2990 IU/L; haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-155); thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue weekly surveillance and repeat the ultrasound in a further four weeks
Arrange repeat suction evacuation of the uterine cavity under ultrasound guidance
Refer to a gestational trophoblastic disease centre for staging and treatment
Cease the combined oral contraception as it is suppressing the fall in the marker
Arrange total abdominal hysterectomy as definitive management of the plateau

subtopic_detail: Persisting vulval plaque despite potent topical corticosteroid
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 67-year-old woman with biopsy proven vulval lichen sclerosus diagnosed four years ago. She has used clobetasol propionate ointment as directed and her itch has settled everywhere except one area.

On the left labium majus there is a 12 mm firm white thickened plaque that has been present for five months and has not changed with treatment. The surrounding skin shows the pale atrophic change and architectural loss typical of her condition, without fissuring or ulceration. Her adherence has been confirmed by tube counts at each review and she has no vaginal discharge.

data_table.Examination: 12 mm firm hyperkeratotic plaque on the left labium majus, surrounding pallor and loss of architecture, no ulcer, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Vulval swab shows no candida or bacterial pathogen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a punch biopsy of the thickened plaque and continue her current ointment
Escalate to a more potent corticosteroid under occlusion and review in three months
Change to topical tacrolimus ointment twice daily and reassess in three months
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to stage the vulval abnormality
Prescribe a course of oral prednisolone and review the plaque again in six weeks

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a single positive antiphospholipid result
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 33-year-old woman who has had three first trimester losses, the most recent six weeks ago. She has one healthy child born at term and no thrombotic history.

Bloods taken at the time of the most recent loss show a positive lupus anticoagulant and a negative anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I. Parental karyotypes are normal, pelvic ultrasound shows a normal uterine cavity, and thyroid function and HbA1c are within normal limits. She is not pregnant now and is asking whether she should start treatment before trying again.

data_table.Examination: No livedo, no leg swelling, no synovitis
data_table.Investigations: Lupus anticoagulant positive at the time of loss; anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I negative; thyroid function and HbA1c within normal limits; pelvic ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start aspirin and prophylactic enoxaparin now and continue through the next pregnancy
Start low dose aspirin alone and repeat the full antibody panel during pregnancy
Reassure her that three first trimester losses need no further testing or treatment
Start prednisolone through the first trimester and repeat the panel after delivery
Repeat the antibody testing at least twelve weeks apart before labelling and treating

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding during tamoxifen therapy
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 61-year-old woman with two episodes of light vaginal bleeding in the past month. She is four years into tamoxifen for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer and her last menstrual period was at age 51.

Transvaginal ultrasound reports an endometrial thickness of 9 mm with a cystic subendometrial appearance and no focal lesion identified. She takes no anticoagulant, the vaginal epithelium appears healthy, and her cervical screening is up to date and negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus.

data_table.Examination: Vulva and vagina healthy, cervix normal, uterus normal size, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Endometrial thickness 9 mm with cystic subendometrial change on transvaginal ultrasound; haemoglobin 131 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in three months and investigate if thickness increases
Arrange hysteroscopy with directed endometrial biopsy under anaesthesia
Reassure her that the thickness is below the threshold requiring further assessment
Cease tamoxifen and reassess the endometrium with imaging after three months
Arrange pelvic magnetic resonance imaging to characterise the endometrial appearance

subtopic_detail: Severity assessment after oocyte retrieval
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 30-year-old woman six days after oocyte retrieval in a fresh in vitro fertilisation cycle. She has abdominal distension, nausea and breathlessness when lying flat, and her weight is 4 kg above her pre-cycle baseline.

She passed only 300 mL of urine in the last 24 hours despite drinking. Ultrasound shows enlarged ovaries with moderate ascites and no adnexal torsion. Embryo transfer has not yet occurred and all embryos have been frozen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, BP 98/60, RR 22, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Tense distended abdomen, shifting dullness, calves soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.49 (0.35-0.45); white cells 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); creatinine 104 micromol/L (45-90); sodium 130 mmol/L (135-145); albumin 27 g/L (35-50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Manage at home with oral fluids, daily weights and review in the clinic in 48 hours
Admit for intravenous fluids with furosemide added to improve her urine output
Admit for observation with oral fluids alone and repeat the bloods in the morning
Admit for intravenous fluid replacement with thromboprophylaxis and paracentesis if needed
Arrange laparoscopy to drain the ascites and assess the ovaries for torsion

subtopic_detail: Assessment before surgery for mixed urinary incontinence
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 54-year-old woman with four years of urinary leakage. She leaks with coughing and also has sudden urgency with leakage on the way to the toilet, and she cannot say which is more troublesome.

She has completed six months of supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy and a three month trial of an antimuscarinic with partial benefit only. Her bladder diary shows nine voids daily with two urgency episodes and no nocturia. Post-void residual volume is 40 mL, urinalysis shows no infection and no haematuria, and she is now asking about surgery.

data_table.Examination: Stress leak demonstrated on cough with a full bladder, no prolapse beyond the hymen, good pelvic floor contraction
data_table.Investigations: Post-void residual 40 mL; urinalysis negative for nitrites, leucocytes and blood; bladder diary shows nine voids daily and two urgency episodes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to mid-urethral sling surgery on the basis of the demonstrated stress leak
Arrange urodynamic studies to define the relative contribution of each component
Start a second antimuscarinic agent and continue the physiotherapy program
Arrange intravesical botulinum toxin injection for her urgency related symptoms
Prescribe topical vaginal oestrogen and review her symptoms again in six months

subtopic_detail: Suspected deep disease with urinary tract involvement
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 34-year-old woman with eight years of increasingly severe period pain and deep pain with intercourse. For the past year she has noticed blood in her urine for two days at the start of each period and has had two courses of antibiotics for presumed infection.

Urine cultures taken during those episodes were negative. She has been on a continuous combined oral contraceptive for six months with partial benefit and has no bowel symptoms. Transvaginal ultrasound performed at a general radiology practice was reported as normal, and renal function is preserved.

data_table.Examination: Tenderness and nodularity in the posterior fornix, fixed retroverted uterus, no adnexal mass palpable
data_table.Investigations: Two urine cultures negative during symptomatic episodes; creatinine 72 micromol/L (45-90); transvaginal ultrasound reported normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat urine culture during the next episode and treat with a longer antibiotic course
Proceed directly to diagnostic laparoscopy without further imaging beforehand
Add a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist for three months and reassess symptoms
Arrange specialist pelvic imaging assessing the ureters, bladder and posterior compartment
Arrange cystoscopy alone to visualise and biopsy any bladder lesions present

subtopic_detail: Preconception antiepileptic optimisation in a woman on sodium valproate
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 27-year-old woman who tells you she and her partner want to start trying for a baby in the next few months. She has generalised tonic clonic seizures that have been fully controlled for three years on sodium valproate 800 mg daily, and she drives to work each day.

She has no other medical history, takes no other medication and does not smoke or drink alcohol. Her cycles are regular and she has never been pregnant. She is not currently using contraception and asks what she should do before conceiving.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Seizure free for three years, no recent antiepileptic drug levels, not taking any supplement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice to give her today?

options.text: Refer for specialist review to change the antiepileptic before conception
Continue the current dose and start folic acid 5 mg daily from now
Stop the antiepileptic now and reassess seizure control in six months
Add lamotrigine to the current regimen and reduce the dose slowly
Advise conception now with folic acid 500 micrograms daily

subtopic_detail: Levothyroxine adjustment for treated hypothyroidism in the first trimester
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31-year-old woman who has just discovered she is pregnant. Her last menstrual period places her at 7 weeks gestation and an early scan confirms a single intrauterine pregnancy with a fetal heart present.

She has autoimmune hypothyroidism diagnosed six years ago and has taken levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily without change for the last two years, with a stable result at her annual check. She takes no other medication, is not on any iodine containing supplement and feels well with no palpitations, tremor or neck swelling. Her thyroid function was checked yesterday.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 108/66, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: No goitre, no tremor, no proptosis, reflexes normal
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 6.8 mIU/L (first trimester target below 2.5); free thyroxine 11.2 pmol/L (10-20)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the current dose and recheck thyroid function at 28 weeks
Measure thyroid peroxidase antibodies before changing the levothyroxine
Reduce the dose because reference ranges fall in early pregnancy
Increase the dose by about 30 per cent and recheck in four weeks
Refer for radioactive iodine uptake scanning to clarify the cause

subtopic_detail: Weight banded enoxaparin thromboprophylaxis after emergency caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetric resident reviewing a 33-year-old woman on the first morning after an emergency caesarean section performed at 39 weeks for failure to progress after fourteen hours of labour. Her baby is feeding well and she has not yet been out of bed because of pain.

Her booking body mass index was 36 kg/m2 and her weight this morning is 98 kg. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism and takes no regular medication. Her blood loss was 500 mL, her haemoglobin is stable and her platelet count and renal function are normal. The regional anaesthesia catheter was removed six hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Weight 98 kg, abdominal wound dry and intact, calves soft and non-tender, mobilising only with assistance
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155); platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400); creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate thromboprophylaxis to prescribe?

options.text: Start enoxaparin 20 mg subcutaneously daily for seven days
Start enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for seven days
Prescribe graduated compression stockings alone until she is discharged
Start enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously twice daily for six weeks
Start enoxaparin 60 mg subcutaneously daily for seven days

subtopic_detail: Choice of technique when a woman requests permanent contraception
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 34-year-old woman in clinic who has three children, the youngest aged 4 years, and has decided she does not want any more pregnancies. She has used the combined oral contraceptive pill for years but now gets migraine with aura and has stopped it.

She has no significant medical history, has never had abdominal surgery and her body mass index is 27 kg/m2. Her last cervical screening test was negative two years ago and her periods are regular and not heavy. She has read about several approaches and asks which operation you would recommend for her.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2, abdomen soft with no surgical scars, normal bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening negative two years ago, pregnancy test negative today

lead_in: Which procedure would you recommend?

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopic tubal occlusion as a day case procedure
Recommend laparoscopic bilateral salpingectomy as the preferred method
Arrange laparoscopic tubal occlusion using Filshie clips instead
Insert a 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system for her instead
Defer the decision and review her again in twelve months' time

subtopic_detail: Suppressive therapy for recurrent bacterial vaginosis
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29-year-old woman who has had four episodes of a thin grey discharge with a strong fishy smell in the past twelve months. Each episode has settled completely with a week of treatment and then returned within six to eight weeks, and she says the smell is worse after sex and after her period.

She is in a stable relationship with one male partner, uses condoms inconsistently and does not douche. There is no itch, no soreness and no pain with sex. Vaginal pH today is 5.2, microscopy shows clue cells with an absence of lactobacilli, and there is no candidal pseudohyphae. Nucleic acid testing is negative for Trichomonas vaginalis, chlamydia and gonorrhoea.

data_table.Examination: Thin homogeneous grey discharge coating the vaginal walls, no vulval erythema, cervix normal
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH 5.2; clue cells present with absent lactobacilli; nucleic acid testing negative for trichomonas, chlamydia and gonorrhoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give a single 2 g oral metronidazole dose and review as needed
Prescribe a seven day course of oral fluconazole weekly for six months
Treat with oral metronidazole then twice weekly intravaginal gel
Prescribe oral clindamycin and treat her regular male sexual partner
Advise vaginal douching with a lactic acid preparation each week

subtopic_detail: Time critical investigation after intrauterine fetal death at 34 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar caring for a 32-year-old woman in her first pregnancy who presented at 34 weeks and 2 days because she had not felt the baby move for two days. Ultrasound has confirmed the absence of fetal cardiac activity and you have broken this news with the midwife present.

She has had no bleeding, no abdominal pain and no rupture of membranes. Her blood pressure has been normal at every visit and is normal now, her urine shows no protein and she has no headache or visual disturbance. Her booking bloods were unremarkable and she is rhesus D positive. Induction of labour is planned to begin later today after she has had time with her family.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88, blood pressure 116/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 31 cm, uterus soft and non-tender, no vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound confirms absent fetal cardiac activity; urinalysis shows no protein; full blood count and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: Which investigation is most important to obtain before the birth?

options.text: Arrange a thrombophilia screen including lupus anticoagulant now
Send maternal blood for a full torch serology panel before the birth
Arrange a whole body magnetic resonance imaging scan of the fetus
Perform amniocentesis for karyotype after the birth has occurred
Take maternal blood for a Kleihauer test before birth is induced

subtopic_detail: Referral pathway for a suspicious adnexal mass after menopause
stem:
