You are the general practitioner seeing a 63-year-old woman who has had three months of persistent bloating, a feeling of fullness after only a few mouthfuls and needing to pass urine more often. She has attributed all of this to getting older and to a change in her diet.

She went through menopause at 51 years, has never used hormone therapy and has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Her weight is stable and she has had no vaginal bleeding. A pelvic ultrasound performed yesterday describes a 7 cm right adnexal mass with solid areas and papillary projections, together with a small volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Her CA125 result is back today.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen mildly distended, no palpable mass, no lymphadenopathy, no ascitic shifting dullness
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound shows a 7 cm right adnexal mass with solid areas and papillary projections and free pelvic fluid; CA125 210 kU/L (less than 35)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a gynaecological oncology centre for definitive surgery
Repeat the pelvic ultrasound and the CA125 in three months' time
Arrange ultrasound guided aspiration of the cyst fluid for cytology
Book a laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy at the local district hospital
Start a trial of hormone therapy and reassess the symptoms after that

subtopic_detail: Whether urodynamic testing is required before continence surgery
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 57-year-old woman who has leaked urine for two years whenever she coughs, sneezes or lifts her grandchildren. She has completed six months of supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist and says it has made no difference to her leaking.

She describes no sudden desperate need to pass urine, gets up once at night and empties her bladder without straining or hesitancy. A three day bladder diary records normal voided volumes with no urgency episodes. Her cough stress test is positive with immediate leakage, her post-void residual volume is 30 mL, and there is no prolapse below the level of the hymen. Urinalysis shows no blood, protein, nitrites or leucocytes.

data_table.Examination: Positive cough stress test with immediate leakage, no prolapse beyond the hymen, good pelvic floor contraction
data_table.Investigations: Post-void residual 30 mL; three day bladder diary shows normal volumes without urgency; urinalysis clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform multichannel urodynamic testing before any continence surgery
Start oxybutynin and reassess her symptoms again in three months
Repeat another six months of supervised pelvic floor muscle training
Refer for a midurethral sling without further urodynamic testing
Arrange cystoscopy and a bladder diary before proceeding any further

subtopic_detail: Decompensating rheumatic mitral stenosis in the second trimester
stem: A 29-year-old at 24 weeks has become breathless climbing one flight of stairs over three weeks and last night woke needing to sit up. She grew up in Vanuatu with repeated childhood sore joints and fever.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 /min and regular, BP 104/68 mmHg, SpO2 97% in air
data_table.Examination: Opening snap with apical mid diastolic murmur, chest clear, jugular venous pressure 4 cm
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram mitral valve area 1.2 cm2, mean gradient 12 mmHg; sinus rhythm on electrocardiogram

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start an intravenous furosemide infusion for negative balance
Start metoprolol to lengthen diastolic filling and limit activity
Arrange delivery by caesarean section within the next 48 hours
Start nifedipine to reduce afterload and improve exercise capacity
Start enoxaparin and arrange balloon valvuloplasty now

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation choice for a mechanical heart valve in early pregnancy
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar seeing a 31-year-old woman who has just found out she is 5 weeks pregnant. She has a bileaflet mechanical aortic valve replacement performed six years ago for congenital bicuspid disease and has had no thromboembolic events since.

She takes warfarin 3.5 mg daily and her international normalised ratio has been stable within target for the last year, including a result of 2.8 taken last week. She has no atrial fibrillation, no left ventricular impairment and her most recent echocardiogram showed normal prosthetic valve gradients. She has heard that her medication can harm the baby and is anxious about what to do.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 112/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Crisp mechanical second heart sound, no murmur of regurgitation, no signs of heart failure
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 2.8 (target 2.0-3.0); echocardiogram shows normal prosthetic gradients and normal left ventricular function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Change to therapeutic enoxaparin twice daily for the first trimester
Change to a direct oral anticoagulant for the whole of the pregnancy
Stop anticoagulation until 12 weeks and use aspirin in the meantime
Change to unfractionated heparin by infusion until 12 weeks gestation
Continue warfarin now and change to heparin at 36 weeks gestation

subtopic_detail: Surveillance plan in the pregnancy after a placentally mediated stillbirth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 30-year-old woman at 12 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first baby was stillborn at 36 weeks two years ago after she noticed reduced movements, and the placental histopathology reported extensive maternal vascular malperfusion with accelerated villous maturation and infarction. The birth weight was on the 4th centile.

She has a body mass index of 24 kg/m2, has never smoked and has no diabetes, hypertension or autoimmune disease. Antiphospholipid antibodies were negative on two occasions at least twelve weeks apart. Her blood pressure today is normal, her urine has no protein and her dating scan is consistent with her last menstrual period.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76, blood pressure 110/68, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, uterus consistent with dates, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Antiphospholipid antibodies negative on two occasions twelve weeks apart; dating ultrasound consistent; urinalysis shows no protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for this pregnancy?

options.text: Start prophylactic enoxaparin from now until six weeks postpartum
Begin weekly cardiotocography from 28 weeks and expect a term birth
Start low dose aspirin before 16 weeks with serial growth scans
Plan elective birth at 37 weeks without any additional surveillance
Reassure that recurrence is not increased and provide routine care

subtopic_detail: Seizure at 33 weeks in a woman with pre existing epilepsy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the assessment unit for a 24-year-old woman at 33 weeks gestation. Her partner witnessed a generalised tonic clonic seizure lasting about ninety seconds at home, with tongue biting and a period of confusion afterwards. She has known generalised epilepsy and takes lamotrigine, and this is her first seizure in two years.

She has no headache, no visual disturbance and no epigastric pain, and her partner says she has had no swelling of her face or hands. She is now fully alert and orientated. Her reflexes are normal without clonus, and the cardiotocograph shows a normal baseline with accelerations and no decelerations. A lamotrigine level taken on arrival has come back well below her usual pre-pregnancy value.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96, blood pressure 148/94, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9, fetal heart rate baseline 140
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, no clonus, normal fundi, no facial or hand oedema, tongue laceration present
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein creatinine ratio 12 mg/mmol (less than 30); platelets 240 x10^9/L (150-400); alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L (less than 35); creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90); lamotrigine level well below her pre-pregnancy value

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the lamotrigine dose after checking the serum level
Give a magnesium sulfate loading dose and plan urgent birth today
Give intravenous labetalol and repeat the protein creatinine ratio
Load with intravenous levetiracetam and admit her for observation
Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain before any treatment

subtopic_detail: Fertility sparing surgery for a suspected ovarian germ cell tumour
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar admitting a 19-year-old university student with three weeks of increasing abdominal swelling and a dragging discomfort in her right side. She has felt her jeans getting tight and has been short of breath lying flat.

She has regular periods, has never been pregnant and takes no medication. There is a firm non-tender mass arising from the pelvis reaching the umbilicus. Imaging shows a 14 cm solid right adnexal mass with areas of calcification, a normal left ovary and no ascites or peritoneal deposits. Her tumour markers have returned and computed tomography of the chest and abdomen shows no metastatic disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 114/70, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Firm mobile pelvic mass reaching the umbilicus, no ascites, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Alpha fetoprotein 890 kIU/L (less than 10); lactate dehydrogenase 520 U/L (120-250); beta human chorionic gonadotrophin less than 2 IU/L; CA125 88 kU/L (less than 35); computed tomography shows no metastatic disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical management?

options.text: Perform total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo oophorectomy
Give three cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy before any surgery
Arrange ultrasound guided biopsy of the mass before any surgery
Perform fertility sparing unilateral salpingo oophorectomy with staging
Observe with repeat imaging and tumour markers in eight weeks' time

subtopic_detail: Biochemical thyrotoxicosis with hyperemesis in the first trimester
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 26-year-old woman at 9 weeks gestation who has been vomiting up to eight times a day for three weeks and has lost 5 kg. She cannot keep fluids down and feels dizzy on standing.

She has no previous thyroid disease and no family history of it. She has no neck swelling, no gritty or protruding eyes, no pretibial skin change and no tremor of the outstretched hands. Her thyroid function and antibody results have just returned. Her ultrasound confirms a single live intrauterine pregnancy with a crown rump length consistent with dates.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 116, blood pressure 98/60, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, no goitre, no lid lag or proptosis, no tremor, no pretibial myxoedema
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); free thyroxine 28 pmol/L (10-20); thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibodies not detected; potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); ketones present on urinalysis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her thyroid results?

options.text: Start propylthiouracil at a low dose and review her in two weeks
Treat the vomiting supportively and recheck thyroid function later
Start carbimazole and refer to endocrinology within one week
Arrange a technetium thyroid uptake scan to clarify the cause
Start propranolol and plan definitive treatment after the birth

subtopic_detail: Tubal ectopic pregnancy occurring after previous tubal sterilisation
stem: A 36-year-old woman had laparoscopic tubal occlusion three years ago and has missed two periods. She has two days of mild left sided ache and light spotting, and can attend for follow-up.

data_table.Examination: Mild left iliac fossa tenderness, no guarding, no cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: beta-hCG 1450 IU/L; empty uterus, 18 mm left adnexal mass, no cardiac activity, no free fluid; liver and renal function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Single dose intramuscular methotrexate with serial hCG monitoring
Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the affected left tube today
Laparoscopic salpingostomy to preserve that tube's patency
Repeat the hCG in 48 hours and rescan once it exceeds 2000 IU/L
Expectant management with weekly hCG until the level falls to zero

subtopic_detail: Mixed incontinence with impaired bladder emptying before continence surgery
stem:
You are the urogynaecology registrar seeing a 62-year-old woman who leaks both when she coughs and when she cannot reach the toilet in time, and who says the urgency episodes bother her far more. She has been referred with a request to consider a sling.

She reports a slow stream, has to sit for a while before anything comes and feels she has not finished afterwards. She has no prolapse below the hymen and her urinalysis is clear with no growth on culture. Her post-void residual volume measured twice is 180 mL and 210 mL. Urodynamic testing shows detrusor overactivity with leakage during filling, urodynamic stress incontinence on coughing, and a low pressure poorly sustained detrusor contraction on voiding.

data_table.Examination: No prolapse beyond the hymen, weak but present pelvic floor contraction, no palpable bladder after voiding
data_table.Investigations: Post-void residual 180 mL and 210 mL on two occasions; urodynamics show detrusor overactivity, urodynamic stress incontinence and impaired detrusor contractility; urine culture no growth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to a midurethral sling to address the stress component now
Start solifenacin now to control the urgency before any surgery
Start bladder retraining and defer surgery until emptying improves
Inject intradetrusor botulinum toxin A at the next available list
Refer for sacral neuromodulation assessment as the first treatment

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic threshold and feeding advice in a lactating woman with a red painful breast
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A woman who gave birth three weeks ago presents with a hot painful area in the upper outer part of her right breast that she first noticed 18 hours ago after a long stretch between feeds. She has been shivery and aching since last night.

She has been feeding from that side but says it hurts so much she has started to skip it. There is a firm wedge shaped area of redness and tenderness in the upper outer quadrant with no fluctuance and no discrete lump. The nipple has a shallow fissure. There is no axillary lymphadenopathy and the overlying skin is not peeling or blistered.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Wedge shaped erythema and induration in the right upper outer quadrant, no fluctuant collection, shallow nipple fissure, no axillary nodes
data_table.Investigations: Breast milk culture not routinely performed; ultrasound not yet arranged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease feeding from the affected breast and express and discard the milk for 48 hours
Prescribe oral di or flucloxacillin, continue feeding from that breast and review in 48 hours
Advise frequent feeding and cold packs alone and review her again in 24 to 48 hours
Arrange a breast ultrasound today and withhold antibiotics until the result is available
Prescribe oral cabergoline to suppress lactation and change the infant to formula feeding

subtopic_detail: Formulation and route of menopausal hormone therapy in a woman with migraine with aura and obesity
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 52-year-old woman has not had a period for 16 months and has 12 or more hot flushes a day with drenching night sweats that wake her repeatedly. She has tried reducing caffeine and alcohol without benefit and says her work is suffering.

She has migraine with visual aura about twice a month, unchanged for years. Her body mass index is 34 kg/m2 and her blood pressure is 128/78. She has an intact uterus, has never had a venous thromboembolism, and has no personal or family history of breast cancer. Her cervical screening and mammogram are both up to date and normal. She asks specifically for something that will stop the flushes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 34 kg/m2, no breast masses, normal abdominal and pelvic examination
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test negative for human papillomavirus 8 months ago; mammogram normal 5 months ago

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Oral conjugated equine oestrogen with continuous oral medroxyprogesterone acetate
Combined oral contraceptive pill containing 20 micrograms of ethinylestradiol daily
Oral venlafaxine titrated for vasomotor symptoms with review of the response in eight weeks
Transdermal oestradiol patch with continuous oral micronised progesterone at night
Transdermal oestradiol patch alone with an endometrial ultrasound every twelve months

subtopic_detail: Emergency contraception method choice at the outer limit of the window with a high body mass index
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 26-year-old woman who had unprotected intercourse 96 hours ago. Her cycles are regular at 28 days and today is day 13. Her body mass index is 36 kg/m2.

She says she does not want to be pregnant and would also like ongoing contraception she does not have to think about. She has no allergies, takes no regular medications and has had one previous uncomplicated vaginal birth. She has never had pelvic inflammatory disease. A urine pregnancy test today is negative and swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea have been taken.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 36 kg/m2, soft non-tender abdomen, no cervical motion tenderness, uterus anteverted and normal size
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative; chlamydia and gonorrhoea nucleic acid testing pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate option to recommend?

options.text: Insert a copper intrauterine device today and treat presumptively if the swabs return positive
Give oral levonorgestrel 1.5 mg now and start a combined oral contraceptive tomorrow
Give oral ulipristal acetate 30 mg now and arrange an etonogestrel implant next week
Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine device today and repeat a pregnancy test in three weeks
Advise that the window has closed and arrange a pregnancy test in two weeks instead

subtopic_detail: Perineal assessment after an apparently second degree tear and the consequence of understaging
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite after a spontaneous vaginal birth. A woman in her first pregnancy has just given birth to a 4100 g baby after a 40 minute second stage with a rotational forceps delivery. The midwife reports a tear she has graded as second degree and asks you to repair it in the room.

The perineal skin and the bulbospongiosus and transverse perineal muscles are torn. On systematic rectal examination with a finger in the anal canal and a thumb on the perineum, you can feel a gap in the fibres of the external sphincter over about a third of its circumference, and the internal sphincter is intact. There is no buttonhole into the rectal mucosa. Estimated blood loss is 350 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88, blood pressure 116/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Perineal body torn, partial defect of the external anal sphincter over less than half its thickness, internal anal sphincter and anorectal mucosa intact
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165); estimated blood loss 350 mL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repair the perineal muscles and skin in the birth suite under local anaesthetic infiltration
Pack the perineum, start intravenous antibiotics and plan a delayed repair in six weeks
Transfer to theatre for repair by an experienced operator under regional or general anaesthesia
Arrange an endoanal ultrasound scan in the ward before deciding on the mode of repair
Repair the tear in the birth suite and arrange colorectal review before she is discharged

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic confirmation before labelling ovarian insufficiency in a woman in her thirties
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in clinic. A 34-year-old woman has had no periods for seven months after a lifetime of regular cycles. She has hot flushes at night and says intercourse has become uncomfortable. She and her partner had been planning a pregnancy this year.

She has never been pregnant, uses no hormonal contraception and stopped none recently. She has had no chemotherapy, radiotherapy or pelvic surgery. Her weight is stable, she exercises moderately and there is no excessive exercise or dietary restriction. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Blood taken three weeks ago showed follicle stimulating hormone 46 IU/L (2 to 10 in the follicular phase), oestradiol 48 pmol/L (110 to 400) and normal thyroid stimulating hormone and prolactin. She asks whether this means she is in menopause.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, no galactorrhoea, no hirsutism or acanthosis, atrophic vaginal appearance, normal sized uterus
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 46 IU/L (2-10 follicular); oestradiol 48 pmol/L (110-400); thyroid stimulating hormone and prolactin within normal limits; urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill and review her symptoms again in three months
Arrange a pelvic ultrasound to count antral follicles and measure anti Mullerian hormone
Refer directly to a fertility service for donor oocyte counselling and treatment planning
Perform a progestogen withdrawal challenge and assess whether she has a withdrawal bleed
Repeat the follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol at least four weeks apart to confirm

subtopic_detail: White atrophic vulval plaques with architectural change and the role of biopsy alongside treatment
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 58-year-old woman referred with two years of vulval itch that is worst at night. She has been given three courses of topical antifungal cream and a low potency hydrocortisone ointment by different doctors with no lasting benefit, and says intercourse has become painful at the entrance.

The labia minora are partly resorbed into the labia majora and the clitoral hood is fused over the clitoris. There are ivory white thickened plaques extending around the vulva and perianal skin in a figure of eight, with two small areas of purpura but no ulcer, nodule or fixed thickening. The vaginal mucosa itself is normal.

data_table.Examination: White sclerotic plaques over labia and perianal skin, loss of labia minora, clitoral hood fusion, purpura, no ulcer or nodule, normal vaginal epithelium
data_table.Investigations: Vulval swab for candida negative; no biopsy performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a potent topical corticosteroid ointment with long term maintenance and review
Prescribe a further course of topical antifungal cream and review the response in four weeks
Prescribe topical oestrogen cream nightly and review the vulval appearance in three months
Arrange a vulval punch biopsy first and withhold all treatment until the histology returns
Refer for surgical division of the fused clitoral hood and resurfacing of the vulval skin

subtopic_detail: Imaging and first line treatment choice in heavy menstrual bleeding with a diffusely enlarged uterus
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar. A 42-year-old woman describes eight years of increasingly heavy periods that now flood through a pad hourly on the worst two days, with deep cramping pain that starts three days before bleeding and continues throughout. Her family is complete and she does not want surgery if it can be avoided.

On examination the uterus is smoothly enlarged to about 12 weeks size, is tender on bimanual palpation and is mobile with no adnexal mass. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a globally bulky uterus with asymmetric myometrial thickening, indistinct border between endometrium and myometrium and small myometrial cysts, and no discrete mass. The endometrium is 6 mm and regular. Her haemoglobin is 98 g/L (115-165) and her ferritin is 8 mcg/L (15-200).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88, blood pressure 112/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Smoothly enlarged tender mobile uterus of about 12 weeks size, no adnexal mass, no cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound as described; endometrial thickness 6 mm; haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-165); ferritin 8 mcg/L (15-200)

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation and start oral iron replacement at the same time
Perform hysteroscopy with endometrial resection and start oral iron replacement afterwards
Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine device and treat the iron deficiency with oral iron
Arrange endometrial pipelle sampling and defer any treatment until the histology is available
Prescribe tranexamic acid on bleeding days only and review her haemoglobin in six months

subtopic_detail: Acute painful vulval swelling and the drainage technique that reduces recurrence
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the emergency department. A 27-year-old woman presents with three days of increasing pain and swelling on the right side of the vaginal opening. She cannot sit down or walk comfortably and has not been able to sleep.

She is not pregnant, has no urinary symptoms and has had no previous similar episode. On examination there is a tense fluctuant swelling about 4 cm across in the posterior part of the right labium majus, distorting the introitus. The overlying skin is thin and shiny but the surrounding vulval and perineal skin is not indurated or discoloured, and there is no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.4
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant 4 cm swelling in the posterior right labium majus distorting the introitus, thin shiny overlying skin, no surrounding induration or crepitus
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Incise and drain under local anaesthetic and insert a Word catheter
Prescribe oral cefalexin and metronidazole with twice daily warm baths
Aspirate the swelling with a wide bore needle and send fluid for culture
Arrange excision of the gland on the next elective gynaecology list
Refer for biopsy of the swelling to exclude an underlying malignancy

subtopic_detail: Household varicella exposure in a seronegative woman in the second trimester
stem:
You are the antenatal clinic doctor. A 29-year-old woman at 16 weeks in her second pregnancy telephones because her 4-year-old daughter developed a widespread blistering rash two days ago and the general practitioner has diagnosed chickenpox. They share a bedroom while her partner works away.

She has never had chickenpox herself and has not been vaccinated. Her booking bloods, taken at 9 weeks, recorded varicella zoster immunoglobulin G as not detected. She feels completely well today, has no rash, no fever and no respiratory symptoms, and her pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated with a normal first trimester ultrasound.

data_table.Examination: No rash on skin survey, chest clear, uterus palpable just below the umbilicus
data_table.Investigations: Booking varicella zoster immunoglobulin G not detected; rubella immunoglobulin G immune; hepatitis B surface antigen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give the live attenuated varicella vaccine and repeat serology in six weeks
Start oral valaciclovir now and continue it until 21 days after exposure
Give varicella zoster immunoglobulin today and advise on warning symptoms
Repeat varicella immunoglobulin G serology and act on the result next week
Reassure that the risk period has passed and review only if a rash appears

subtopic_detail: Viral load threshold for antiviral prophylaxis to prevent perinatal hepatitis B transmission
stem:
You are the doctor in a hospital antenatal clinic reviewing a 31-year-old woman at 26 weeks in her first pregnancy. Her booking bloods showed hepatitis B surface antigen positive, and she has known about her infection since a screening test in her teens but has never needed treatment.

She feels well, has no jaundice or abdominal pain, and takes no medication. Her liver is not enlarged and there are no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Her partner and her mother are both hepatitis B surface antigen positive. Fetal growth and liquor volume were normal on the morphology scan.

data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis B surface antigen positive; hepatitis B e antigen positive; hepatitis B virus DNA 3.2 x10^7 IU/mL; alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L (less than 35); bilirubin 9 micromol/L (less than 20); platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Examination: No hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly, no ascites or spider naevi

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to reduce transmission to her baby?

options.text: Plan an elective caesarean section at 39 weeks to reduce transmission
Rely on neonatal immunoglobulin and vaccine at birth without an antiviral
Start entecavir now and stop it at the onset of established labour
Advise formula feeding from birth to reduce the risk of transmission
Start tenofovir disoproxil at 28 weeks and continue it after delivery

subtopic_detail: Counselling and timing at 41 weeks in an uncomplicated first pregnancy
stem:
You are the doctor in the antenatal clinic seeing a 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 41 weeks and 0 days. Her dates were confirmed by a crown rump length measurement at 9 weeks.

The pregnancy has been uncomplicated, with normal growth on clinical assessment and normal fetal movements reported today. The fetus is cephalic with the head engaged, the cardiotocograph is normal, and vaginal examination gives a Bishop score of 4. She tells you she has been reading about induction and would prefer to wait for labour to start by itself, and she asks what you would do in her position.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 112/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8, fetal heart rate 140
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 39 cm, cephalic presentation with the head engaged, cervix 1 cm dilated, 1 cm long, mid position, soft, station minus 2
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocograph normal with baseline 140 and moderate variability, no decelerations

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Arrange twice weekly cardiotocography and fluid assessment until 42+6
Offer a membrane sweep today and book induction before 42+0 weeks
Admit her today for prostaglandin induction whatever her preference is
Recommend an elective caesarean section given the unfavourable cervix
Review her in one week and reassess only if she has not laboured then

subtopic_detail: Storage symptoms in a midlife woman and the sequence of conservative and drug treatment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 54-year-old woman who has been rushing to the toilet for the past eight months and has twice not made it in time. She passes urine about ten times a day and wakes twice at night.

She does not leak when she coughs, sneezes or lifts her grandchildren. She drinks four cups of coffee and two cups of tea daily and has cut her water intake right down to try to control the problem. Her last period was three years ago and she takes no medication. Pelvic examination shows well oestrogenised vaginal skin with no prolapse beyond the hymen and a good pelvic floor contraction, and her post-void residual measured on bladder scan is 30 mL.

data_table.Examination: No prolapse beyond the hymen, no leakage on cough with a full bladder, good voluntary pelvic floor contraction, post-void residual 30 mL
data_table.Investigations: Urine microscopy and culture no growth; fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.0-5.4); bladder diary shows 10 daytime voids and 2 nocturnal voids

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Start oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily and review her symptoms in six weeks
Refer for a mid urethral sling procedure on the gynaecology waiting list
Refer for urodynamic studies before deciding on any further treatment
Prescribe vaginal oestrogen cream three nights a week for three months
Start bladder training with caffeine reduction and normalised fluid intake

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding with a focal endometrial abnormality on transvaginal ultrasound
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the outpatient clinic. A 58-year-old woman was referred after two episodes of light vaginal bleeding, six years after her last period. She has never used menopausal hormone therapy and has a body mass index of 34 kg per square metre.

Her cervical screening test last year was negative for human papillomavirus. Speculum examination shows a healthy cervix with no visible lesion and no blood in the vault today. Transvaginal ultrasound reports an endometrial thickness of 11 mm with a discrete echogenic lesion 14 mm across within the cavity, which has a single feeding vessel on colour Doppler, and normal ovaries.

data_table.Examination: Healthy cervix with no visible lesion, mobile non-tender uterus of normal size, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound endometrial thickness 11 mm with a 14 mm intracavity echogenic lesion and a single feeding vessel, normal ovaries, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopy with directed biopsy and removal of the lesion
Perform an office endometrial pipelle biopsy and act on the histology
Reassure her and repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in three months
Measure serum CA125 and arrange computed tomography of the abdomen
Start cyclical oral progestogen and review her bleeding in three months

subtopic_detail: Severe oligozoospermia on a first semen analysis and the workup it triggers
stem:
You are the doctor in a fertility clinic seeing a couple who have been trying to conceive for 14 months with intercourse every two to three days. The woman is 29 with regular 29 day cycles, a normal pelvic ultrasound, an anti-Mullerian hormone in the expected range for her age, and patent tubes on hysterosalpingogram.

Her 32-year-old partner has fathered no previous pregnancies. He is well, takes no medication and does not use anabolic steroids. His testes are of normal volume with no varicocele and both vasa are palpable. His first semen analysis, produced after three days of abstinence, is shown below and he has not previously had one.

data_table.Examination: Normal secondary sexual characteristics, testicular volume 18 mL bilaterally, both vasa palpable, no varicocele
data_table.Investigations: Semen volume 2.8 mL; sperm concentration 4 x10^6 per mL; progressive motility 20 per cent; normal morphology 2 per cent; no antisperm antibodies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to intrauterine insemination in her next ovulatory cycle now
Repeat the analysis in three months with testosterone, FSH and LH levels
Refer directly for intracytoplasmic sperm injection using this sample
Prescribe clomifene for him and reassess his semen in three months' time
Advise another 12 months of timed intercourse before further assessment

subtopic_detail: Cyclical pain with primary amenorrhoea and a uterus present on imaging
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 15-year-old girl brought by her mother because she has never had a period, and for the last eight months has had lower abdominal pain that lasts three or four days and comes at roughly monthly intervals.

Her breast development and pubic hair are fully developed and her growth has followed the 50th centile. She has no cyclical nasal or urinary symptoms. On examination her abdomen is soft with a tender suprapubic mass palpable two finger breadths above the pubic symphysis. Inspection of the introitus shows a normal hymenal opening with no bulging blue membrane, and a gentle cotton bud examination meets a smooth blind end after about 3 cm. Ultrasound reports a uterus containing echogenic fluid, both ovaries normal, and both kidneys present.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 5 breast and pubic hair development, tender suprapubic mass, normal hymenal opening, vagina ending blindly at about 3 cm
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound shows a uterus distended with echogenic fluid, normal ovaries and two normal kidneys

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Incise the membrane at the introitus under local anaesthetic in clinic
Request a karyotype and serum testosterone before any further imaging
Start a continuous combined oral contraceptive to suppress her cycles
Arrange pelvic magnetic resonance imaging and refer to a specialist unit
Book diagnostic laparoscopy to inspect the pelvis and drain the uterus

subtopic_detail: Median nerve symptoms in the third trimester with motor signs
stem:
You are the doctor in the antenatal clinic seeing a 33-year-old woman at 32 weeks in her second pregnancy who has had pins and needles in both hands for six weeks. It began at night and woke her, and she used to relieve it by hanging her hand out of the bed.

For the past fortnight the numbness in the right thumb, index and middle fingers has been constant rather than intermittent, and she has dropped her cup twice and cannot fasten her bra. Her blood pressure is 110/70 with no proteinuria and her ankles are only mildly swollen. On the right, thumb abduction is weak against resistance and there is early flattening of the thenar eminence. Sensation over the thenar skin itself is preserved.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88, blood pressure 110/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7, fetal heart rate 145
data_table.Examination: Reduced sensation over the right thumb, index and middle fingers with preserved sensation over the thenar skin, weak thumb abduction, early thenar wasting, symmetrical reflexes
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick no protein; thyroid stimulating hormone 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); haemoglobin 116 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Fit night wrist splints and reassure her that it settles after delivery
Start oral prednisolone for two weeks and review her hands in the clinic
Refer for nerve conduction studies and urgent hand surgical assessment
Take preeclampsia bloods and arrange review in the day assessment unit
Arrange cervical spine imaging after delivery for a possible radiculopathy

subtopic_detail: Breast lump in a lactating woman that has not resolved with appropriate treatment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who is nine weeks postpartum and breastfeeding. Three weeks ago you treated her for a hot tender left breast with a full course of flucloxacillin, and the fever and redness settled within four days.

The lump itself has not gone. She says it feels the same size or slightly larger, and the skin over it has become dimpled and thickened in the last week. She is afebrile and systemically well and milk supply is good. On examination there is a firm irregular 4 cm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, tethered to overlying skin with peau d'orange, and a 1.5 cm firm mobile node in the left axilla. The breast is not warm and there is no fluctuance.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76, blood pressure 116/70, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Firm irregular 4 cm mass in the left upper outer quadrant tethered to skin with peau d'orange, no fluctuance or warmth, 1.5 cm firm mobile left axillary node
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 7.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe a second longer course of flucloxacillin and review in two weeks
Advise her to wean from the left breast and review the lump afterwards
Refer for incision and drainage of the collection under local anaesthetic
Reassure that this is a blocked duct and teach positioning and massage
Arrange urgent breast imaging with biopsy and continue breastfeeding

subtopic_detail: Sequencing antibiotics and evacuation in secondary postpartum haemorrhage
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar called to the emergency department. A 29-year-old woman is 12 days after a normal vaginal birth at term with an estimated blood loss of 350 mL at delivery. Her lochia had almost stopped, but for two days she has been soaking a pad every hour and passing clots.

She has lower abdominal pain and offensive vaginal discharge. She is not dizzy and has passed urine normally. On examination the uterus is bulky and tender at the level of the umbilicus, the os admits a fingertip, and there is no cervical or vaginal laceration. Bedside ultrasound shows heterogeneous echogenic material of 22 mm within the cavity with vascularity on colour Doppler. Bleeding continues while you examine her.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112, blood pressure 104/62, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.3
data_table.Examination: Bulky tender uterus at the umbilicus, offensive lochia, os admits a fingertip, no genital tract laceration
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-165); white cell count 18.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5); ultrasound shows 22 mm of vascular echogenic intracavity material

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give intravenous antibiotics and evacuate the uterus once cover is running
Take her directly to theatre for curettage before antibiotics are started
Start oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and review her in the clinic tomorrow
Give intramuscular ergometrine and observe her on the ward overnight
Arrange uterine artery embolisation as the initial definitive intervention

subtopic_detail: Entry dyspareunia with normal vulval skin and repeatedly negative swabs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24-year-old woman with 12 months of burning pain at the vaginal opening that starts as soon as penetration is attempted and lasts for hours afterwards. She has no pain at other times and no pain with tampons at first, although she now avoids them too.

She has taken four courses of oral fluconazole prescribed for presumed thrush over the past year, each with no benefit. She is in a stable relationship, describes the relationship as supportive, and has no history of sexual assault. On examination the vulval skin is normal in colour and architecture with no fissures, whitening or loss of the labia minora. A cotton bud applied to the vestibule reproduces her pain sharply at the 5 and 7 o'clock positions but not on the labia majora or perineum, and the pelvic floor is tight with tenderness of the levator muscles.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulval skin colour and architecture, allodynia localised to the vestibule at 5 and 7 o'clock on cotton bud testing, hypertonic tender levator ani
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab no candida or bacterial vaginosis; nucleic acid testing negative for chlamydia and gonorrhoea; vaginal pH 4.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a six month course of weekly oral fluconazole for recurrent thrush
Apply topical clobetasol propionate ointment nightly for four weeks
Refer for pelvic floor physiotherapy and start topical local anaesthetic
Refer for surgical vestibulectomy on the next elective operating list
Change her combined oral contraceptive to a progestogen only preparation
